inline.s: Jinming is a famous monastery of Jiahe. Behind it lies Fan Li’s Lake; today that is the prefectural city — blue seas and mulberry fields indeed. The monastery began in the Qiandao era of the Song, when Chan Master Jinghui opened the mountain. Its rise and decline have not been uniform, yet the ground of the monastery has been guarded by gods and spirits, and never once did it fall to wild grass. Formerly, though the halls and buildings had collapsed, the monks did not lack for offerings. Recently, in the gengzi year, the venerable Xian of Qiutan first rebuilt the Buddha Pavilion; it was not finished when he passed away. The Chan monk Daoxian, by the vow of his ordination master, undertook to continue his work, and the pavilion was at last completed; the Buddha Hall, the Hall of the Great Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, and the Deva Hall were all made new. Master Yexi was invited to lecture on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, and so it became a full monastery. To the right of the monastery there is some ten mu of land, formerly the site of the Chan hall, which had long been held by a powerful man. The laymen Bao Xinxian, Shen Runa, Wang Jichang, Shen Erhou, and Zhongzhen and the rest donated funds to redeem it. Afterwards Master Xuanjin was invited to lecture on the Lotus, Perfect Enlightenment, Diamond, and other sūtras, and those who returned to the faith grew ever more numerous. Again they built the Chan hall, the refectory, the kitchen, and the storehouse; what had before been lacking was all made complete in one season, a magnificent sight for a place of practice. When I came to Shuangjing and Yunqi to mourn the two great elders, I first passed through Wumen and met Master Yexi. Seeing his venerable countenance and his joy in the Dharma-gate, I was glad that the southeast had a teacher and model. I had been dwelling on Nanyue and had completed my Comprehensive Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, which was printed at Gusu. It happened that the Master was then in his lecture period; seeing it, he sighed and said: “This parts the heavy clouds over the scholastic teachings. I beg to be allowed to finish it, so as to spread the gift of Dharma.” When the lectures ended and he returned, he passed through Jinming. Master Xian had long attended his Dharma seat and served him as a disciple. The Master then vowed to expound it here. Ten days after returning to his mountain, he passed away. Alas! Birth and death are a dream; must they depend on men? Seeing him bear his aspiration away with him as he departed, one knows that there is that which does not depart and remains. Master Xuanjin was Master Ye’s rightful heir, one who truly carried on his aspiration and continued his work. I was lodging at Jingci, and Xuan served as keeper of the Danguo guest hall. When I returned to Mount Kuang, Xuan escorted me to Jinming. Seeing the monastery and moved by its story, I directed Xian to invite Xuan so as to fulfil the former aspiration, and so I inscribed its hall as Great Samādhi. This is the name of the Śūraṅgama great samādhi; here it means firm and indestructible. Now when the Buddha first sat at the site of enlightenment, that ground was firm, made of diamond, and therefore it was called araṇya, the true place of practice. This place has passed through five hundred years, through the kalpas of formation, dwelling, decay, and emptiness; and yet in the end it is a place of practice. As to its flourishing, it began with the Śūraṅgama; now that it is complete, it ends with the Śūraṅgama. Yet the practice and realization of the Śūraṅgama takes the diamond mind-ground as its root and beginning, and what it realizes is just this. Seen in this light, whether mind or realm, both alike are diamond, permanently abiding and indestructible; and so I named its hall Great Samādhi. Truly so. Those who dwell in this hall dwell with this mind; those who expound the Dharma expound with this mind; those who hear the Dharma hear with this mind. Even when bell and drum answer one another, when the chanting of Sanskrit verses blends together, and even the many voices of the marketplace and the laughter of men and women, all enter the gate of the great samādhi. How then could there be a division of stillness and confusion, a distinction of mountain forest and city? The brethren escorted me to Linxi, where we received the meal offering of the layman Shen Erhou — surely a karmic gathering that completes the beginning and completes the end. Therefore I have made this record.
Dream Roaming Collection of Elder Hanshan, Fascicle Twenty-Five
Record of Fayun Monastery on Wuru Peak of Mount Lu

Mount Lu takes its vein from Nanyue. Turning back, it crosses the Xiang hills to border western Yue; turning north, it passes Xingzi and Linwu to border eastern Yue; at Guiyang it borders Wu and Chu. At Yu Ridge it divides its branches, and drawing out a main trunk it runs east through the Wugong range, stretching over two thousand li, straight to Xunyang, with Pengli Lake before it and Jiujiang behind, coiling over more than two hundred li like a blue lotus rising from the water, thrusting high into the Milky Way. It faces Wu and Yue to the south and gazes toward the Central Plain to the north, contending in majesty with the Five Marchmounts — truly a vast magnificence within the world. Its incoming vein reaches the Yuantong gorge, where the Ma’er and other peaks rise abruptly, then winds east for more than twenty li until one peak stands out alone, called Peach Blossom. It leans against the highest heavens and is the host of hosts of this mountain. From it two great trunks divide. One runs east, arraying the Nine Marvels like a screen, to the Hanpo Mouth; turning north it raises Qiangang Ridge, the guest within the host. Its force runs out to the northeast, embraced by river and lake, winding and coiling. From the head of that ridge a great trunk is drawn off to the southeast and becomes Five Elders Peak, looking back at Peng Lake and standing as the gate-guard of the Western River, ending at the Three Cascades — the most wondrous and peerless spot of all. Among the retreats below that peak is Jingmiao; five li before it lies White Deer Hollow, the academy of Hui’an, and tradition says there was also Li Qinglian’s study hall, though this cannot be verified. From the head of the Five Elders a ridge is dragged along, following the divided waters of Hanpo, winding west and then south down to Xingzhu, which is the seat of Nankang commandery — this is the south face of the Five Elders. Its main ridge runs north to Songguang Ridge and splits into two branches. The northeastern trunk is Lotus Peak, which descends as Wuzhang Mountain and reaches straight to Hukou; within it are Huiri and other retreats, while outside it spreads into level ridges, and ten li on is the grave of Zhou Lianxi, facing Lotus Peak; twenty li further is the seat of Jiujiang commandery. The northern trunk of that ridge bends west to Wulong Pool, from which a branch is drawn down; ten li on it enters the plain and becomes Taiping Palace. Winding left for another ten li is the place of Elder Huiyuan’s Lotus Society at Donglin, looking back at Incense Burner Peak, where Bai Xiangshan’s thatched hut stands; its foundation still remains. The Wulong branch runs west past Lion Rock, Dalin, the Water Mouth, the Imperial Stele Pavilion, the Bamboo Grove, Buddha’s Hand Rock, the Sūtra-lecturing Terrace, Incense Burner Peak, and other wonders, and knits itself into Tianchi Pool; looking back at Peach Blossom, it is therefore the chief monastery of the mountain. Below the rock is Stone Gate, which is the water mouth of the whole mountain. In the midst of the mountain is Yellow Dragon Pool, like a single pistil at the heart of a flower; the various monasteries and retreats are arrayed about like fragrant stamen-banners. This completes the configuration of the eastern trunk. The great trunk sent forth southward from Peach Blossom runs west against the back of the incoming dragon, with a valley clasped between; the highest point is Great Hanyang Peak, the master mountain of the south face. It towers in mid-heaven, its face swallowing the two lakes, drawing Jiangnan from afar; the belt of peaks is arrayed along the horizon like stars bowing to the north, a thousand li at a glance, reaching straight to Hukou and embracing the Five Elders in return. This is truly a great vista of the southeast. At Hanyang’s western end is Valley Curtain Spring; below and before it the land opens into plains, which are Chaisang, the old home of Tao Yuanming. Halfway down, a branch is drawn off to the south, and at its waist rises a solitary peak several hundred feet high, like a stūpa floating in the air; it is called Golden Wheel. In the Jin, the Indian master Yaśas carried iron on his back and built a stūpa, enshrining a Buddha relic at the summit. Two li or so below is Dong Feng’s apricot grove, famed to this day. In the plain below the peak is Guizong Monastery: Wang Youjun, while governing Jiangzhou, built his residence here; later he met the Indian master Buddhabhadra and gave up the house as a monastery. Today there are the Ink Pool and the Goose Pool, and so the monastery vied with Donglin. From the Tang, when Chan Master Chiyan taught the Dharma here, more than thirty masters succeeded one another. In former times the Dharma-way of the Western River alone flourished, and so it was the foremost monastery of this mountain. Such is the general configuration of Kuang’s south. As for the Five Breasts: from the very centre of the south face of Great Hanyang Peak a single branch is drawn out, rising and falling through several nodes, then opening into a great screen. Behind it on the left is Peach Blossom; the peaks called Stone Man run east and downward, and outside they knit into Qixian, facing the Five Elders. Following the divided waters of Hanpo down and around Qixian is Jade Abyss Pool, whose waters gather into a river and enter Xingzhu. The left screen wraps inward like a lotus rolled backward; within it are the three retreats of Stone Buddha, Striking Bamboo, and Baoqing, and Baoqing was the hermitage of such great elders of old as Dahui Gao, Ying Shaowu, Yue Gonghui, Baofeng Yue, and the chief seat Yuan. Long in ruins, it has now been rebuilt. Further west is Crouching Dragon Ridge; below the ridge is a valley, and in the valley a hermitage, where Zhu Huiweng, while governing Nankang, came and went, carving the Memorial on Sending Out the Troops on the rock. The hermitage is ruined, but the carving remains. This is the left screen before Hanyang. Its right screen arrays the peaks of Guozi Fort and reaches Yellow Cliff, where a waterfall falls from the sky into a pool. On the great rocks above the pool are many carvings by ancient worthies. Before it is Kaiguang Monastery, which Li the Middle Ruler bought and built as a monastery, a place where the patriarchs taught the Dharma. Huang Shangu wrote the verses of the Seven Buddhas on the cliff, and Wang Yangming left an inscription when he defeated Chenhao. Turning left from the monastery and crossing a ridge brings one to Wanshan Monastery. This is the right screen before Hanyang. From the very centre of that screen a single branch is drawn out alone, hanging down like a horse’s mane. In the belly of the peak a peak springs up like a unicorn’s horn, called Hu’s Nose. To the left it trails like a screen; seven peaks stand abreast, piercing the highest heavens — the Seven Worthies. In former times the Tang recluse Liu Ke studied below the peaks; later Hui’an brought his son, his disciples Chen Zhengsi, Chen Yanzhong, and Yu Jiqing, and his nephew Wei Yu, and often wandered there, and so they were named. The local people vulgarly call them the Seven Points — a corruption. Below the Seven Worthies are five protrusions like breasts, hence the name Five Breasts; they join above and below and reach east to Crouching Dragon Pool, dividing the waters as they descend. This is the left dragon of the Five Breasts. From Hu’s Nose, bowing and saluting, one peak rises in succession, called Stone Drum. Gently descending, it winds like a dragon roaming in the clouds, twisting in a thin thread for several li, drawn out alone and wrapping around, opening a palm’s breadth at its centre — the site of the old monastery. It leans on the Seven Worthies and faces the Five Elders, like a lotus on a halberd’s branch; the monastery is deeply hidden like the young shoot within a lotus, the most secluded spot on the southern flank of the mountain. There the many waters return to the ravine and flow down around the monastery, issuing from a stone crevice for about five li to the foot of the mountain, where they join the Jade Abyss river. Winding within, it encircles Jade Capital Mountain and enters the lake hills — this was Yuanming’s old dwelling. As his poem says, “In former days I made my home at Jade Capital” — that is it. At the water mouth of the Five Breasts is a stone peak several zhang high, and on it a flat rock a zhang square, called Liu Ke’s Reading Terrace, still so named by the local people. The gazetteer records that Liu Ke had a study hall there, later changed to Lingyun Hermitage, below the Seven Points. The old monastery was destroyed by soldiers, and its story cannot be verified; only its foundation stones remain. Afterwards a cliff carving was seen: “In the fourth month of the renshen year of Zhizheng, the rebuilding was completed.” The monastery’s mountain lands and fields first passed into private hands in the early Jiajing era. In the bingchen year of Wanli I travelled east from Nanyue and took my summer retreat at Jinzhu. Probing the hidden reaches, I came to this place, and loving each hill and gully, I meant to rest here and even divined for a dwelling. It happened that Xing Maoxue, a licentiate of Huangmei, bought it at its price to be a place for my leisure in old age. At that time Lord Wang Kesou, Grand Minister of War of Huangmei, wished to be the donating patron for its construction, and Lord Chen Dashou, Sealbearer of Fuliang, agreed with certain others to donate funds and gather timber, and so the monastery was completed. Lord Yu Yuli of Jinsha and the layman Miao Xiyong donated incense-offering fields, and thus we could dwell in peace. The work began in the dingsi year and was finished in the jiwei year. The prefect Yuan Maozhen wrote an essay to record it. From this, monks from all quarters came daily in greater numbers, and so it became a full monastery, sitting as it were within a single petal of the lotus. On the ridge to the left of the monastery there was formerly a Lake-Viewing Pavilion built by Hui’an; its foundation still remains. In that valley there are retreats. One, below Stone Drum Peak, is called Chongmo Studio, for which I wrote an inscription; it is the most secluded, superb, and lofty, and from it one looks at the hills beyond the lake, a thousand li at a glance, spread out before one — as though sitting on a lotus terrace and putting forth the broad, long tongue to the assembly of Dharma-hearers come like clouds from the ten directions. One, below Seven Worthies Peak, is called Hibiscus Hermitage, facing the Five Elders and treading on Crouching Dragon, with all the peaks arrayed as though at one’s table. Entering several li from the hermitage, the great valley is called Fragrant Vale; there is a stone screen, and before it a great rock whose face is like a low table; below the rock is a cave, from which a rare fragrance issues, wafting over one without cease. One, on Dragon Water Cliff near the monastery, is called Wood and Stone Hermitage, as the name declares; I also wrote an inscription for it. All these are within the precinct, like the pistils at the heart of the flower. In the valley to the left of the monastery is the site of Guanyin Hermitage; the gazetteer says there were two old wells there, their whereabouts unknown. Now they have been found amid the tangled brush. Again, on the left arm is Guiyi Hermitage, which joins the divided waters of Crouching Dragon and gathers into the great river — another precinct altogether. Dongpo said: “We cannot see Mount Lu’s true face, only because we are ourselves within the mountain.” Because the mountain resembles a lotus and those who dwell here sit within the flower, its true face lies only on the south side, and of that only the Five Elders and Seven Worthies are the most superb. The monastery sits in a ravine, leaning on the Hanyang peaks as its screen. Looking back at the Seven Worthies and Five Elders, they sit amid the clouds; Peng Lake encircles them without, and beyond the lake the cloudy mountains arch inward from a thousand li, secretly arrayed before one — truly a hidden capital of the Huazang world. The monks daily recite the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, their voices ringing clear; bell and drum answer one another and, with the soughing pines and the sound of springs, together perform the sound of the tide, lending fresh colour to this mountain. Only we have not been able to emulate Elder Huiyuan by carving the lotus water-clock and keeping the six periods of worship.
Record of the Zongjing Hall (Mirror of the Source Hall) at Jingci Monastery on West Lake

On West Lake at Wulin there is a hill called Nanping, and on it stands a monastery called Jingci. When Emperor Gaozong of the Song crossed south, he honoured the Five Mountains and Ten Monasteries, and this one headed them all. The monastery began in the Xiande era of the Zhou, built by King Zhongyi of Wuyue of the Qian family; at first it was Yongming Cloister, and Chan Master Zhijue Shou was welcomed as the first abbot to open the mountain; later it received its present name. The Master received the Dharma from National Master Shao of Tiantai and was a bone-descendant of Fayan, wondrously attuned to the singly transmitted mind-seal, thoroughly versed in the three baskets, and comprehending the Buddha’s whole canon. In particular he made manifest the meaning that the three realms are mind-only and the ten thousand dharmas are consciousness-only. After the Buddha’s extinction, the teaching masters of the western regions, on the basis of mind-only and consciousness-only, established the two schools of nature and characteristics, which attacked each other like ice and fire, until they divided the river and drank apart, destroying the true Dharma. When the great teaching came east, not three hundred years had passed before Bodhidharma came from the west, not setting up words, pointing directly at the human mind, seeing one’s nature and becoming Buddha — this is the Chan school. Thereupon there was the way of the special transmission outside the teachings. After six transmissions it came down to Caoxi, and then to Nanyue and Qingyuan, and next into the five houses. From Tang to Song its way flourished greatly, and then Chan and the teachings opposed one another even as nature and characteristics contended — all because they did not comprehend the meaning of mind-only and consciousness-only, but each set up its own gate. For four hundred years, from Liang and Tang to Song, students within the seas wrangled noisily and contended, and in the end none could rouse the Great Enlightenment to adjudicate between them. Therefore the Master, grieving that the sun of the Buddha had grown dim, gathered more than a hundred scholars of the three schools of scholastic learning — Xianshou, Cien, and Tiantai — who were versed in the meaning of the Dharma, lodged them in two pavilions, where they read widely through the ocean of meaning and challenged one another in turn, and the Master weighed and levelled them with the balance of the mind school. He further collected sixty Mahāyāna sūtras and treatises and three hundred works of the words of sages and saints of India and this land, to prove and establish mind-only, making a book of one hundred fascicles entitled the Record of the Mirror of the Source. Hence the hall was named after it, the meaning being that the one mind is the source and the ten thousand dharmas are illumined as in a mirror. It tore down the fences of the three schools and revealed the profound meaning of the one mind, as though hanging the image of meaning in the sky of nature and gathering the various streams back into the ocean of Dharma. Not only are nature and characteristics fused, but the nine streams and hundred schools, and the crafts that sustain life, none but are led back to reality. How then should teaching and Chan not be one, how should views and opinions not be dissolved? Truly, beings have long been mired in attachment. Though nature and characteristics, teaching and Chan, all reveal the wonder of the one mind, the Buddha’s opening and closing were medicine for the sickness of the mind; his final twirling of the flower made him seem to speak and yet differ from himself, and in the end there was no way to make them one. Hence those who cling to the trap lose the moon by taking the finger for it — who could set them right? It is two thousand years since the World-Honoured One entered extinction. Had the Master not risen up and made it all thoroughly clear, I fear the clamour would go on to the end of time, and there would never be a day of return and peace. Thus we know the Master’s merit is great: he gathered the great accomplishment of our Dharma; were Śākyamuni to rise again, his merit could not surpass this. Is this not that the Master was far worthier than Yao and Shun? Someone may say: all the patriarchs of former times were themselves enlightened to their own minds, and yet they said that of the matter one step above, the Buddhas of the three times are not permitted so much as a glance; and again, that the whole canon is scrap paper for wiping the pus from sores; and seeing the World-Honoured One at birth pointing to heaven and earth, they wanted to kill him with a single blow; even when he ascended the hall and addressed the assembly, they never failed to denounce words bitterly, forbidding any approach to the teachings. Now the Master harmonizes nature and characteristics and forcibly joins them to the one mind — is this not contrary to the purport of Bodhidharma’s coming from the west? Or did the ancient worthies violate the meaning of the one mind? I answer: it is precisely because the great purport of the coming from the west was not clear that men set up partial views against one another; hence this work of his life. As for the records of the ancients’ encounters, they all reveal the Tathāgata’s great mechanism and great function, and are never other than the Buddha’s design. Thus Mañjuśrī, having given rise to the view of a Buddha and the view of dharma, was banished towards the Iron Ring Mountain; and Mañjuśrī also once took up a knife to kill the Buddha. And when the various disciples entered Vimalakīrti’s ten-foot room, they were reproved in various ways. All these are the workings of the patriarchs, merely medicinal Dharma-remedies to block, drive off, and tame beings — they are not the real Dharma. But beginners of shallow wisdom today do not awaken to the Tathāgata’s equal dharma-realm, and so cannot comprehend the purport of being free from marks. Now the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma seals and settles all dharmas with the ocean-seal samādhi. It says that space is a sapphire jewel, empty and bright as a mirror; the great earth, mountains and forests, grass and weeds, men and beasts, the myriad forms in their array, none but show their images within the empty mirror. And when the great ocean’s waves are stilled and its emptiness is bright and thoroughly clear, then the images of the empty mirror appear within the sea like the text of a seal. The Tathāgata teaches the Dharma with equal great wisdom, perfectly illumining the dharma-realm; the thoughts of beings, he knows all their number; the raindrops over Jambudvīpa, he knows every one. This is called the ocean-seal samādhi. From this we see that there is no thing that is not Buddha-mind, no dharma that is not Buddha-work, no practice that is not Buddha-practice. How could any dharma, by a hair’s breadth, fall outside of mind-only? Thus we know that the title Mirror of the Source means illumining dharmas with the one mind and dissolving the ten thousand dharmas back into the one mind; and then what dharma is not the patriarchs’ mind-seal, and what distinction is there between nature and characteristics, teaching and Chan? Therefore, one who destroys characteristics does not comprehend the Dharma-nature; one who denounces the teachings does not comprehend the Buddha-mind; not having fathomed the wondrous function of the Buddhas and patriarchs, such a one takes it for real dharma. This is why the treasury of the true Dharma-eye is hard to make clear. Is it not cause for grief? Now the monastery faces West Lake, whose waters are like a mirror; the four hills are arrayed about, and on the six bridges are flowers and willows; boats come and go, and the people are fair and plain; songs and flutes sound near and far; bell and drum answer one another through the six periods of day and night, unbroken from ancient times to now upon the lake. Yet the Tathāgata within the hall sits serene and silent, as though entered into the ocean-seal samādhi, never by a hair’s breadth departing from the Mirror of the Source. Even today the wind in the pines and the sound of springs, the humming of earthworms and the croaking of frogs, are still the Master sitting in the Zongjing Hall, waving his fly-whisk, meeting the meaning, and teaching the Dharma. What need is there of pen and tongue? Thus we know this mountain’s ground is foremost in the central region, this monastery heads all monasteries, its Dharma surpasses teaching and Chan, and its mind and realm are the most superb. One who arrives at the Zongjing Hall should be as lasting as the lake and hills themselves. It is more than four hundred years since the Master entered extinction; his relic stūpa sank into the tangled brush. In a certain year of Wanli the monastery monk Dahe sought and found it, and moved it to the rear of the hall. Truly this is the Master’s dharma-body, hidden and appearing again, and it should abide imperishably with this hall. The hall had no record, and Dahe begged me to write one.
Record of Lingxiao Peak at Jingshan

According to the gazetteer, the Dragon-Roaming Pavilion stood on the summit of Cui Peak, with painted arches and jade-inscribed eaves, bearing the clouds and admitting the sun, and beyond its open eaves was the Lingxiao Pavilion; so the summit had a pavilion. The record adds that five-colored ray-lights were often seen on the summit, and hence there was a Precious Light Hall, which suggests a hall stood before the pavilion. Both are now in ruins. Long ago Chan Master Yuanzhao dwelt on the summit for ten years and left the lines: “Sitting through Lingxiao, ten years already; upholding the school and supporting the teaching, all according to conditions.” Afterwards Chan Master Gu Ding dwelt there ten years as well. From this we see that the mountain-dwellers of former generations all loved its solitary remoteness. Yet the summit has no water, the wind is high, and the place is utterly cut off; it is no ground for hidden cultivation. Dharma Master Yueting once expounded the Avataṃsaka Sūtra here for the assembly, for this peak is the lord of the five peaks and the ancestral dragon of the twin paths of Jing. Recently Master Fanhuai Hui built a hut on the summit and has lived there thirteen years. He had long suffered for want of water; the master chiseled the rock and found a spring that can supply a hundred people and does not fail even in great drought. With his own hands he planted pines along the path, hoping they might turn into dragons. In the first month of the ding-si year I climbed the peak. Gazing in all four directions, all was vast and open, a thousand li at a single view. I therefore inscribed his hut: “Dwelling in the Void,” to mark a transcending of the world. At the time I wrote a poem to record it. The spring water is sweet and cold, welling out of the void like heavenly sweet dew, and so I gave the spring its name.
Record of Zunsheng Hermitage at Haiyu

Haiyu lies tucked away in the eastern corner, where the Buddha's transforming influence has naturally been slow to reach. Not long ago I passed through and looked about: those there who devote themselves to the Three Jewels flourish beyond other places, neighborhood emulating neighborhood, for the district has many retired gentry who have long been protectors of the Dharma and are stirred to arise by what they see and feel. Truly the Buddha-nature is innate and the Dharma's transformation pervades all things; every blade of grass and mote of dust becomes a seed of Buddhahood. It depends only on how the one who opens the way does it. The present Zunsheng Hermitage was founded by Dharma Master Yuehui, Master Ming, a son of the Chen family of this district. As a child he was already murmuring the Buddha's name, and in learning ordinary trades he understood nothing; his whole aspiration was to leave the world. At seventeen he took the monk Yiyuan of Yufeng Hermitage as his teacher, received the full precepts from Master Yunqi, and then went to the southern capital, where he attended Dharma Master Xuelang's lecture seat and studied the doctrine of the Xianshou school, enduring hardship for seven years. In the autumn of the ji-hai year he returned home to visit his mother, and on the sunny terrace of Mount Yu he shut himself away for three years, investigating the ancestral meaning of the coming from the West. In the ren-yin year he again went among the various regions. Everywhere he saw the aged and the sick, whom the monasteries mostly would not admit, leaving them with nowhere to turn. So he made a vow: if ever I have so much as a thatched hut, I will share it with the aged and sick of the ten directions. Sadly it was never realized, and ten years slipped past. In the autumn of the ren-zi year the district's juren Weng Zhaoji offered to give a plot of open ground before the monastery, about ten mu, on which to build a ten-direction Chan cloister and a quiet hall for the care of the aged. The master rejoiced, feeling that with the ground in hand his old vow could be repaid. The district gazetteer records a Zunsheng Hermitage long fallen to ruin. When they broke ground, more than a fathom down they found an old well whose water was very sweet and cold, and guessed it was the old site; the blue sea turns to mulberry fields — is this not the working of the kalpa? Work began in the summer of the ding-si year of Wanli and was completed in the autumn of the wu-wu year. Because the master had upheld the Zunsheng mantra all his life, the hermitage took the name Zunsheng. He sent a letter asking me to record it.
I said to him: Throughout the great earth there is no being without the Buddha-nature; throughout the worlds of the ten directions there is no dust that is not a place of practice. It is only that conditions meet and stimulus and response intertwine, and then in a snap of the fingers it appears. With Master Weng's gift of land, why need a Jetavana? With Master Ming's building of the teaching, why wait for Baizhang? Simply let the Chan companions dwell in peace, bowing and chanting at the six periods, the sound of sūtras and the Buddha's name with bells and drums answering one another, so that the aged are at ease and the sick are comforted, the foolish become wise and the lazy diligent, the weary rest and the hungry eat, the thirsty drink — which of these is not the merit of Zunsheng? Let the pure rules of Yunqi not fall, let the Dharma-way of Vulture Peak endure forever. As for the heavenly emperor twisting a single blade of grass into a brahma-monastery, that is hardly to be sought by thought or calculation. And so, above, to offer blessings for the sovereign's years, and below, to bring the people of this age together into benevolence and long life, a hidden current in the great sea that moistens without end. I am without ability; how could I presume to put a name to it?
Record of the Bronze Aśoka Relic Stūpa Made by King Zhongyi of Wuyue of the Qian Line

When the World-Honored One entered nirvāṇa, his cremation yielded eight hu and four dou of relics, which were divided into three portions — for the heavens, for humans, and for the nāga palace — and in each a stūpa was built for veneration. King Aśoka himself received one portion and scattered it over Jambudvīpa; the land of Cīna obtained nineteen, and the Aśoka stūpa at Mingzhou was one of them. Its design too came from the Western Regions. The relics blazed brightly and their light transformed, so that each person saw something different, and some saw nothing at all, because the obscuration is thick or thin. Two thousand years later, in the Five Dynasties, King Zhongyi of Wuyue of the Qian line, inheriting the work of his forebears, reverently served the Three Jewels and had small bronze stūpas made after that design, eighty-four thousand of them, buried among the famous mountains of his realm, and the world knew nothing of it. In the early Wanli era of our Ming, at Changshu, Gu Gengguang, while building the grave of his father the vice-commissioner, dug out a small bronze stūpa about five inches tall, in the style of King Aśoka's stūpa. Inside was engraved: “King Qian Hongchu of Wuyue reverently made eighty-four thousand precious stūpas. Recorded in the yi-mao year” — nineteen characters. On the four outer faces were carved Śākyamuni's past causes and former conduct, showing their marks: in front, King Śibi cutting his flesh to feed the hawk and save the dove; behind, King Cili cutting off his ear to light a lamp; on the left, Prince Sattva casting himself from the cliff to feed the tigress; on the right, King Candraprabha giving away his precious head — four scenes in all. The carving was fine and closely wrought, inlaid with gold. Gu was the maternal uncle of the Hanlin scholar Qian, and because the gentleman was a descendant of King Zhongyi, he gave him the stūpa. Having obtained it, the gentleman styled himself Layman Gathering Sand, to record its cause, and sent it to Xingfu Temple. On my journey east I visited the Hanlin scholar, and calling on the senior monk Dongwen, I saw the stūpa. Marveling at the affair, I recorded it, saying:
The Buddha takes the dharma-realm as his body, so that even a blade of grass or a knotted thread becomes the Buddha's true substance — how much more that which is enshrined in an image? It is because beings are deluded about their original dharma-body that it turns into the three poisons and becomes the eighty-four thousand afflictions. The Buddha, by the radiance of universal wisdom, perfumes the three poisons into the secret treasury of the three virtues, and so turns afflictions into eighty-four thousand merits. What King Aśoka made was meant to show the measure of that merit. The King of Wuyue had bronze stūpas imitated in that number and buried them all in the earth, intending to show that merit is stored in the mind-ground of beings: whoever opens one stūpa sees one kind of merit and beholds the whole body of the dharma-realm, as one sees boundless space through a single crack. How could this be looked upon as mere form? The dharma-body is firm and indestructible through kalpas, appearing in response to conditions. This stūpa of the Hanlin scholar — is it not a single crack through which the emptiness of nature is shown from the causal ground? Recorded on the Buddha's birthday in the forty-fifth year of Wanli.
Reading the Record of a Strange Dream

The Illusionist traveled east through Wu and Yue and returned west to Mount Lu. As his boat passed Wuguan, the pass-keeper Master Liu Yushou invited him to stay a night or two. It happened that Guan Xizhi, a xiucai of Wumen, came by another road; the next morning Xizhi came first to the boat, and asking after the Illusionist, told him of Yushou's strange dream. The Illusionist was astonished. When he questioned Yushou, the latter brought out his Gancheng Travel Sketches, and the record of the strange dream was read in full. At first, when Yushou had accepted a post in Qianzhong, he fell ill on the road and lay in the post-house at Xiajun. At night he dreamed of a giant of a man with a long snout who burst in, seeming to seek something, his bearing still fierce and resentful. He bowed to Yushou and sat down with him. Asked his clan and name, the man answered in a loud voice: “I am Cao Han, general of the Song. Because of the campaign at Jiangzhou I killed many innocents and brought this sorrow on myself. What is there now to say?” In the dream Yushou did not know the details of the Jiangzhou affair, but remembered that Han had served as a general alongside Cao Bin, and said: “You were under the command of Cao Bin, commissioner of military affairs, who was humane and would not kill; how did you bring this sorrow on yourself?” The man said: “I was enraged that Jiangzhou had long resisted the royal command, so I first killed the defending general Hu Ze and then massacred the city, taking pleasure for a moment. How was I to know that after death I would receive the punishment of the dark realm? All who shared in it at the time fell into other paths; I alone became a pig. For in life I was prone to angry cursing, my tongue a keen and deadly weapon. Having received the pig's retribution, my voice is mostly a grunting squeal; when I am seized and caught, my cries ring in every direction. The penalties of the dark realm miss not a hair's breadth. I beg you, sir, to save me.” Yushou heard this with terror, and said: “I am still an ordinary man; how can I free you?” The man said: “You are compassionate by nature; whenever you see such as us you feel genuine pity. Do you recall that some years ago you had a dream in which someone owed his rebirth to you? That was I.” For in the spring of the wu-shen year, when a household slave of Yushou's was in debt for rent, several pigs had been taken in repayment; that night he dreamed of a man begging for his life, and at once ordered the slave to keep the pig. It died of itself a year later. In the dream he clearly recalled the matter and answered: “It is true, but I did not know it was you.” “And now where am I to find you?” The man said: “The retribution of karma is unfixed. Yesterday I was paying a debt to someone of a nearby county; unexpectedly, by karmic affinity, I have met you again here. This time I do not know where the working of karma will carry me.” As he spoke he wept most bitterly. Then, slowly drying his tears, he said: “I had the good fortune to live in the reign of Emperor Taizong of Tang as a petty clerk. Hearing a Dharma master expound the Sūtra of Forty-Two Sections, I made an offering of food, and I was rewarded with birth after birth as an official. By the early Song my reward was exhausted, and I suddenly committed evil karma and turned to receive this fruit. Yet happily, on account of good roots planted long ago, I have met you today. From now on I beg you: whenever you meet such as us — whether you see us caught, hear our cries, or see the leftover flesh being eaten — recite the Cundī mantra for us, or call Amitābha Buddha's name, and I shall for a while be able to bear the suffering. I will surely escape this retribution, be born among humans, and vow never again to commit evil karma and betray you.” Yushou said: “This has long been my wish; and now that you have instructed me, how dare I break the pact?” The man rejoiced, bowed in thanks, and departed. How strange indeed! Karmic retribution is so clear and misses nothing. See how Cao Han began as a petty clerk: by hearing the Buddha-Dharma and making the merit of one meal offered to a monk, he received blessings life after life. But when his good reward was about to end, he became a great general and gave free rein to the karma of killing. Is it not that evil habits grow along with the reward of merit? Truly it is to be feared. For the horror of his killing karma he suffered the torment of the chopping block and the knife for more than six hundred years; yet still, through the good roots planted long ago, he appeared twice in dreams to Master Liu, and at last begged to be freed from his painful destiny. Was Master Liu, then, perhaps the Dharma master who had expounded the sūtra to Han in a former life? Seeing how Cao Han's evil retribution missed nothing, one may know that Master Liu's good roots, too, had their source. When the Illusionist first heard the account he was astonished; and on reading the Record of a Strange Dream in Master Liu's Gancheng Travel Sketches, he therefore told the story, to proclaim it widely to gods and humans and to exalt the virtue of releasing life and abstaining from killing, making it plain and manifest. Moreover, if merely hearing a cry or seeing flesh, with the recitation of a mantra or the Buddha's name, can yet bring hope of enduring and escaping that bitter retribution, how much more so for one who acts from true compassion and abstains from killing and releases life? Hence I feel this deeply regarding the life-releasing pool at Yunqi. I respectfully write this to inform the officers of this monastery: follow the rules. All creatures released here have karmic affinity with us; tend them diligently, expound the Dharma for them, and recite for them at death — these are matters of truth. Pray do not grow weary. Seen in the light of the Buddha-nature, the provisions for the path are theirs to share as well; pray let there be no lack, nor let them go hungry and empty.
Record of Zhenru Hermitage in Taihe County

Forty li northwest of Taihe, at Zaohe Market, there is a Zhenru Hermitage built by Guang Guo, a disciple of Yunqi. Guo was a man of Ji'an. In his early years he ate vegetarian food and reverently served the Three Jewels; in middle age he took his wife and children and left the home life, receiving ordination at the Pure Karma Hall on Mount Lu and the precepts from Master Yunqi, and then trained to full ordination under the monk Guxin. Returning to his home district, he came to Taihe, where the juren Luo Shaokui donated five mu of land, and a hermitage was built for him to dwell in and receive travelers. Eight years have passed thus. In time his assembly gathered and grew daily larger; two halls were built, and the cloud hall, refectory, and kitchen and all else were fully provided, so that it became a proper place of practice. Fearing he could not support the assembly, he gathered the faithful and held a “hundred sons” lantern festival, storing its proceeds, and bought some mu of land as a permanent endowment, so as to provide for the assembly forever, with the four requisites complete and peaceful dwelling possible, enabling them to cultivate the Pure Land path in earnest without seeking outside. When matters were settled, Guo came to Mount Lu and asked me for a record.
I said to him: I have heard that the Pure Lands of the ten directions are transformed by mind alone; when the mind is pure, the land is pure. It is like a dream: a nobleman dreams of suffering and groans, a poor man dreams of gold and jewels and rejoices; though all is empty after waking, in the dream it was certainly there. It is said that birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are like last night's dream — how much more the conditioned adornments and merits of worldly truth? Long ago Bodhidharma said to Emperor Wu: “Conditioned practices have truly no merit. Pure wisdom, wondrous and perfect, is in its essence empty and still.” Yet if one has not understood the essence of the empty school and casts aside conditioned practice, is that not an empty belly waiting for the king's feast, hoping to relieve its hunger? As it is said: conditioned deeds, though false, if abandoned leave no accomplishment of practice; the unconditioned, though true, if merely imagined, makes the sage's fruit hard to win. If one can penetrate the emptiness of nature and yet establish the ten thousand practices, that may be called cultivating both principle and phenomena and fusing the true and the false in one. Why then should building be treated as mere activity? As for the Chan man Guo — he was an ordinary layman; in middle age he took his wife and children and left the dust of toil, at once cultivating the pure precepts, and within ten years a place of practice rose in his wake. Is this not the Pure Land being mind-only? Moreover, this hermitage was once barren salt land and is now a place of practice — truly accomplished in a single thought. From this we see that the Western Pure Land is not apart from what lies before our eyes. How can one not believe it?
Record of the Qingchang Studio

Jingkou is a meeting place of rivers and mountains, and Qu'e is a region especially secluded and wonderful. Mount Hui backs upon the city wall and pillows the flowing water; its woods are dense and luxuriant, the lake's gleam vast and rippling, one expanse of green like a mirror. Ridges wind away, ten thousand pines massed in verdure. When the wind of heaven blows from time to time, all sounds arise at once, piercing the heart and filling the ear. This is the finest spot within the dust. The layman Tunan cleared the brush and built a hut, sitting at ease within it, and inscribed it “Qingchang,” Clear and Free, taking the sense of Xu Miao of the Jin, who was frugal and pure in his cultivation. In early summer of the ding-si year I passed by Mount Hui; the layman attended me and asked about the Dharma. When I returned to Mount Lu, the layman sent a letter asking for a record.
I said to him: “Chang,” free flow, is the opposite of “yu,” pent-up. Thus when heaven and earth are pent up, baleful vapors arise; when dung and soil are pent up, poisonous fungi grow; when human feelings are pent up, a hundred diseases appear. Hence we know that free flow is the harmony of the vital breath and the ease of the feelings. Alas, those who wallow in wealth and honor, abandoned to the desires of things, and take a moment's pleasure as their freedom — they take pent-upness for free flow. It is like eating poison that pleases the palate, never thinking that in time the poison will erupt and destroy one's life. Once there was an official in western Yue who was fond of the taste of partridge; since the region produced many, his craving was fully supplied, and without it he would not eat. In time he returned from office and fell ill; his whole body swelled and broke open, and the best physicians were helpless. A knowledgeable man said: “This is pinellia poisoning. The partridge feeds on pinellia, and with long indulgence the poison filled his five viscera; he is past saving.” Those in the world who crave a pleasing malady until the poison erupts are all of the partridge kind. The layman regards rank and office as shackles and wealth and honor as floating clouds. Widely learned and retentive, he has given his mind to the Buddha's truth, investigating the source of nature and destiny and comprehending the why of death and life. He lets his feelings range the skies and lodges his delight in cloudy forests, wandering with the Maker of Things. What he means by free flow is to be open and unobstructed in every direction: he will broaden the great void into his dwelling and dive into the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss for his home — how should he merely be one who is frugal and pure in cultivation and vaguely resembles its spiritual principle? The layman in his leisure assigns his sons their reading, hoping thereby to hand down this free flow as the family's calling. I have written this record for him especially.
Record of the Merit of Releasing Living Beings

The Buddha teaches that the dharma-body is no body, and takes living beings as its body; that the bodhisattva's wondrous practice is no practice, and takes the saving of living beings as its practice. Hence all ten thousand practices are gathered into the six pāramitās, and dāna stands first among them. Yet giving that dwells on marks is what the Tathāgata condemns, because when self and other are not yet forgotten, one cannot regard all with equal eye; and the merit such giving produces mostly becomes outflows. It is like shooting an arrow straight up into the sky, and its fall is a matter of course. Only a practice free of marks, its essence one with true emptiness, so that among all manner of adornments none surpasses the merit of releasing living beings. Why is this? Because the womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born and metamorphically born, the crawling worms and the winged insects, one and all are regarded by their Buddha-nature; one pities them for sinking into the path of suffering, and resolves to rescue them from the butcher's block and the cauldron, from the place where they are minced and scorched and rotted. Once let out of the cage and the snare, set free to fly through the sky and dive into the depths, they roam at ease in a land of utmost bliss. Such kindness proceeds without any condition, such compassion is not the compassion of love and views; seeing all as one body, one holds not the least thought of expecting reward. Therefore the measure of the merit and blessing is like empty space, inconceivable. Is this not the supreme, most excellent wondrous practice? Yet though people and creatures differ in grossness and fineness, their Buddha-nature is equal. And take a person: for a single meal he repays a thousand pieces of gold; for a bowl of broth he requites it with his life; gratitude and the remembrance of kindness are things he does not forget. How much more so when one has been delivered from boiling water and fire in a place of certain death? If one gives while contemplating Buddha-nature, one will be requited in accordance with dharma-nature. Cause and effect are clear as black and white; such is the principle. Moreover, people are limited, but creatures are without limit. Now if by giving up the food of one meal one saves millions of lives, what one has given can hardly be measured or reckoned at all. Therefore the Buddha taught his disciples that protecting life is the supreme practice. That, however, still confines itself to what is outside the world. As for engaging with the world, ordering the noble and the base, and settling the wise and the foolish, nothing is as wondrous a practice as releasing living beings. In recent times Yunqi made a special point of this practice, of abstaining from killing and releasing life, and the merit and the responses it brings he set down in his writings. Throughout the land it has been practiced very widely. When I formerly passed through Wancheng, I saw that its customs were much given to serving the Buddha, owing chiefly to Minister Wu, who led the way in his own person, so that every household was instructed and every family understood it: a vast and overflowing air of the land of the Buddha. Kejing, Master Zhan, upholding the Yunqi dharma, established a society for releasing life and set up permanent property, so as endlessly to turn the great wheel of the dharma of compassion. I heard of it and was delighted, saying: In former days Great Master Zhiyi used the sea as a pond for releasing life, and afterwards the Tiantai school flourished greatly in the countries beyond the sea. Those who know say that this was the ground on which the released living beings repaid their gratitude. Master Zhan draws along the stream of dharma of the officials and lay householders of the time and saves living beings beyond measure, all returning to the sea of nature. If the true and eternal is not obscured, then those who receive the grace will be transmuted and reborn as human beings, and we shall see loyal ministers and righteous scholars, filial sons and compassionate grandsons, gathered together in one region, of one mind in protecting the dharma, becoming wall and moat for the Three Treasures, and raising the great dharma banner. Nor will it stop at the various southern lands embracing the dharma. Yet this can be verified within one or two twelve-year cycles; the reward is not distant, and there must be those who witness its proof with their own eyes. How could the merit ever fail?
Record of the Pine Revived at Guizong Monastery

The Buddha teaches that mountains, rivers, the great earth, grasses, trees and groves all accomplish the Buddha's true body and together turn the wheel of dharma. This is meant to reveal the purport that the three realms are mind only. As for insentient things accomplishing Buddhahood, the world finds it hard to believe, but that is only because it does not penetrate the meaning of mind only. Guizong Monastery on Mount Lu was the place where Chan Master Chiyan taught the dharma; thirty-six clear-eyed spiritual teachers succeeded him there. The site commands the finest prospects of Mount Kuang and has long been numinous. After it fell into ruin, its jeweled halls and brahma abodes were left to the thickets and wild grass, and only one ancient pine before the monastery still stood upright, propping up the sky. Its base had been stripped and peeled away by woodcutters, more than half of it gone; its branches and boughs were withered, and it was on the point of breaking. At that time Chan Master Daguan passed by and asked about it, and sighed: This Guizong has only this one staff-pole left, and now it has suffered the axe; without it, every trace of the place of practice would be wiped out. So he led his disciples to set a stone wall around it and bank it up with earth, made a spell and a vow over it, and swore: If this monastery is to rise again, may this pine come back to life as before. Then he lingered there, wrote a verse about the old man of the piled pellets, and departed. In less than a few years the tree did indeed grow again, its bark whole and close, its branches and leaves luxuriant. Before long there was a great famine, and the remnant monks of the monastery traded the pine for rice to eat. The stonecutters eyed it askance, turning to cut it down, when it happened that a beggar was resting in its shade and begged to give rice to redeem it. The craftsman was moved by him and stopped. Within a few years, sure enough, Master Qing Zhan restored that monastery, and in the end moved the emperor to bestow the great canon upon it. For a time those in authority built halls and shrines for it, turning rubble into a pure land. Was not the turning point of all this foreshown in a single withered trunk? If one calls it insentient, could it have done such a thing? And yet grass and trees have no consciousness; it lies in sincere devotion moving and transforming, and the meaning of mind only is thereby made plain. See how Meng Zong wept and the bamboo put forth shoots in winter, and how Master Sheng preached and the stones nodded. The dharma is not outside the mind, and the transformation wrought by devotion comes from the person. Even the withered turtle that tells people of good and ill fortune, though drilled seventy-two times, never fails in its reckoning: it lies wholly in single-minded sincerity, and the response is like an echo. Hence it is said that one who can transform things is the same as the Tathāgata; that people and things are one body and together turn the wheel of dharma is here made evident. I therefore record it to tell those who come after, that they may know this pine to be the dharma-body, ever abiding. Should later generations harm a single hair of it, that would be to wound and slay the dharma-body and cut off the Buddha's wisdom-life. Can they fail to bear this in mind?
Record of the Relic Stūpa of Śākyamuni Buddha on Golden Wheel Peak at Mount Lu

The Buddha's dharma first entered China in the Yongping era of the Han. In the Chiwu era of Wu, the Western monk Kang Senghui came to Jiankang, set up images and practiced the way, and sought relics in Changganli; the King of Wu built a stūpa to enshrine them and founded the first monastery. This was the beginning of stūpas and monasteries in the south of the river. In the Xiankang era of Emperor Cheng of the Eastern Jin, the brahma master Dharmatrāta arrived bringing the meditation scriptures. At that time Wang Xizhi, the General of the Right, was governor of Jiangzhou; he saw him and was struck by wonder, so he gave up his residence and built Guizong Monastery for him to dwell in. In the Yixi era, Master Yuan came to Mount Lu and opened the White Lotus Society at Donglin. The brahma master the Elder Yaśas arrived, and Master Yuan invited him into the society; then with the relics of Śākyamuni Buddha that he had brought, he built a stūpa on the summit of Golden Wheel Peak at Guizong, carrying iron on his own back to make the pagoda. This was the first of the stūpas and monasteries of the western river. In the Tang, in the Yuanhe era, Chan Master Chiyan Chang received the mind-seal of Mazu and opened his teaching at Guizong, and all the famous monasteries south of Mount Kuang were led by his eminent disciples. The excellence of that time was such that it was called a dharma pit, and the way of the single transmission from the West was greatly roused on this mountain. From then on more than thirty men in succession taught the dharma there, all of them recorded in the Transmission of the Lamp. Down to the Five Dynasties and the Song, the way gradually declined and the monastery gradually fell into ruin. In the Jingde and Huangyou eras of the Song it was repaired twice. In the Yuanfeng era the monk Wenjing revived it again. At the end of the Yuan it was destroyed by soldiers, and from that time the stūpa and the monastery were abandoned, and its mountain lands and fields all became the property of the people. In the guichou year of the Wanli era, Master Daguan's disciple Guoqing Zhan, while paying reverence at the stūpa, passed by and sighed, and thereupon roused the resolve to restore it. He visited all the officials and benefactors far and wide, and all at the same time put forth their strength, so that in the end the emperor was moved to issue an edict granting one copy of the great canon, and a warrant made his disciple Xiuzi the abbot. Those in authority built the halls and shrines, and Xing Maoxue, a licentiate of Huangmei, donated funds to redeem all the mountain lands and fields, so that it became a great place of practice once more. In that guichou year Master Zhan wished to rebuild the stūpa and bought several tens of thousands of catties of iron, but before he could do so he passed away. In the jiayin year Xiuzi made a great Vairocana image in Wu, and on his return the stūpa relics emitted light three times, illuminating the valleys, and the pines behind the monastery bore five cones shaped like stūpas, some eight inches tall, each with thirteen tiers; near and far all marveled at it. In the spring of the yimao year, Ci, carrying out his master's dying command, smelted iron and cast a thirteen-tiered pagoda and reopened the relic repository, where he saw several hundred relics, whose five-colored jewel light dazzled the eyes; all who beheld them bowed in reverence and were moved to joy. In the ninth month of that autumn, at the time appointed for enshrining the relics, the valleys shook and roared like thunder seven times, and all who heard knew it to be a portent of the relics. Ci feared the iron would soon corrode, so on the outside he had porcelain ash and rice broth pounded together to protect it, seeking a firm and close seal that would last. In the summer of the bingchen year I came from Nanyue to pay reverence, and saw that wondrous peak, sheer and towering, standing alone and propping up the sky, its form like a stūpa. The summit is scarcely two zhang across, with a stone cavity a few feet wide that just holds the stūpa repository: surely made by heaven and set by earth, and no accident. I made this record of it, saying: When Śākyamuni Buddha entered extinction, his cremation yielded eight hu and four dou of relics, which the gods above, the people in the world, and the dragon palaces each divided and enshrined in stūpas. King Aśoka distributed them throughout Jambudvīpa, and in our land of Zhenshan there were nineteen; those at Mingzhou and Jiankang are the most famous, while the rest have not been made manifest. Might not this be one of them? Relics are the residual perfume of precept and samādhi, congealed from the four elements. Because they come from flesh, blood, hair, teeth and bone, which are not the same, there are differences of five colors. Their substance is hard and firm, able to pierce metal and stone; their radiance seizes the eye and surpasses all worldly treasures. Some are firm and congealed and do not move; some flow and move up and down, their forms changing without constancy: each accords with the response and is so. Ah, all Buddhas and living beings alike receive this mind. Living beings, perfumed by ignorance, the three poisons and false thinking, therefore have a body that stinks and is foul and in the end decays. The Buddhas, perfumed by the diamond mind of precept and samādhi, therefore have a body firm and solid, whose light shines forth and abides without decay. The direct retribution is thus; the circumstantial retribution is likewise so. The circumstantial retribution of living beings brings the evil world of the five turbidities, filled with every defilement; the pure lands of the Buddhas are adorned with the seven treasures. Hence the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says: its ground is firm, made of diamond. This is what is meant by being transformed by mind only; how could it be the power of another? A Buddha does not dwell where there is no pure land, and so relics are not borne where there is no auspicious site. As for this Golden Wheel, standing out on the southern face of Mount Kuang, towering into the sky and pressing down the assembled peaks, it is a celestial dwelling among men, and the Buddha's dharma-body relics abide within it forever: how could this be a small matter? Though the true and eternal does not decay, yet the marks of the world change, and so its pagoda rose and fell again and again. To hand it down forever, and to trace the mind of him who first built it and the resolve of those who restored it, there must be a vow-power abiding in it. Therefore I make this record.
Record of the Relic Stūpa of King Aśoka at Mount Mao, Mingzhou

In Sanskrit, sharīra means the bones of the body. Our World-Honored One alone, through vast kalpas, with a diamond mind cultivated the diamond samādhi, until he became Buddha, with never a single divergent thought. Thus he transformed the condition-born five aggregates, this illusory body, into a diamond substance, which is the Tathāgata's dharma-body, ever abiding and undecaying, forever free of birth and death. Among the Buddha's ten bodies, one is the body of sustaining power, and this is that. The Tathāgata appeared in the Sahā world, showed his birth in Kapilavastu, taught the dharma for forty-nine years, and when the work of his teaching was done, entered great nirvāṇa in the city of Kuśinagara, between the twin trees of the sāla grove. Then the king of that country, according to the dharma, cremated him and obtained eight hu of relics, which were divided into three shares, and the gods above, the people in the world, and the dragon palaces each raised stūpas in offering. The people in the world divided theirs among eight kingdoms. The kingdom of Magadha, King Ajātaśatru, received one share, with eighty-four thousand grains. In the time of King Aśoka, who had great spiritual power and could command ghosts and spirits, he ground the seven treasures to powder and made eighty-four thousand stūpas, scattering them throughout the four continents. Since the southern Jambudvīpa is the land of his body-teaching, stūpas are many there. Of those that came to Zhenshan there were nineteen, and those at Changgan in Jinling and at Mount Mao in Mingzhou are the most illustrious. In my youth I left home at Changgan and repeatedly beheld light and auspicious signs, of many kinds beyond naming. Though I have never been to Mingzhou, I long ago heard the evidence of its responses. Now seeing the Record of Mount King Aśoka sent by Master Li, and reading it, I was moved and sighed: This is where my own original teacher is present in the world, turning the wheel of dharma. What then is a relic? It is the one true dharma-realm, the ever-abiding true mind, the substance of vast and great radiance. The Buddhas realize it as the pure dharma-body; bodhisattvas cultivate it as the diamond mind-ground; living beings are deluded about it as the ālaya consciousness. What does not decay in them is the seed of Buddha-nature, called the Buddha's knowledge and vision. Because it is originally complete in living beings, the Buddha came into the world expressly to open and reveal it and enable them to awaken and enter. The patriarch came from the West and pointed to it as the mind-seal. Thus we know that living beings and the Buddha are not two and not different; the only difference lies in the defiling or purifying perfume and transformation. Through the power of living beings' ignorance and karma, thought after thought fumigating them, they receive a body of the four elements and five aggregates, rank and foul and stinking and impure, impermanent and decaying. What does not decay in them is the karmic fruit of rebirth, unforgotten through kalpas. Bodhisattvas take it as samādhi and wisdom and, perfuming and cultivating it, attain the mind-born body, taming living beings and purifying Buddha-lands. What does not decay in them is subtle merit, the perfection of adornment. Only the Buddhas realize it as the pure dharma-body, abiding forever in the land of tranquil light, where body and land are not two. When they manifest the great body, it is the boundless radiance and marks, dwelling in the adornment of the Huazang, called the reward body. When they manifest the small transformation, it is the golden body of sixteen feet, showing birth among men and sharing the troubles of the people. Yet those who see it see only the condition-born Buddha, not the true substance of the dharma-body. To show that dharma and transformation are not two, that the impermanent is the permanent, he entered parinirvāṇa, and left the relics to gather in living beings, which is called the body of sustaining power, revealing the diamond, undecaying dharma-body as ever abiding in the world, which from the first has no marks of birth, death, coming or going. Therefore the radiance and marks he manifests, and the various auspicious responses, are inconceivable. What responds and appears according to the minds of living beings is the dharma-body teaching according to capacity, and by the samādhi beyond words it points directly to the Buddha-nature inherent in living beings, wishing to enable those who see it to awaken at once to their own mind and suddenly see the unborn and undying nature of the dharma-body. How is this different from sitting on Vulture Peak at the end and holding up a flower? Thus the Buddha's coming into the world to teach the dharma was nothing but a pointing to this one great matter, and in the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra he opened and revealed to living beings the Buddha's knowledge and vision. This knowledge and vision is the wisdom-life of the dharma-body; hence it is said that wherever this sūtra is, one should raise a stūpa of the seven treasures. How much more so the Buddha's knowledge and vision, which is in turn obstructed by words and letters! As for the patriarchs who pointed it out to people directly and showed it in blows and shouts, in mockery and abuse and angry scolding, people labeled it clever repartee and supposed there was some other mystery in it; hence those who awaken are few. Now here one sees the dharma-body with one's own eyes; the Tathāgata faces one and speaks the dharma of no birth and death, yet people do not awaken to it within themselves, but on the whole look on it as radiance and auspicious marks. Truly this is meeting it face to face and missing it. Is it not pitiable? Alas, we have sunk down through many kalpas, wandering in birth and death. How fortunate, what causes we have now, to meet a rare and hard to encounter matter, and still to be deluded about our heads and take shadows as real! Do we not then betray the true compassion above and obscure what is inherent in ourselves? Must we not grieve greatly over this? Formerly the Buddha, in the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra, himself spoke of the measure of the dharma-body's life, abiding and undestroyed. But that was only put in empty words; there was nothing so deeply and clearly shown in actual deeds as this. Only Samantabhadra, by his ten great vows, revealed the dharma-body, saying: Pray the Buddha to remain in the world; urge him to turn the wheel of dharma; always follow the Buddha in learning. These three meanings are made manifest here. At first, when Seng Hui came to Changgan, the Wu ruler Sun Quan ordered him to seek relics, setting a term of seven days, and there was no response. The term was extended to twenty-one days, and still at midnight there was no response. Seng Hui bowed his head and pleaded in grief, saying: The Buddha takes compassion as his heart; if he does not respond, then the living beings of this region will have the Buddha-seed cut off. Thereupon he cried the Buddha's name with all his strength, three times, and from every pore of his body blood and sweat burst forth. At once he heard a clanging sound in the vase, and its light lit up heaven and earth. When it was opened, the relics were there in the vase. Liu Sahe had fallen into hell, with no term of release; then he heard a brahma monk direct him to seek relics as a ground for confessing his offenses, and so he moved a jeweled stūpa to spring up from the earth. Thus we know that Kang sought them for others and Liu for himself, and both were the meaning of Samantabhadra's prayer and entreaty. As for all the various adornments and offerings, the guarding and the praise, are these not always following the Buddha in learning? Moreover, the Buddha-nature in living beings is indeed deluded. But the radiance of prajñā shines forever without being obscured, and issues in action: as when loyal ministers and filial sons, persons of aspiration and benevolence in the world, in all they do, bring benefit to their ruler and grace to the people and accomplish undying works, is this not the outflow of the dharma-body? And when the emperors of successive dynasties revered and prospered it, was this not the beneficial manifestation of the Dharma King? In sum, there is no living being who does not possess this nature. Hence those who see and hear and rejoice, who bow and make offerings, are no different from those who personally receive and support his feet; even giving up body and life, emptying all one has, exhausting inner and outer gifts to make adornment, is but for the enjoyment of one's own nature. As for one who at a single sight of the relics suddenly shatters ignorance and awakens to the dharma-body, bidding farewell to birth and death and forever escaping the road of delusion, that depends on one of sharp faculties and keen wisdom whose hearing and perfuming are from former lives and whose conditions ripen at this moment; such a person is not lacking. From this we see that kings and ministers of many generations built it up before, that Minister Lu restored it in the past, and that Minister Guo of the army revived it again today; and that he entrusts the dharma-body to the samādhi of a hair's tip, to show what does not decay. All this too is upheld by Samantabhadra's wheel of vows. Is Master Li one whom the Buddha called Elder, as he called Śāriputra? I am confident that the assembly on Vulture Peak is solemnly present before my eyes, and that the sound of the dharma being taught goes on blazing without interval. Therefore I write this especially, to tell all who see and hear, who rejoice and bow and make offering: you must not seek it by marks and appearances.

Record of the Great Compassion Repentance Hall at Mount Lu

The Buddha’s dharmakāya has no bounds: in its entirety it becomes sentient beings. The deluded thinking of sentient beings has no bounds: in its entirety it becomes the deluded karma of birth and death. Because deluded karma is not dissolved, the sea of suffering of sentient beings is likewise boundless, and in the end they do not know the way out. Were it not for the power of the great compassionate vow, there would be no means to drain the sea of suffering, dissolve deluded karma, escape birth and death, and realize the original ground. Therefore the Great Being Avalokiteśvara, according with the mind of the dharma-realm, practices the practice of great compassion and secretly enters the ocean of deluded thinking of all sentient beings to ferry them across. He established a dhāraṇī and had them recite, uphold, and permeate themselves with it, wishing to bring sentient beings out of the sea of suffering, to see their original dharmakāya, and to reach the shore of nirvāṇa. This is why the Great Compassion Repentance was established. Its mantra comes originally from the Vajrašekhara section; it flows forth from the dharmakāya of the middle way and is the mind-seal of Vairocana. It was first composed by the Venerable of Siming in accordance with the Great Compassion Sūtra, and its lineage is ancient. Truly, because the storehouse consciousness of sentient beings is a hidden fastness, nothing but a secret mind-seal can break it open; this is the sovereign remedy for escaping suffering. Master Man of Zhizhi received the teaching from Yunqi and retired to cultivate at Nanyue, taking repentance rites as his Buddha-work; many believed in and followed him. Later he went to Mount Lu and dwelt alone in a hidden retreat, vowing to spread this practice widely in order to save the four assemblies. So he built a Repentance Hall to set forth the manner of cultivation. When the hall was complete he asked this old man for a record, and I said to him: “All sentient beings are originally the dharmakāya; having become deluded, they turn into a sea of birth-and-death karma. When they are made to use the mind-seal of the dharmakāya to permeate and transform their karmic nature, it is water poured into water, emptiness merged with emptiness; whoever has faith will escape the suffering of birth and death without ever intending to. With a mind of great compassion the Master is the kindly oar of the boat that crosses the sea of suffering; he points out the Dharma that everyone inherently possesses. It is like sprinkling sweet dew on scorched and withered things: the ground of their minds is cooled, and they know it without being told. The Dharma-nature is inexhaustible; the realm of sentient beings cannot be exhausted; and so this practice too is inexhaustible. Why, then, reckon in terms of forever and ever?”
Stele Record of the Ten-Direction Permanent Estate of Yunzhong Temple on Mount Lu

The Chan groves of Mount Lu are closely spread. At the mountain’s very summit, below the Nine Wonders Peak, lies the most secluded and lovely spot, commonly called Yangtian Ping, Gazing-Heaven Flat, because it is high and has nothing above it. In former times it was a den of tigers and wolves. There stands Yunzhong Temple, founded by Master Zhong of Jingtang. The Master’s dharma-name was Fazhong, a native of She. At nineteen he took the monk Daji of Lingyin in Hangzhou as his teacher and became his disciple. He tended the kitchen fire for three years, then reflected that the great matter was not yet settled. He therefore attended the lecture halls and listened to the sūtras of definitive meaning, yet still found words and letters an obstruction. He crossed the river to Shaolin and relied on Master Daqian, investigating the purport of Bodhidharma’s coming from the West. He stayed ten years, then sought out the capital and again paid his respects to great learned masters such as Bianrong, sealing his resolve in the essentials of mind. He then went to Wutai, where he met me and Master Miao, and in our hearts we knew him to be a hero of the Dharma gate. When I departed for the Eastern Sea and Master Miao returned to Luya, Master Miao drew him along. He stayed three years, and in all that was undertaken he was much consulted. Before long he gave it up and entered Niu Mountain; not long after he moved on to Mount Kuang. At first he built a hut at the Sutra-Expounding Terrace and lived there three years. Finding the coming and going a burden, he moved to the Five Elders Peak. After four more years he came to Yunzhong. Loving its lofty isolation, he cut thatch and bound rafters to dwell there. Clad in grass and eating wild fare, he was joined by many spirited patch-robed monks from the ten directions. The Master cast off bodily form and knew no you or me, forgetting one another in the Way. He laid down no rules and imposed no constraints; each person disciplined himself. He put on no worldly airs. The four requisites came as conditions allowed, and when they ran short he went out begging in person to supply them. Even an inch of silk or a grain of rice, his thought was always for the community. He refined the three karmas and was entrusted with the illumination of the one mind. After twenty-two years it became a monastic grove. Later he built a round thatched hut for rest and repose. The mountain gate bore the placard “Yunzhong, In the Clouds,” to record that it is the highest of all. The Master loved to plant pines, more than a hundred thousand in all, hoping that when they turned to dragons they would mark the years. I came from Nanyue to visit this mountain, and the Master talked with me through the night. He said to me: “I am old. In this phantom world I have dwelt on this mountain as conditions allowed for thirty years. Now the floating light will not last long, and as for this practice-place, though it was brought about by illusory conditions, my original intent was to provide it for the dragons and elephants of the ten directions, not for this petty self alone. I beg you, Master, for a word to serve as its record.” I rejoiced and sighed: “How great is the Master’s mind! The sūtra says: ‘Taking the great perfect enlightenment as my monastery, body and mind dwell at peace in the wisdom of universal equality.’ This is the Buddha’s regard for the ten directions. West River has a saying: ‘Gathered together from the ten directions, each one studies the unconditioned; this is the field for choosing Buddhas; with the mind emptied, one passes and returns home.’ This is the patriarch’s mind set upon the ten directions. The Master’s lifelong aspiration was selflessness, and so whatever he established was selfless. Now in a single stroke he hands it over to the ten directions: this is selflessness in the ultimate sense. Should there be one able to carry on his work and shoulder it with bare body, taking the Master’s mind as his own, then if he sets his will on the Way, will there not be heroic men who pass with emptied minds? Then the hues of the mountain and the light on the lake, the flowing water and the moving wind, all proclaim the Dharma-sound of selflessness, and the Master’s broad and long tongue is ever present and never extinguished. As for the succession of the permanent estate, there is a separate deed, not written by me. I have briefly recorded the Master’s life from beginning to end, to tell those who come after.”
Record of the Adorning of the Buddha Images at Wanshou Temple on Mount Lu
