South of Mount Lu the tops of monastery banners face one another. The greatest of its valleys is called Qixian, its cliffs and ravines steep and craggy, its woods dense. The peaks Taiyi, Hanyang, and Taolin stand ranged amid the clouds, and all the waters gather in a great torrent. Within is a temple called Wanshou, built by the Tang monk Deying as a place of Chan. Through the years it fell into ruin. In the Zhengtong era of our Ming the monk Ming’an rebuilt it, and now it too has collapsed. The monk Huileng gathered it together and dwelt there. The ancient hall of several bays could not keep out wind and rain, and the golden countenances of the Buddha images, dimmed by dust and eaten by time, looked desolate among green moss and old tiles. Huileng therefore made a vow to renew it and asked me for an appeal, sending his disciple Bensheng to beg in his native Xincheng. The provincial graduate Mr. Tu Shiyan, because in a former life he had been a monk, had taken the courtesy name Wulai, Mistaken Coming, to record that he did not forget his origin. Seeing the appeal, he roused his mind, was the first to lead the crowd, and donated a sum of gold. Bensheng carried it back and used it to adorn the golden images, and hall and buildings shone entirely new. The mountain light veiled and revealed them as if one beheld the radiant marks on Vulture Peak, when the Buddha preached for gods and men. He then asked me for a record, and I said: “Buddha means the Awakened. He is the great root of living beings, namely the self-nature of sentient beings’ awareness. Since a person has this mind, everyone has this awakening; awakened, sentient beings are the Buddha; unawakened, the Buddha is a sentient being. Hence it is said: mind, Buddha, and sentient beings, these three are without distinction. To adorn this image today is not merely to embellish an illusory form of gold and wood; it is truly to open the Buddha-nature of one’s own mind. As for Mr. Tu, in a former life he was a monk: he was one who wished to climb the path of awakening. Now he has turned into this present body: wishing to be awakened, he has grown dim again, like a man deep in sleep who is about to wake but sinks back into drowsiness, only because there is no one beside him to call out and rouse him. The patriarchs of the Transmission of the Lamp opened wide their furnaces and bellows to smelt and refine the deluded multitude; sometimes in the space of a single blow or shout they made a person exhaust ordinary feeling at once and instantly ascend the ground of awakening. This is what is meant by waking from the great dream at a single call. Seen in this light, my one appeal is no less than the blow and shout of Linji and Deshan. Should Mr. Tu be touched once and awaken to his original nature, he could manifest the eight phases before his eyes and perfect the three asamkhya kalpas in the present moment; he may be called one of swift and keen faculties. Then all the good men and women who give together are of the company of the four assemblies at Vulture Peak, jointly forming the condition of the Buddha-seed. In lives to come, life after life within the house of dreams, they will call and rouse one another in turn, and all will reach the great awakening before it ends. This is what is meant by the one great matter’s cause and condition. How could it be merely a matter of giving unstinting wealth and embellishing an illusory image? Of this condition of Buddha-nature the sūtra says: it is like a person who swallows a little diamond; in the end it will pass out through the skin. This speaks strongly of how the truth of the nature is not obscured. I beg to have it recorded, as a pledge of the Dharma gate for days to come.”
Record of the Fields for Feeding the Sangha at Ziqing Temple in Pinghu County, Jiaxing

The Ziqing practice-place at Pinghu was built by Master Jianquan Hui. He set aside seventy mu of monk-feeding fields to supply the Three Jewels in perpetuity; this is the permanent estate. In the dingsi year the Master entered quiescence, leaving a testament to his disciple Zhida not to neglect his work. Zhida came to Mount Kuang to receive the precepts, and asked this old man for a record, saying: “In the world, what is called a field is where the seed is entrusted and does not decay, producing without end. Thus filial devotion to father and mother is the field of reverence; relieving the poor and suffering is the field of compassion; offering to the Three Jewels is the field of blessing. If people in the world abandon these and cultivate blessings for body and life, they have no ground to stand on. In the fields left by Master Hui all three are present, and on them indeed depend both worldly and world-transcending life. Those who later guard these three fields but do not till them with effort, letting them go wild and foul: losing reverence they become rebellious; losing compassion they become thieves; without blessing, the Buddha’s wisdom-life is cut off. And whoever fails to bring this to mind is no true human, nor is he a disciple of the Buddha. Yet those who eat from these fields should also know to extend this mind, so that the seeds of wisdom and the sprouts of the spirit blossom day and night, and the fruit of bodhi may be hoped for. Otherwise they fall away into scorched sprouts and rotten seeds.”
Record of the Founding of Changhua Hermitage at the Sancha River, Quanjiao County

Reverently reflecting on our Sagely Ancestor, who soared as a dragon in the Huai region and first traced his steps at Chuyang: the numinous power of its mountains and rivers has long been present. Quanjiao lies west of the prefecture; though it is a mere pellet, a black speck, tucked away in a corner, it is the deep recess of Chu, like an inch of jade, storing its radiance and gathering its moisture, so far held in and not yet released, like the growth of warm spring, which has its season. Through more than two hundred years of our Ming, at the time of the Jiajing and Longqing reigns, the fortune of letters first opened; that was still the bright ascendancy of the Ming, and now it is the broad and flowing air of a Buddha-land. Not only in the city’s outskirts, where bells and drums are heard one from another; even in poor villages and remote lanes those who serve the Buddha and purify their minds stand shoulder to shoulder. Is this not the great transformation of Heaven and Earth, flourishing with the times? The waters of the county town run from west to south, and twenty li on they join the waters of Mount Huang. The three forks are the county’s water outlet. On the left of the river a mountain crouches like a guarding gate, but on the right the embankment is flat and open, so the outflow has no check; the energy scatters and the center is hollow, as though Heaven had a gap in it. A villager, Xia Rang, by nature deeply good and fond of serving the Buddha, resolved to build a Buddha temple on the north bank of the river: main hall, mountain gate, refectory, kitchen, and storehouse, a noble practice-place indeed. Its position stands in match with the mountain and checks the flow of the waves, so that the impounded waters do not spill away and their outflow remains ample. When the hermitage was complete he came to Mount Lu to tell of it and to ask me for a plaque. This is my native place, and I know its circumstances well, so I inscribed it Changhua, Flourishing Transformation, meaning that the fortune of Dharma-transformation will flourish from here. And with this to pray for the Sage’s longevity and to protect its people, may it also greatly prosper the kingly transformation, so that all alike attain benevolent long life and ascend to the land of Ultimate Bliss. I have therefore briefly recorded the matter, and made this inscription:

The Sagely Ancestor took flight
On Chu’s fair shore in dragon light;
This Pepper Hill stands, summit high,
Upon the western ridge hard by.

Barren without, within it rich,
It holds the spirit’s hidden worth;
Like jade within the stone, in which
Lie stored the gleam and dew of earth.

Heaven’s way moves silently,
As spring within the flower lies;
The threefold yang in harmony
Bursts forth in bloom before our eyes.

The tide of letters turns anew,
And Dharma’s transformation streams;
Heaven’s working and the hearts of men
Are like a boat that rides on water’s gleam.

Three waters meet and join; and high
A guardian gate stands steep and sheer.
One lone fist of a hill stands by —
As if the right arm were not here.

Then rose this man; the light of heaven
Burst on him, sudden and bright;
And by the river’s bank was built
This Brahma-shrine of Dharma’s light.

Its halls tower up in majesty,
The people’s shield and surety;
Bells and drums clash, boom, and ring,
The Dharma-sound goes echoing.

All who see take refuge there,
All who hear are glad at heart;
Straightway is this people placed
In the Blissful Land apart.

The Way’s transforming power flows wide;
The letters’ fortune truly grows;
This far-flung blessing here is laid:
Hills are high, and long the water flows.
Stele Record of the Circumstances of the Revival of Dongchan Temple at Jinsha

The worlds of the ten directions are wholly the light of eternal quiescence; there is no place that is not a bodhimaṇḍa. All the gates of affliction are the practice of Samantabhadra; there is no dharma that is not Buddha-work. What matters is that conditions meet and the work then rises, and that the right person is found for it to appear. In this world of the five turbidities, how hard it is to set up the Dharma-banner! Looking at Dongchan in Jinsha, one may see it in outline. According to the county gazetteer, some three li east of the seat of government there was an ancient temple, at first named Xinxing Chan Cloister. It was founded in the Guangqi era of the Tang, and in the Jianyan era of the Song, through Duke Zhang Zhongmu, it was renamed Duzhong Xianqing Cloister; afterward it was called Dongchan. It fell to ruin at the end of the Yuan. Our dynasty restored it, and in time it too sank into tangled brush and tall grass. In the winter of the gengyin year of the Wanli era, the Chan Master Daguan was copying sūtras in the gardens of the Yu and Wang families. With the Hanlin scholar Mr. Wang Sun’an and others he passed by and was moved to sighs. In the thickets they found a broken stele, pieced it together and read it, and learned that it was a record of the Bell Tower composed by the tribute student Lu Yilin in the Daguan era. Master Daguan restored its text and preserved it, and thereupon made the vow to revive the temple. After Master Daguan left, his disciples Jianyin Xiuzi and Gutan Ruqing vowed to shoulder it as a cloister of the ten directions. At that time, amid the waves of wheat, there stood three broken bays of houses, used by a Daoist priest for farming. Master Qing at once established a water-and-gruel fast there to rouse the faith of the crowd, and before long people gathered from near and far. The laymen Sun Yunyi and Yunreng built three bays of Chan hall, and on the twenty-eighth day of the eighth month of the xinmao year of Wanli they divined the raising of the beam. Word came that Yunyi had passed the provincial examination, and he donated his archway allowance to complete the building. In the renchen year Yunreng was specially selected for tribute, and in the guimao year the Hanlin scholar’s nephew Maokun passed; in the renzi year Maowu passed. Each gave archway funds according to precedent. Thereupon they built five bays of Chan hall and three bays each of the Sangharama hall and the Patriarchs’ hall. Earlier, because Master Daguan’s disciple Mizang Kaigong had solicited offerings to support the Chan companions, the practice-place was brought to completion. Master Qing guarded it with all his strength, pacing in meditation around the temple, holding dhāraṇīs, and planting pines, hoping it would become a monastic grove. Before long Master Qing left, and those who followed him either left or passed away. So they invited Master Gaoyuan of Shu; he too left. Then they made Bian’s disciple Langya Haiyao abbot. Yao was a man of resolve and gave his whole life to raising it up. It happened that Xiuzi arrived, and with Dharma companions such as Haiyin Daocheng he took counsel to found a Dharma society, honoring the Buddha’s three trainings and taking the sūtras, the vinaya, and the śāstras as its standard: the sūtra being the Lotus, the vinaya the Brahma Net, and the śāstra the Awakening of Faith. At first they took reading, reciting, receiving, and upholding as their work; when that was familiar, they practiced as taught. Yet their meditation was chiefly the wondrous school of calm and insight, devoted to the Pure Land. The society was named Blue Lotus, and Master Yao presided over it. This is one of the most excellent Dharma conditions of the Dharma-ending age. When the agreement was settled, the Hanlin scholar’s nephew Jing, carrying out the dying wish of his father Yuwang, donated a hundred pieces of gold to help begin the work. In the gengxu period the Hanlin scholar, having no heir, wished to give up his residence as a temple; he therefore sold his other estate for more than a thousand gold and gave it all toward the building. In all he made three bays of main hall, three bays of the Western Pure Land hall, and five bays of new Chan hall. The plan was a four-sided enclosure, broad and open in scale, seen clearly at one glance: a great practice-place indeed. When the hall was finished, the images were supervised by Master Yao, modeled on the painting copy of Guanxiu of the Tang, wrought of lacquered cloth and hollow dry-lacquer work of matchless excellence, a choice piece of the age. At first the old hall faced north, so the main hall was made to face east, and the mountain gate was placed to the north, because the Hanlin scholar was skilled in geomancy. In the autumn of the guichou year the Hanlin scholar unfortunately passed away, and by his dying command his own portrait was enshrined in the temple, with the vow to be its Sangharama guardian, as Nangong was to Helin. In the spring of the bingchen year Master Yao gathered the benefactors and sent a letter inviting me to preside over the society, so that he might rest in old age. Because of the unfinished bond of mourning for Master Daguan, I gladly accepted, and arrived in the tenth month of that winter. I had not been there long when I went to Shuangjing. The next year, in the spring of the dingyi year, I resolved to spend my old age back at Mount Kuang. Master Yao wept and clung to me, but in the end it could not be. It happened that Master Yao wished to leave for other conditions; while I was at Mount Kuang I heard of it and at once sent a letter, keeping Master Benhuai Yin there to guard it. Before long Master Jianyin Ci arrived from Wancheng, and the faithful, glad that he was the original vow-maker, firmly kept him there. The layman Yunreng, as founding benefactor, recounted the whole story of its origins and asked me for a record. He also asked me to set down rules and establish a Dharma covenant, so that it might be forever a permanent estate of the ten directions. I sighed in dismay and said: From of old it has never been easy to establish and complete a work. Is it only states and dynasties that are so? The monastic grove is the same. Now the Dharma King’s rule over the world takes the Practices of Ease and Bliss as its household model and the Brahma Net precepts as its covenant, with rewards and punishments so strict, how clear it is! What is called the government of Wen and Wu, spread out in the records: when the man is there, the government is raised; it truly depends on what kind of person one gets. Śramaṇas, sons of Śākyamuni, if they know that our Buddha, through countless kalpas, gave up body and life in quest of bodhi, and even at his appearing in the world still endured six years of cold and hunger in the Snow Mountains, and so won the offerings of gods and men to nourish the sons and grandsons of later ages; and if they think how hard this temple’s founding was, and that every mote of dust and drop of water was the fat and blood of the faithful, then at a single thought of it their body hairs will stand on end. Even a grain of rice or a stalk of greens is a shard of diamond. How could one bear to be unafraid of the Niraya hells and recklessly create black karma? Those who dwell here hereafter need only seek clear faith in cause and effect, not be blind to their first resolve, diligently uphold the three trainings, keep and observe the sūtras and precepts, and hold the great matter of birth and death in mind in every thought. What need is there to seek the Buddha-Dharma elsewhere? This is the record.
A Record of the Wondrous Response to the Portrait of Master Baozhi of Yangshan in Xin'an

The four barrier mountains of Xin'an are the most wondrous and fair in all the southeast, and Yangshan among them is especially secluded and superb. It was a mountain opened in the Liang dynasty as the practice ground of Master Baozhi, and it became renowned in the Tang through Chan Master Ji; long fallen into ruin, it was heard of no more. The country folk there had never known the Buddha, yet they revered Master Baozhi with uncommon strictness. Whenever they prayed for rain or for offspring, or sought portents of fortune and calamity, their prayers were answered at once, and so the sacrifices to him never ceased. At the beginning of the Longqing era, Master Jingxuan of Shoujing practiced the ascetic discipline of the dhutaṅgas with extraordinary austerity, and all far and near were converted by him. The great clans of the valley gathered their kin to take counsel and begged him to restore Yangshan, and he consented. When he entered the mountain, he found the old foundation sunk in thick grass and thorny brush, while every field and slope within the bounds had passed into the hands of the powerful. He therefore first collected contributions from the various clans and bought farmland at the foot of the mountain in order to exchange it for that land, and he led his disciples Xingyu and Xingjue to brave wind and rain, clearing the weeds and cutting the brambles as they worked. In less than ten years the old was torn down and all made new, and it became a great practice ground, as though it had fallen from heaven or welled up from the earth. Within all the four borders everyone came to know of the Three Jewels. When the monastery was finished, the elders passed down the tradition that there had once been three portraits of Master Baozhi, scattered among the common people, no one knowing where they were. In the xinchou year of Wanli, when the reliquary stupa at Bao'en Monastery in Jinling was being repaired, the workmen found them inside a jeweled vase at the golden peak. They were from the hand of Zhang Sengyou of the Liang; the man rolled them up and carried them home. He was a certain Li of Jixi in Xin'an. He had three sons, and each took one. Before long Li died, and the second and third sons grew poorer day by day. Learning that Master Baozhi's practice ground was at Yangshan, they presented their portraits there, and Masters Yu and Jue received them and held them to be sacred objects. After a long while the eldest son's house caught fire, and he urgently warned his family to throw down the portraits and snatch up the deeds instead. When they searched, the portraits had survived and the deeds were burned. This happened three times, and so he grew suspicious and took it for a ghostly thing. Some years later, returning from a long journey, the eldest son lost his way and by mistake came to a hermitage at the foot of the mountain. At the time all the monks had gone to a meal, and only the meditation monk Jingguang remained. Presently a visitor bowed and asked the way, and Guang pointed it out. The visitor was moved and asked his name, and he answered, Jingguang. The visitor was dumbfounded, and Guang did not know why. Some days later, when the community had again gone to a meal, Guang stayed behind once more. Presently the same visitor arrived, and Guang sat with him. The visitor said, My late father was a stonemason who repaired the Bao'en stupa, and he obtained three portraits of the great being Master Baozhi. They were divided among us three brothers. My two elder brothers have already returned theirs to the great monastery above. As for the one I kept, my house has been burned three times and it was thrown out yet not destroyed, and by this I know it is not mine to keep. Now I bring it to you, Master, to be joined again with the first two. Guang received it and unrolled it, and saw written at the top that Emperor Wu had bestowed it upon the great being's disciple Jingguang for his support. Thus he understood why the man had been dumbfounded before: he was astonished that the names were the same. In the twelfth month of the first year of Taichang, Jingguang came to Mount Kuang to receive the precepts and told the whole story of these causes and conditions. When I heard it I found it most strange. The great being's responsive bodies are beyond measure, yet each appeared once and then transformed away; only in the form of the monk Baozhi did he manifest at length and become ever more renowned. At first Emperor Wu commanded Zhang Sengyou to paint the great being's true likeness, and though he tried again and again it was never a true likeness. The great being then split the skin of his face with his fingernail and revealed the appearance of the great being Avalokiteśvara, and so it was known that he was a transformation body. The records say that in his lifetime he often came and went between Qianshan and Lake Tai, but I have never heard that he was at Yangshan. When the great being entered cessation, Emperor Wu made a shrine of two clay jars and buried him on the sunny side of Mount Zhong. When our August Ancestor fixed the capital at Jiankang, he himself divined a resting place in that mountain and settled it from above; digging the earth, they found the clay jars. Opening them, they saw the flesh body as if alive, with hair and nails grown full, and a tablet held in its hand inscribed: Baozhi of the Liang. Our August Ancestor marveled greatly at it and moved the burial to Linggu on the eastern side of the mountain, building a stupa and monastery to honor it. He set up an image in Jiming Monastery within the city and established spring and autumn sacrifices using dough in place of living victims, a rite of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices that continues to this day unaltered. Who would have said that amid the wild brush and brambles of Yangshan he would emit light and display auspicious signs, showing that the perfected one's responsive transformations have no fixed place and are wondrous beyond reckoning. I have traced the causes and conditions of the three portraits. Of the first two, one is the title of investiture granted in his lifetime, and the other is Emperor Wu's encomium after his death; both must be from Zhang Sengyou's hand. The inscription on the last one bears an edict in golden characters recording that after the great being's death Emperor Wu longed for him and bestowed one hundred and eight thousand taels of silver, commanding Wu Shiliang, Vice Minister of Works, together with the August Master's disciple Jingguang, to build and enshrine them in succession. He also ordered three pictures to be engraved in a single block: the plan of the hall, Emperor Wu's own visit to offer incense, and the great being preaching the precepts to his ministers. Only two prints were permitted, one kept in the palace for offerings and one bestowed on the great being's disciple, Chan Master Jingguang, who was also granted fields, though the place is not recorded. Thus these three portraits were originally not in one place. Yet from the Liang to the founding of our dynasty is more than a thousand years; what survived was not all of one piece. How then could the elders of Yangshan have heard of them and known of them? This is the first wonder. Moreover, in a thousand years and more, through changes of dynasty and the chaos of war and fire beyond counting, public and private holdings scattered and shifting without constancy, how did the three portraits come at last into the imperial treasury entirely undamaged? This is the second. The Bao'en stupa was built between the Yongle and Xuande eras; would its deposit have lacked other treasures, that the three portraits should be placed in the air of it? And once the portraits were on the summit of the stupa, how could the elders of Yangshan have known of it and carried the tale down to this day? This is the third. But the portraits being set on the stupa top, there was no further reason for them ever to be seen among men again. Why then did the restoration of Yangshan fall exactly at the time of repairing the stupa? This is the fourth. Even if the portraits came out of the stupa, had one fallen into another's hand, what hope would Yangshan have had? Who could have expected that the stonemason would be a man of that very commandery? This is the fifth. Though the portraits were gathered in Xin'an and the two younger sons did return theirs to the mountain, had the eldest not met with three fires, there would still have been no day of reunion. This is the sixth. And the portraits began in the great being's lifetime, while those from after his death came back in due order; the practice ground was completed and the pictures then appeared. Had the name of Jingguang been different, there would have been no way to awaken the eldest son's faith. This is the seventh. Therefore when I heard it I found it most strange, and my sighs of wonder would not cease. It shows that the perfected one hides his form to benefit beings: the dharmakāya is clear and still, pervading the ten directions without division, enduring the three calamities without ruin, passing through a thousand ages without fading, forever dwelling on gray cliffs and stone walls to arouse the roots of goodness in the heedless. The Buddhist monasteries of Xin'an rose to prominence at Yangshan; the jewel of the Saṅgha first appeared in Master Xuan, and the complete return of Master Baozhi's portraits came about through Masters Yu and Jue and the descendants of Jingguang, on the day the brahma monastery was made new. Is any of this not the power of my great being's ever-abiding dharmakāya and the gathering embrace of his compassion and awe-inspiring spirit? I have therefore set it down in full to make it known forever, so that those who see it may, through the causes and conditions of the three portraits, understand the wonder of the great being's responses and be moved to arouse faith and continue the life of wisdom.
Stele Inscription on the Restoration of the Sixth Patriarch's Ordination Platform at Guangxiao Chan Monastery in Guangdong, with Preface

When the Buddha's Dharma entered China, the teachings came west on a white horse, traveling by land to Luoyang; Chan crossed the vast seas and came by water to Wuyang. Was it not that the single vein of the ocean of the nature flows secretly beneath the great earth? In the Jin dynasty the Elder Yaśas came by foreign ship to Xiancheng, built a brahma monastery, and planted terminalia trees until they formed a grove, which is why it was called Helin, the Terminalia Grove. In the Song dynasty Guṇabhadra brought the four fascicles of the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra and stayed at Helin, where he established an ordination platform within the grove. His prophecy said: Later there will be a great being in a flesh body who will transmit the precepts at this place. In the Putong era of the Liang, the Indian master Tripiṭaka Zhiyue brought a bodhi tree and planted it beside the platform, recording: After one hundred and seventy years a person of great wisdom will leave home here. Then our Master, the Sixth Patriarch, received the robe and bowl at Huangmei and had his head shaved beneath the bodhi tree, exactly fulfilling the prophecy. He then followed Vinaya Master Zhiguang and ascended Guṇabhadra's platform, receiving the complete and perfect precepts, and afterward returned to Caoxi. The Chan school truly has its source from this. The precepts are the root of becoming a Buddha. When the Master opened the teaching at Caoxi, he took the ordination platform as his fundamental ground, and his disciples came and went within it; hence the monks of this monastery today all issue from the robe and bowl. For a thousand years the incense and lamps have been offered as though he were living, yet the workings of nature shift in secret and the ways of the world are no longer as of old. In time the monks did not know there were precepts, and men did not know there was a platform; the pure ground of awakening became a fox's den. As the years passed it changed hands several times. In the spring of the bingshen year of Wanli, I received imperial grace and was banished beyond the seas, and I opened the teaching amid the fortifications. Beneath the trees I had several tens of disciples, Tongjiong and Chaoyi among them, all of whom received instruction from me, and many of the scholar-officials' sons also came to take refuge. Seven years later, in the renyin year, the disciples gathered and sighed, saying: The ordination platform is the fundamental ground of our Patriarch; how can we bear to sit by and watch it sunk in ruin and overgrown? Jiong and Yi gathered funds and materials, and the layman Wang Anshun and others joined together in counsel and redeemed a corner of the platform's foundation, and within less than a year the work was completed. Eight years after I left Wuyang, Yi grew old on Mount Kuang; Jiong and Yi followed me in my wanderings without ever leaving my side, just as when they dwelt beneath the trees. One day the two of them bowed and requested, saying: The causes and conditions of the ordination platform depended on you, Master, from first to last. You are old, Master; we beg a word from you to record it. I spoke to them, saying: Within the ocean of the Dharma-nature there is fundamentally no emerging or perishing; in the land of everlasting quiescent light, how could there be coming or going? The changes of the human world follow their course; the purity or defilement of a Buddha-land accords with the mind. This is what is meant by the Way depending on men to spread it and the Dharma responding to the capacities of beings. This is a chance of a thousand years in a single hour, raising up the ruined and glorifying what came before, and there will surely be those who meet it without prior arrangement. How do we know that those who revive it now were not the people of old, and that those who come hereafter are not the assembly of today? This is the Buddha-seed arising from conditions, undimmed through kalpas of dust, lamp passing to lamp in unending continuity. Thereupon he made this inscription, saying:

The great sea flows hidden beneath,
throughout the lands of the four continents.
The single vein of Chan
came from the south to this place.
Then there appeared a perfected one;
the Terminalia Grove was first opened.
The ordination platform was founded
to await the coming of the Sage.
Bodhi is no tree,
yet its root is planted in the precepts.
The Buddha-seed arises from conditions,
and depends upon branch and leaf.
One hundred and seventy years —
the prophecy was not in vain.
He came forth from the hunting band
to nurture this planting stock.
The robe appeared,
and hair and beard fell away of themselves.
Splendid true response,
his radiance shining clear.
One peal of the Dharma thunder,
and the Dharma rain pours down in torrents.
It moistens and enriches the great thousand worlds,
making branch and bough grow again.
The shade it spreads is dense,
and those who gather grow ever more.
Sage and common are not divided,
dragons and snakes are mixed together.
When branch and bough are broken,
the root is no longer firm.
And so upon this adamantine ground
fox and hare take shelter.
The great cycle turns,
and nothing that goes fails to return.
The people of old came in due time;
restore to me my former things.
The jeweled palm opens once,
and they are taken as from a bag.
The Dharma banner is raised again,
and this Way shines forth anew.
Leaves fall and return to the root;
when he came, he had no mouth.
Truly it is our Patriarch
who cut open his own mind.
Now that this platform is restored,
it is like gold from the ore.
To the end of future ages
this mind will be transmitted.
Space itself may perish,
but the mind's light is undimmed.
Only this practice ground —
thus it is, thus it is.
Record of the Stele of the Practice and Conduct of Master Daguang Yue of Shuangfeng Reception Monastery in Wuchang Prefecture

Chu is a great metropolis south of the Han, standing at the crossroads of the empire and on the necessary route of wandering monks with their bowls and staffs who come and go among the four great sacred mountains. Formerly there was no place to rest, and so on the long road, in wind and rain, hunger and cold, who would take thought for them? Had Master Yue not given away body and life, how could such a wayside lodge have been made? The Master's courtesy name was Zhenyue, and he was a man of Fenyang in Jin. His surname was Yan; his father was Weishi and his mother of the Song family, who conceived him after an auspicious omen. At thirty he suddenly abandoned wife and children and went out beyond the world. He first went to Wudang and studied under the Bueri monk, who instructed him in the method of Buddha-recitation. He then had his head shaved and was named Zhenyue by imperial decree. He served as attendant only a short while before entering Baicaoping in Zhongnan, where he dwelt on rock, eating greens and drinking water, sitting facing the wall for nine years without any awakening. Then he left the mountain and went on pilgrimage, traveling everywhere and seeking instruction from teachers for twenty-two years. He went again to the Demon-taming Ground at Funiu, where he sat in a long seven-week session, and at this point his mind had a breakthrough. He then sought confirmation from masters everywhere. In the yiwei year of Wanli he came to Tanxi in Xiangyang and met the monk Wuwen, whose minds were mutually attuned, and who gave him the courtesy name Daguang; at that time he took refuge with him. The Master considered that his practice had not yet reached true substance, and so he sat three more seven-day fasts and went a full year without eating rice. Afterward he followed his teacher to worship at Putuo. In the dingyou year he came to Wuchang, and seeing monks of all quarters coming and going with nowhere to lodge, he resolved to build a place of reception. Taking up his bowl, he went about begging until he came below Shuangfeng at the eastern wall of the city, where there was an old monastery wholly ruined, with only the image of the white-robed great being buried in mud and earth. The Master grieved a long while, then called the name and prayed, vowing to restore it. Thereupon he sat in the wild brush without food for fourteen days, fainting and reviving, and then kept a water fast for a hundred days. Those who saw his utter sincerity were all stirred and shaken. The Master disciplined himself most strictly, willingly content with the plain and meager, sharing every grain of rice and every stalk of vegetable with the community, receiving people without weariness, and dealing with offerings and profits so that cause and effect were plainly clear and not a hair's breadth awry. The benefactors of that region trusted and honored him more each day, and in less than ten years he had made a monastery. In the summer of the bingchen year I was going from Nanyue to Shuangjing and lay at anchor on the river, where I saw how he conducted himself, dignified and utterly sincere, and I believed he was indeed one in whom the four assemblies could take refuge. I have read the Avataṃsaka Sūtra and know that the bodhisattva's benefiting of beings is not of one kind only, but that all is done with a vast and profound mind that regards others as oneself: taking the body as the great earth to bear up beings, taking the body as a bridge to ferry beings across, even to head, eyes, marrow, and brain without stint, through a hundred thousand kalpas without weariness. At first I was astonished; in the end I believed it to be true practice. The reason beings forever lie in birth and death is that they take a self, and this is the obstruction. The bodhisattva who saves beings must first save himself; when the self is saved, beings are saved of themselves. Once self and others are empty, the realm of beings is exhausted; and when the realm of beings is exhausted, where can affliction and karmic fruit take their stand? There is no accomplishing of wondrous practice beyond this. All causes and fruits of sage and common are established depending on mind and perfected according to vow; when the mind is empty and the vow firm, they appear at the very moment of thought. The adornment of the Pure Land is fundamentally no outside matter. A man like the Master began with a life as tenuous as a single thread, bound it to a vow, and at last accomplished such vast Buddha-work — was this not building from emptiness? Seen in this light, these conditioned and phantom causes and conditions are hardly enough to exhaust the measure of the Dharma-realm. Yet one may taste a drop and know the great ocean, glimpse a crack and see the great void; by this there is a way to know the Master. Moved by his conduct, I have recorded it to be cut into firm stone, as encouragement for those of the Dharma gate who come hereafter.
Record of the Restoration of Changqing Monastery on Buddha Hall Mountain in Duchang County

Some seventy li east of the seat of Duchang County there is a mountain named Buddha Hall, a place of surpassing wonder. On it is a monastery named Changqing, first founded in the Tang. Chan Master Leng of Changqing passed here and transformed the place, and so it became a famous monastery. It continued down to the Yuan dynasty, when it was destroyed in war, and for a long time it lay waste as private property. In the jiyou year of Wanli of our Ming, a monk named Xingnian came wandering here and, seeing the purity and wonder of the mountain setting, resolved to restore it. Thereupon the Liu family of Tangxi donated their foundation garden, and the Liu family of Tangshan gave materials and gathered workmen, and a small monastery was first built as a place for retreat and cultivation. Four years later, in the renzi year, Nian invited the Dharma-grandson of Chan Master Daguan, Master Guyu Zhuo, and took him as his teacher. The Master devoted himself wholly to rebuilding, leading his disciples Xingting and others in bitter effort and tireless strength, soliciting donations to assist the work. Presently the Master's father and his younger brother, who had long practiced Confucianism, suddenly aroused the mind that leaves the world and gave away the whole of their family wealth, several hundred pieces of gold, to aid the adornment, and so the practice ground was completed. Buddha hall, Chan hall, refectory kitchen, and mountain gate were all made complete. Afterward both the Master's father and brother shaved their heads and donned the black robes. His father was named Benneng, courtesy name Xuenan; his brother was named Dazhe, courtesy name Anxing. Together they cultivated the pure karma with diligence, and those who took refuge with Master Zhuo grew more numerous by the day. Xingmin, You, Gan, Zhong, Mao, Min, Xiang, and others were all his disciples, and all had a part in the work. When the monastery was finished, I was at Mount Kuang, and Master Zhuo came to consult me on the essentials of the Dharma. He still delighted in dwelling alone, and cutting thatch he built a hut below Wulao Peak at Shiziyan, within sight of the features of Wuru. From time to time he was able to come and pay his respects. One day he took up incense, bowed, and told me the whole story of the causes and conditions, begging me to write a record. I sighed deeply and said: The whole Dharma-realm arises from conditions. Therefore it is said, all dharmas are born when conditions meet. Being born when conditions meet, before that they did not exist; not existing before, their arising is fundamentally nonexistent. Worldly and world-transcending dharmas are all like this. Thus we know that the great earth and its mountains and rivers are all the one true Dharma-realm, and that everywhere is nothing but a practice ground; it depends only on whether conditions meet or not. Before Changqing came to this mountain, its wondrous peaks and sheer ravines held only dense grass and brush, the cry of gibbons and cranes, and serpents and tigers ranging at will. But once Changqing passed by, a Dharma banner was at once set up, so that those who saw or heard, gazed or paid reverence, straightway aroused the mind of unsurpassed bodhi; and all the sounds of mountain forest and grass and trees became the mark of the broad and long tongue, proclaiming the Dharma of no-birth and non-duality. When conditions scattered and it perished, it was again as in the time before Changqing came. Now the rising of this practice ground began with Xingnian, met its conditions through Master Zhuo, and was brought to completion truly through the father and son of the Xue family. Was the meeting of one family a small condition? The sūtra says, the mind of thought congealed becomes a land. Those who now restore, those who give, those who assist, those who lend their strength in between — unless they shared one adamantine mind-ground, how could they have straightway accomplished so imperishable a wonder, so that mountain forest and grass and trees together gave forth light, surpassing the cultivation of former times to such a degree? May those who dwell and guard here hereafter understand the mind that established it, so that every blade of grass and every leaf becomes a diamond seed; then in this mountain and this ground the sound of pines and the echo of springs will all proclaim the Dharma, forever a bodhi practice ground, and morning bell and evening chant will forever invoke blessings on the imperial longevity without bound. How then could such an establishment be measured by the leaky standards of gods and men? I have therefore recounted its causes and conditions from beginning to end, to make them clear to those who come after.
Record of the Permanent Community of the Reception Monastery in Wujiang

The Flower Adornment Sutra declares: Vairocana's body pervades the whole dharma-realm, adorned by the practices of wisdom and compassion. In our land of China the three mountains of Wutai, Emei, and Putuo are the fields where the three great beings gather and transform living beings; throughout the realm, all men and women of understanding turn their hearts to them as to treasure-grounds. Of these, the Southern Sea is both near and easy to reach, so monks of the ten directions come and go in an unbroken stream, endless as a thread. Yet on the road they grow weary, and without a conjured city in which to rest awhile there is no way to relieve their hunger, thirst, and toil. The provision of reception is therefore the foremost and most excellent of practices. Wujiang is a thoroughfare and ferry-crossing between north and south, and the Reception Monastery stands right at its pivotal point. The monastery was founded in the Shaoxi era of the Song, when the monk Jizhao opened the mountain and its plaque read Chengtian Wanshou. In the Zhizheng era of the Yuan the monk Zhengshou enlarged and repaired it, and it was renamed Jiedai, Reception. At the beginning of the Wanli era the monk Liaokong reopened the Reception Cloister. The Minister Lu Wutai, the Censor Shen Taisu, the lay benefactor Wu and others donated funds to build the Chan hall and to establish a perpetual community of the ten directions. After Liaokong, the Venerable Wubian Hai succeeded him, and in the gengxu year Hai passed away. The gentry and lay devotees of the county then invited the Venerable Nianyun Qin to dwell there. Qin was a dharma-grandson of Chan Master Daguan and the foremost disciple of the Venerable Micang Kai. Since the Chan master had long taught and transformed beings here, the dharma affinity was the ripest; the Venerable Qin was upright and firm in conduct, no disgrace to his lineage, and the whole region esteemed him. The monastery flourished day by day. Mindful that the aged of the dharma gate had nowhere to turn, he established the two halls of Retirement and Long Life and built a common stupa — the most excellent practice of compassion. The various dharma-protectors, planning for the long term, established perpetual fields, reckoned at three hundred and sixty mu a year, so that the monastery had lasting property with which to provide for those who came. When the conditions were complete, they urged the Venerable to send a letter asking me for a record, saying: Since ancient times in the monastic community it is not the founding that is hard, but the keeping of the inheritance. Because the Buddha taught the bodhisattva to take benefiting others as his sole task, Baizhang established the pure regulations: whatever belongs to the sangha within the monastery — down to a hair's breadth — is all set apart for the permanent community of the ten directions, not to be likened to the property of worldly heirs. How stern are its precepts! It is said that the goods of the sangha of the ten directions are like deadly poison: no sooner does one touch them than the whole body breaks out in sores — the strongest way of saying that one must not lightly lay a finger on them. One grain of rice or a stalk of greens one dares not take privately; how much less when it is much. The seeker's first intention was from the outset for the sake of the sangha, and the donor's resolve was at root a seed in the field of merit. The Buddha said that one who eats such food, if he be not a good field, will not escape the suffering of repaying it with his own body — how much more if he feeds the poison of greed and nourishes the karma of the hells? These are the clear and unfailing workings of cause and effect; should one not feel a chill at heart? As for the founding of this place of practice: had the Venerable Qin's heart not been all-embracing, this work could never have been accomplished; and those who guard it hereafter, if their hearts be not like his, will surely be unable to continue the thread. But if they keep themselves pure and exert all their strength to uphold the Buddha's precepts, then for the cloud-and-water wanderers who come and go the hungry will eat, the weary rest, the sick be eased, the aged have repose, and the dead find a home: is this not an everlasting field of merit, a ford and bridge across the sea of suffering? If one discerns the minutest hair and is not blind to cause and effect, one guards it with Mañjuśrī's great wisdom. Keeping it and never losing it, practicing it without weariness, one has Samantabhadra's great practice. To aid and save without end and let the field of compassion grow ever wider is Avalokiteśvara's great compassion. With these three complete as cause, one perfects the fruit of Vairocana's dharmakāya. This is the wondrous practice of attaining buddhahood; there is nothing beyond it. Why then need one climb mountains and ford rivers, seek far and wide among the wise, and look elsewhere for a mysterious and wonderful buddhadharma? In past years, when I traveled east to mourn Master Daguan, I lodged there for two nights and learned of the Venerable Qin's discipline of mind and conduct. Marvelling that this merit is the most excellent of all, I have written this account in full.
Record of the Universal Deliverance Hermitage

East of Panyu lies Nanshawan, the old home village of Li Zhongjian, a prime minister of the Song. Its clan is the largest there, with more than ten thousand households. The layman Li Yizhen, courtesy name Yanzhou, studied the classics in his youth but found no sale for his talents. He often reflected that human life is illusory and that men merely bustle to no purpose, and he sought a way to escape suffering. Arousing his mind toward the Way, he took refuge in the Three Jewels. Coming upon Longshu's Pure Land Essays, he sighed: “This is a compass for one who has lost his way.” Then he obtained Yunqi's commentary on the Amitābha Sutra and read it over and over, believing the more firmly and without doubt. He vowed to keep a perpetual fast, to embroider Buddha images, to shut out all family ties, and to devote himself single-mindedly to the pure karma — for three years now. Reflecting that the dharma gate is vast and takes universal deliverance as its heart, he built a monastery, enshrined an image of the Great Being Avalokiteśvara, and named it Pudu, Universal Deliverance. He wished that old and young of his village might each arouse a heart of sympathetic joy and together knit the bond of escape from suffering; this was no idle gesture. When I first arrived at Caoxi, the layman came from afar to pay his respects and asked me to write a record of it. Hearing this, I praised him, saying: Excellent! This is a vast and great heart. This Buddha-nature is equally endowed in sage and commoner and is shared by every wriggling, sentient thing. But being deluded they do not awaken; though they use it daily, they do not know it. They turn this Buddha-nature into delusive thought and commit greed, hatred, and delusion, killing, stealing, lust, and falsehood — all manner of evil karma — and so bring upon themselves the acute suffering of the three evil paths; for hundreds, thousands, and millions of kalpas there is no way out. Consider, for instance, killing other living beings and taking their flesh and blood to feed one's mouth and belly: in the space of a single meal, within a single bowl, hundreds and thousands of lives are destroyed. If one reckons the repayment, cause and effect never fail: the karma of a single day already draws down the suffering of hundreds, thousands, and millions of lives — how much more all that is done in a lifetime? The single karma of killing is already boundless; how much more the many karmas. Accumulated karma, deep and wide, is what we call the sea of suffering. If there be no boat to ferry one across, how shall one ever reach the other shore? Truly this is pitiable. Therefore the buddhas and bodhisattvas, in compassion for the deluded, appear in the world and manifest in various bodies to save them. Our Avalokiteśvara, the Great Being, with his thirty-two responsive manifestations, appears according to kind: in whatever body one should be saved, in that body he appears and speaks the dharma, causing them to escape suffering. Seen in this light, the layman's heart is the Great Being's heart; to save living beings with compassion is to be the Great Being's responsive body. The people dwelling here number no fewer than a hundred thousand; if through this hermitage they attain deliverance, then the buddhadharma will have transformed one village. Extending and enlarging this, joining village to village and town to town, reaching the great cities, it will spread through the whole realm and on to all under heaven; and if everyone were to forsake evil and turn toward good, all would become the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Then this foundation of Universal Deliverance is but a single leaf of the genial spring. All men share this same heart; would not any who see, hear, and rejoice leap to follow it? This too is a great matter and a weighty cause. This is the record.
Record of the Golden Lotus Hermitage in Ningdu

Ningdu in Zhanggong lies where three provinces meet, a region of deep mountains and waters. Forty li west of the county town stands the highest of the mountains, called Lotus Peak. Winding down from it, a single ridge rises abruptly, called Precious Peak; its woods are dense and luxuriant, clear springs wind about it like a girdle, and a thousand peaks encircle it in green — truly a place of the highest excellence. The site is high and broad. Long before, the elders told, several golden lotuses suddenly appeared there, and it was known that a place of practice might be made of it. In the dingwei year of the Wanli era the Venerable Ruxiao, loving its seclusion, built a hermitage upon it and gave it the plaque Golden Lotus. One day the Venerable fell ill and, in a daze like a dream, suddenly saw all the varied appearances of the hells, which in a moment turned into the realm of the Western Pure Land. Awakening, he sighed: “Heavenly palaces and hells are but transformations wrought by good and evil according to one's own mind.” Thereupon he made a great vow, resolved earnestly on cultivation, and devoted himself to reciting the great Avataṃsaka Sutra day and night with unflagging diligence. By this the whole region was moved and transformed. In the winter of the gengshen year, my fourth year dwelling at Mount Kuang, the Venerable came with the Venerable Nanming Dao to visit me and asked for a few words to record the matter. I said to them: Mountains, rivers, and the great earth — wherever the eye falls is a place of practice; the Pure Land and this Sahā world change with the mind. So the ancients, picking up a single blade of grass, would found a monastery; how much more one who raises halls and monks' quarters with all things complete. This truly is founded from the vajra mind. Yet just as one mind can turn thorns into a precious monastery, it can also turn a place of practice into a sea of karma. If those who guard it hereafter can embody the founder's mind, and within it diligently purify the three karmas and make single-minded purity their aim, then this place is made of solid vajra, forever enduring, unmoved and undestroyed. But if, taking their dwelling as they please and the four requisites as ready to hand, they give free rein to body and mind and pursue worldly affairs, until outside insults invade and the permanent community is damaged, that is to trade the kāṣāya for horns and fur, to exchange a precious land for the hells. Should one not fear this? Liaoci's secular surname was Liao, a prominent family of the county. He left home at eighteen, and his dharma name was Ruxiao. His disciples, so-and-so and others, joined in recording it.
The Releasing-Life Society of Xingjiao Monastery in Yangzhou Prefecture Builds the Pavilion of the Welcoming and Guiding Buddha

Yangzhou is a great metropolis of the southeast. The founding of the dharma gate there began when Xie An of the Jin gave up his residence to make a monastery and invited the Venerable Buddhabhadra to translate the Avataṃsaka Sutra; hence it was called Xiao Xingyan. While the Venerable was translating, two youths were moved to bring water every day; when asked, they said they were dragon descendants. From this the place of practice first flourished. Through succeeding ages it was renamed Xingjiao. In the Jiajing and Longqing eras my late master, the monk Wuji, spread the dharma in Jiangnan, and scholars from all quarters came and went. The chief seat, the Venerable Baotang Zhang, hung up his staff here. Zhang's dharma-grandson, the Venerable Lingyi Deng, went to study under my late dharma-brother Xuelang and cultivated pure karma with diligence; for a time the gentry of the region esteemed him. Thus he drew them into the practice of compassion, and they formed a society for Buddha-recitation and releasing life, meeting on the eighth day of each month. They built the Pavilion of the Welcoming and Guiding Buddha to show that there is a place to which the heart may return, hoping to hand on the teaching forever. They asked me for a record. Hearing this I praised it, saying: This is what our Buddha established — the most excellent practice of benefiting self and others. I have heard that Buddha means the awakened; it is the nature of knowing awareness that we human beings inherently possess. Above, it is shared with the buddhas; below, it extends to all living beings — equally bestowed and commonly endowed. Pei Xiu said: All that has blood and breath must have awareness, and whatever has awareness must share one substance — that which is called true, pure, wondrous, and luminous, empty and penetrating, spiritually unobstructed, standing alone and self-abiding. This nature, when undeluded, is Buddha; deluded, it becomes a human being; inverted, it becomes a creature. Our Buddha alone realized this; pitying beings who are deluded, he appeared in the world to open and reveal it universally, so that they might awaken and enter. Of the many gates of skillful means, Buddha-recitation is the simplest and most direct. Yet reciting the Buddha's name is nothing else than calling upon the Buddha innate in one's own nature. One awakened thought is one Buddha; when every thought is awake, every thought is Buddha. If one is always awake and never benighted, then one is a permanently abiding Buddha. In the work of self-benefit there is nothing beyond this. Yet when one is oneself awakened, one pities others still deluded. As for the flying, the swimming, the crawling, and the wriggling, how can they be made to awaken themselves? Therefore one extends the compassion of shared substance to pull them up and relies on the Buddha's true kindness to gather them in; and so one recites the Buddha's name many times on behalf of many living beings. Yet each life released is a Buddha accomplished. Thus in a flash one causes the living beings born from womb, egg, moisture, and transformation — countless, numberless, boundless — to all enter nirvāṇa without residue; and in truth not one living being attains deliverance. Is this not then the most excellent practice of the two benefits? So it is that by my vow, relying on the Buddha's power, the image of the Welcoming and Guiding One is set up and a pavilion built to enshrine it, so that those who see, hear, and rejoice may, with a single gaze and a single bow, arouse the heart of universal salvation. Then the compassion of shared substance grows ever wider and the true seed of buddhahood ever deeper. Such merit — how could it be conceived or discussed? This is the record.
Record of the Permanent Community of the Reception Hermitage at Beihaitai in Gaoyou Prefecture

The three great beings manifest throughout the ten directions to deliver all living beings universally, and there is no place they do not reach. In our land of China, three famous mountains serve as the permanently abiding places of practice of their dharmakāya. Emei lies secluded in western Shu, far off in a corner; only Wutai and Putuo face each other north and south and are the places of resort for the monks of the ten directions. On the roads they come and go in an unbroken thread. Where the Huai and the Yang meet, in the region of Gaoyou, beside the Grand Canal, the county stands cut off midway; the cloud-and-water wanderers who pass through have no pause for their feet. The road is long and the traveler weary; the day darkens and the way runs out. In windy mornings and rainy evenings, treading snow and walking on ice, bodies still subject to outflows, pressed by hunger and thirst, tormented in the flesh — such cases cannot be counted. The pilgrimage wanderers with none to turn to are not one person on one day. There was a layman, Lu Hong, who resolved to build a reception hermitage as a place of rest. Fearing that provision would not be constant, he gathered donations and bought one hundred and eighty mu of land, using its yield to fill the alms-bowls. So the black-robed monks who come and go — the weary find rest, the hungry food, the thirsty drink — and those who arrive feel as though returning home. This is the foremost and most excellent field of merit in the human world. I am passing my old age in retirement at Mount Kuang. The layman came to take refuge and asked me to write a record. Gladly I spoke to him, saying: All living beings cling to the notion of a self and think only of benefiting themselves. Though it be a blade of grass or a thread of a leaf, they look on it as a nine-tripod cauldron, and all their plans are for their descendants. Who can harbor a single thought of benefiting and aiding others? Only our Buddha taught the bodhisattva's great heart, which takes benefiting others as its sole task. Of the six pāramitās he practices, giving is the first. What he gives is of three grades: outer, inner, and uttermost. The outer is wealth and goods; the inner is body and life; the uttermost leaves nothing remaining. Unless one's selflessness is complete, who can do this? In this age of the dharma's decline living beings have slender merit and grow daily more miserly and greedy; this practice is hard. Yet if one can extend a single thought to this, one is a bodhisattva of the great heart. I say the three grades of giving are all one mind. Since living beings regard wealth as their life, to give up wealth is to give up life. If the greedy mind is not exhausted, not a hair can be pulled out; but once the mind of renunciation arises, it is uttermost, leaving nothing behind. Yet mind, Buddha, and living beings — these three are without distinction. So a single thought of renunciation fills the whole measure of the dharma-realm and becomes the substance of buddhahood. It can cause the rejoicing thought of the receiver to enter the dharma-realm as well. Thus this mind, the Buddha, and the realm of living beings are all equal. This is why giving is the root of attaining buddhahood. If one can use this mind of renunciation to benefit beings, thought after thought without interruption, then in every thought one attains buddhahood together with all living beings. The great sutra says: “I now accomplish perfect enlightenment within the minds of all living beings” — it is for this reason. Thus the bodhisattva's myriad practices are gathered into the six pāramitās, and giving is made their dhāraṇī. Because the heart is great and the deed hard to perform, the virtue is broad and the benefit great. Thus Mañjuśrī's wisdom, Samantabhadra's practice, and Avalokiteśvara's compassion all equal the dharma-realm, for they carry the selfless mind to its utmost. So this hermitage, though small, contains the whole dharma-realm, and the three great beings permanently abide within it. Its merit and benefit — how could they be conceived or discussed? Therefore I gave the layman the name Field of Merit, to mark his practice. This is the record.
The Dream Roaming Collection of Old Man Hanshan, Volume Twenty-Seven
Stūpa Inscription for Chan Master Daguan Ke of Jingshan

In this great earth of birth and death, men lie benighted through the long night; the gate of feeling is fast shut, the lock of consciousness is hard to open. For one to spring up and shatter it with a single blow, to shake off his sleeves and go on alone — unless he be a fierce and mighty man, one whose measure transcends the world, this is not easily attained. Looking back over the elders of the Transmission of the Lamp, they were all such men. And now I have seen such a one in Chan Master Daguan. The master's personal name was Zhenke; his style, Daguan; in later years he took the sobriquet Zibo. His disciples called him the Venerable — out of reverence for the Dharma. His forebears were men of Gouqu; his father, Shen Lian, lived for generations at Wujiang, on the bank of Lake Tai where the shore breaks away. The master was his youngest son. His mother dreamed that a stranger gave her a great fresh peach with its leaves still on it; she woke to find the room full of fragrance, and so conceived. When the master was born he did not speak until he was five. A strange monk came to their gate, stroked his crown, and said to his father, “If this child leaves home, he will be a teacher of gods and men.” With that he suddenly vanished, and the master could speak. Before that, huge footprints had appeared in the courtyard; from then on they were seen no more. In his boyhood his nature was fierce and bold, generous and ardent; his countenance was grand and unlike other boys'; young as he was he had no taste for play. From birth he disliked the sight of women and would not let them bathe before him. One day his elder sister by mistake went in to bathe ahead of him, and the master flew into a rage. Thereafter even female relatives dared not come near him. As he grew, his resolve grew greater day by day; his parents could not restrain him. He once wrote in a poem, “The bold heart of a dog-butcher is not easily quenched” — a true record of himself. At seventeen he was bearing a sword on a long journey to the frontier. Coming to the Chang Gate of Suzhou, he was strolling in the marketplace when a great rain fell. He met the monk Mingjue of Huqiu; each looked at the other, and Mingjue, struck by his powerful bearing, sheltered him with his umbrella. So they went back to the monastery together, where supper was set out and they rejoiced greatly. Hearing the monks chant the names of the eighty-eight buddhas by night, his heart was filled with joy. Toward dawn he went into Mingjue's room and said, “You and I have a great treasure — why defile it in here?” He untied the money at his waist, more than ten pieces of gold, and gave it to Mingjue, having him set out a feast and ask that his head be shaved. So he took Mingjue as his master, and that night sat upright until dawn. Often he would murmur to himself with a sigh, “Looked at, there is no flesh; eaten, it has savor.” Mingjue wished to collect ten thousand catties of iron to cast a great bell. The master said, “I will help you.” So he went to a great house at Pinghu and sat cross-legged outside the gate. The host offered food, but the master would not eat. Asked what he needed, he said, “Ten thousand catties of iron to cast a great bell; have it, and I will eat.” The host at once brought ten thousand catties of iron outside the gate. The master smiled, finished his meal, and had it carried straight back to Huqiu. On returning he shut his door and read, and for half a year did not cross the threshold. Seeing monks drink wine or eat meat, the master would say, “A man who has left home behaving like that deserves to be killed.” The monks all stood in awe of him. At twenty he received the full precepts from a lecturing master. He once went to Changshu and met the Grand Secretary Yan Yangzhai, who recognized him as a vessel of rare worth and kept him more than a month. He went to the East Pagoda Monastery in Jiaxing and saw a monk copying the Avataṃsaka Sutra. Kneeling, he watched for a long while and sighed, “If we could do that, it would be enough.” Then he went to Jingde Monastery at Wutang and sealed himself in retreat for three years. Returning to Wumen, he took leave of Mingjue, saying, “I must go and wander through the regions, calling on the teachers one by one, to settle the great matter.” And he set off with his staff. One day he heard a monk recite Zhang Zhuo's verse on seeing the Way: “To cut off delusive thought but adds to the sickness; to turn toward suchness is likewise perverse.” The master said, “That is wrong. It should be, ‘Only then is there no sickness; it is not perverse.’” The monk said, “You are wrong; he is not.” The master was thrown into great doubt. Everywhere he went he wrote the two lines on the wall, and his doubt grew until his face and head swelled. One day, in the midst of a meal, he suddenly awakened, and the swelling at once subsided. Thereafter he bestrode all the quarters. He once said, “Had I been under Linji or Deshan, one slap would have woken me. What need of all this how-so and what-so?” Passing Mount Kuang, he plumbed the profound meaning of the Faxiang school. Walking twenty li in a day, his feet hurt; so he rubbed the soles of his feet with stones until he could walk two hundred li a day, and then stopped. He traveled to Wutai and came to a sheer cliff and an empty crag, where an old monk sat alone. The master bowed and asked, “What is it when not a single thought has arisen?” The old monk raised one finger. He asked again, “And after it has arisen?” The old monk spread both hands. At these words the master grasped the purport; but when he sought the old monk's traces, the place was gone. He came to the capital and called on the great elder Bianrong. Bianrong asked where he had come from. “From Jiangnan,” he said. “And what have you come here to do?” “To study lecturing.” “And why study lecturing?” “To penetrate the meaning of the sutras and proclaim the Buddha's teaching in his stead.” Bianrong said, “You must expound the Dharma in purity.” The master said, “Even now I am unstained by a single mote of dust.” Bianrong ordered the master's robe to be stripped off and given to a monk beside him, then turned to the master and said, “Strip off one layer, and there is still another.” The master smiled and accepted it. He stayed on, lodging at the pagoda. He called at the gates of such worthies as the Dharma Master Xiaoyan and the great elders Xianli, and then departed. In the ninth year he returned to Huqiu to visit Mingjue. Then he went to Songjiang and kept retreat for a hundred days, and then to Wu County. Mr. Fu Guangzhai of Liaocheng was magistrate there; his son had sharp faculties, and he ordered the boy to pay his respects to the master. The boy was displeased. One day the boy held up two flowers and asked the master, “Is this one or two?” The master said, “It is one.” The boy opened his hand and said, “These flowers are two; why does the master say one?” The master said, “I speak of their root; you speak of their tips.” The boy then bowed. He went to Tianchi and met Mr. Guan Dongming, who, hearing his words, esteemed him deeply. The master then took up a rose with one stem and two blossoms and questioned him. The gentleman said, “These flowers are born of the same root.” The master separated them into two and questioned him again; the gentleman had no words. So he was made to stand a vegetarian feast, and thereafter they were fast friends. In the third year of the Emperor's reign, Master Darun of Daqian opened the hall at Shaolin. The master, with his friends Chaolin and Jieru and others, went to call upon him. When they arrived and he saw them mount the hall and lecture on kōans, taking mouth and ear for the mind-seal and a handkerchief for the true transmission, the master was ashamed of it and sighed, “Is the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West really like this?” So he did not join the assembly, and soon returned south. Coming to Jiahe, he met the Grand Minister Lu Wutai, and their hearts were in deep accord. Earlier there was one Mizang Daokai, a man of Nanchang, who had cast aside the scholar's gown, left home, and had his head shaved in the South Sea. Hearing of the master's manner, he came to take refuge with him. The master knew him to be a vessel of the Dharma and kept him as an attendant. The Surangama Monastery in the prefectural city was where Changshui had expounded the sutras; long in ruin, it had been encroached upon by a powerful man and made into a garden pavilion. The master wrote a poem to lament it: “A single wheel of bright moon, cold beyond the blind — / Deep in the night it once shone on the one who sat in Chan.” He resolved to restore it, and charged Master Daokai with the work, entrusting the Grand Minister with its protection as Dharma-patron. The Grand Minister's younger brother, Mr. Yuntai, donated the building of a Chan hall of five bays. When it was finished, the master was asked to write an inscription for its pillars, and he made this couplet: “If one does not investigate the mind, sitting in Chan only multiplies the suffering of karma; / If one can but guard the mindfulness, even reviling the Buddha still profits true cultivation.” Then he took an awl and pierced his arm, and wrote it in a bowlful of his blood. From then on he received and met those who came and went. More than twenty years later the prefect Cai Huaiting was at last able to restore it — upheld, surely, by the master's vow-power. Seeing the Dharma decline in this age of the semblance-dharma, the master made the spreading of the Dharma and the benefiting of beings his household business. Reflecting that the volumes of the Tripitaka were heavy and many, and that in far regions and remote corners there were those who would never so much as hear the name of the Buddha-Dharma, he wished to have it carved in the Fangce booklet format, so that it might easily circulate, so that all who saw or heard might plant the diamond seed; and should any slander it, he would bear the guilt himself. So he took counsel with the Grand Minister, with Feng Mengzhen the Director of the Directorate of Education, with Zeng Tongheng the Chief of the Court of Judicial Review, and with Qu Ruji the Chief of the Court of the Imperial Stud, and they resolved the matter, appointing Master Daokai to oversee the work. In the jiyou year of Wanli they began the carving at Wutai. After four years there, because of the bitter cold of ice and snow, they moved it to the Jizhao Hermitage on Jingshan. Once the work was under way, Master Daokai withdrew to hide away on account of illness. Those who continued and completed the task were his disciples Hanhui Ruqi, Ruqi's disciple Huanyu Benji, and the last disciple Danju Kai. At first Wu Yongxian of Tongcheng, then a bureau secretary in the Ministry of Rites, visited the master in his room, and in the course of talk the matter of carving the canon came up. The master said abruptly, “You have a great karmic bond with this Dharma.” After the master's passing, Mr. Wu went out to head the provincial administration of Zhejiang and, following the Director Feng's original proposal, restored Huacheng as a lower cloister of Jingshan, to store the printing blocks of the sutras. This was indeed due to Mr. Wu's power of faith, but it was also a prophecy the master had made beforehand. When the resolution to carve the canon at Jiahe was settled, the master returned to Wumen to visit Mingjue, the master who had ordained him. Mingjue had already returned to lay life and was known as a physician. Hearing that the master was coming, he was greatly intimidated. The master disguised himself as a merchant, lay stiff in a small boat, and asked Mingjue to examine him. Mingjue saw the master and was much startled. The master wept and said, “How has your delusion gone this far? What is to be done now?” Mingjue said, “Your command is my only law.” The master at once had him shaved and carried him away. Mingjue was ashamed and submitted, wishing to serve him with a disciple's reverence. On the day the master came, as Mingjue ate his evening meal, his rice bowl suddenly fell to the ground and shattered — such was the power of the master's sincerity. When the master first passed through Wujiang, the Shen and Zhou clans gathered their families and took refuge with him. At Qu'a and Jinsha, the He, Sun, Yu, and Wang clans brought their whole households to pay him homage. At Yuyuan the master copied the Lotus Sutra to repay his parents' kindness, and inscribed the place where he copied it “Ink-Light Pavilion,” which still stands. Hearing that Master Miaofeng was building an iron pagoda at Luya, he sent the sutra to be placed within the pagoda, and discussed with him the affairs of the canon. He returned to the capital, and came to visit me at the Eastern Sea. It was the seventh month of the autumn of the bingxu year of Wanli. Because of my connection with Wutai, word of me had reached the palace, and I had fled renown to the Narayana Cave by the Eastern Sea. The Empress Dowager Cisheng, to protect the imperial person and prolong the nation's fortune, had printed and distributed fifteen copies of the Tripitaka; the Emperor sent them down to the famous mountains of the realm, and the first reached the Eastern Sea. I went to Chang'an to give thanks for the favor. The master, taking Master Daokai with him, traveled along the coast and came to Jiaoxi, where the autumn waters had flooded and risen; the others judged that they could certainly not cross. The master stripped off his clothes and waded in first, calling urgently to the rest. The water was already at his shoulders, yet he leapt forward. Having crossed, he turned to his disciples and said, “At the pass of birth and death one must go straight through — that is what counts.” The hearts of all were filled with admiration. Hearing of it while in Chang'an, I hurriedly packed to return and traveled by double stages to Jimo. The master had already come out of the mountains and was at a monastery at the foot of the mountain; at dawn he was to set out. That night we met and laughed aloud for joy. At daybreak I asked him to return to the mountain with me. He stayed ten days, and our minds sealed in mutual accord. From then on the master took me as one who understood his words, and pledged me his friendship for life. The master returned to the capital and visited Shijing Mountain, bowing at the stūpa of Master Wan of the Sui. Reflecting that Master Wan, fearing that the three disasters would destroy the kalpa and the true Dharma be utterly extinguished, had begun to carve the canon in stone and store it in the rock caves, the master was moved by the depth of his resolve to protect the Dharma and wept tears like rain. The land of Master Wan's stūpa-cloister had already passed into the hands of the powerful; he vowed to recover it but did not succeed. So he resolved to journey west to Emei. Passing through the three Jin regions and across the Guanzhong plain, he crossed the plank roads into Shu, paid homage to Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, and went downriver through the Qutang Gorge. He passed Jing and Xiang, climbed Taihe, and came to Mount Kuang. He sought out the old site of Guizong Monastery, where there was only a single ancient pine. The monks had sold it for five pecks of rice and the masons were about to cut it down; a beggar, taking pity on it, begged the rice to redeem it, so that the monastery's trace might remain. The master heard of it and was moved. The tree's root had been hacked by woodcutters' axes and was about to break; the master laid stones and filled earth about it, and with mantras vowed that it might live again, as an omen by which to divine the monastery's restoration. Afterwards the tree grew daily, and the monastery was in the end restored. Such indeed was his vow-power. Xing Maoxue, a provincial graduate of Jiangzhou, invited him to stay at the Long Pine Lodge. The master gave Dharma talks there, which were titled “Long Pine Vegetarian Fare.” Zou Erzhan, Supervising Secretary, and Ding Shaoyuan, Assistant Administration Commissioner, urged him to reside at Mount Kuang, but it came to nothing, and he set out. Passing Anqing, Mr. Ruan Zihua invited him to visit Mazu Hermitage on Mount Wangong. The master delighted in the surpassing excellence of the place and had a monastery built there. The layman Zhao Woen of Jiangyin came to beg leave to leave home, and was shaved in the mountains; the master named him Fakai — the “last disciple” of whom I spoke. The master traveled north again to Tanzhe. The Empress Dowager Cisheng, hearing of his arrival, sent her close attendant Chen Ru with offerings of vegetarian food and specially bestowed on him a purple robe of the sanghati.
