The master firmly declined, saying: “I am ashamed that these poor bones can hardly wear the purple; / Give it to a man of high worth, and the merit will double.” Chen Ru accompanied the master to Yunju, where they paid homage to the stone sutras at Leiyin Monastery. They opened the stone chamber, and beneath the Buddha's seat found a golden casket containing three relics of the Buddha, whose light illumined the cliffs and ravines. So he asked that the relics be brought into the palace and offered for three days; then, with silver from the treasury, they were enshrined again in the stone cave. With the surplus of the Empress Dowager's feast-offering he redeemed Master Wan's stūpa, and then drew me along to visit and pay homage, asking me to write a record of it. Returning, he lodged at Cishou, and we stayed together in a garden in the western suburbs, conversing for forty days and nights without our eyelids meeting — truly the happiest event of my life. The old master Bianrong had already entered nirvāṇa; he wrote a piece mourning him, containing the phrase “he inherited the virtue but not the Dharma.” While at Tanzhe the master ordinarily ate only after bowing to the Buddha. One day a guest came and he mistakenly took a bite beforehand. So he said to the director of affairs, “Today someone has broken a precept; I order you to give him thirty hard blows. If they are light, you shall make them up.” The director was astonished and did not know who it was. Presently the master handed him the staff, prostrated himself on the ground, and received the full number of blows before the Buddha, until both his thighs were black as ink. Then he said, “The beginningless habitual tendencies of beings are like oil worked into dough — not to be broken by force. Unless the cutting away of feeling hurts, they are not easily tamed.” The master and I planned to compile a Transmission of the Lamp for our own dynasty. Because the Chan school had withered, I agreed with the master to go and dredge out Caoxi, to open the Dharma-lineage afresh. The master went ahead to Mount Kuang to wait. It was the seventh month of the autumn of the guisi year. Three years later, in the yiwei year, I had enshrined the Tripitaka granted by the Empress Dowager and completed the building of Haiyin Monastery. Through some other affair I incurred the Emperor's wrath, was summoned, arrested, and thrown into prison. Interrogated, I had nothing else to answer; by grace I was spared death and sent into exile at Leiyang, and my monastery was destroyed. Hearing the news at Mount Kuang, the master vowed to recite the Lotus Sutra a hundred times, hoping thereby to shield me from death. He went to inspect Caoxi and, on his return, was about to go to the capital to save me; then, hearing that I had been banished to the south, he waited for me on the riverbank. In the eleventh month of that year we met at the Traveler's Rest Hermitage at Xiaguan. The master took my hand and sighed: “You bear the great Dharma at the risk of death. The ancients, for the Dharma, had the hearts of Cheng Ying and Gongsun Chujiu. What man am I? If you do not return alive, I shall have no birthday to keep.” I consoled him again and again. As I was about to set out, the master charged me: “If I should die before you, my affairs are entrusted to you.” And so we parted for the last time. In the fifth year after I crossed the mountain passes, the gengzi year, the Emperor, for the building of the three halls, levied a tax on mines, and the eunuch commissioners were stationed at Hukou. Wu Baoxiu, the prefect of Nankang, impeached them and was arrested. His wife, in grief and rage, hanged herself. Hearing of it at Mount Kuang, the master said, “Affairs have come to this — what is to be done for the way of the world?” So he took his staff and went to the capital. When Wu entered prison, the master protected him by every means and gave him half a verse of the Visvabhu Buddha, charging him to recite it a full hundred thousand times, and he would leave prison. Wu recited it to eighty thousand, and the Emperor's mind was appeased, so that his sentence was reduced. Because I had not yet been restored to my former status, the master would often sigh, “The Dharma-gate has no men left. If one sits by and watches the banner of Dharma destroyed, where then should one who would perpetuate the Three Jewels apply his mind? If old Hanshan does not return, it is one great burden on my leaving the world. If the mining tax is not stopped, it is one great burden on my saving the world. If the Transmission of the Lamp is not continued, it is one great burden on my life of wisdom. If these three burdens were released, I should no longer run to Rājagṛha.” In the autumn of the guimao year I was at Caoxi and sent a flying letter by a disciple who was going up to the capital for the examinations, inviting the master into the mountains. His reply said simply, “I will give up this one poor body.” Before long the “wicked book” case suddenly broke out and shook the court and the realm. Those who envied him seized the occasion to impeach him, and in the end he met disaster through it. Earlier, the Emperor, as a wheel-turning sovereign riding on the power of past vows, revered the great Dharma, and had written out the Diamond Sutra in his own hand. It happened that a drop of his sweat fell and stained the paper, and he wondered whether he ought to copy it again; so he sent his close attendant Cao to consult the master. The master presented a verse: “One drop of the imperial sweat — / A bridge for ten thousand ages; / The inexhaustible Dharma-store / From this sends forth its light.” Reading it, the Emperor was greatly pleased, and from this turned his attention to him. When he later saw the memorial, his heart was very compassionate; but under the law it could not be avoided, and so the arrest followed. The edict came down: “Let him be examined, and no more.” When the imperial guards interrogated him, he answered only with the matter of the three burdens, and had nothing else to say. He was delivered to the Ministry of Justice. The chief minister of the time wished to put the master to death. Hearing of it, the master said, “The ways of the world are like this — what use is it to remain long?” So he asked for a bath; when it was done, he charged his attendant, the young priest Xingtian: “I am going. Pray thank all the Dharma-protectors of Jiangnan.” The priest wept, and the master scolded him: “You have served me twenty years, and still you behave like this?” Then, having spoken a verse, he sat upright and peacefully passed away. The censor Cao Xuecheng, who had been arrested and imprisoned for remonstrance and had questioned the master about the Way, heard and hurried to him. Stroking him, he said, “The master has gone well.” The master opened his eyes again, smiled, and took his leave. It was the seventeenth day of the twelfth month of the guimao year. The master was born on the twelfth day of the sixth month of a guimao year. His worldly life was sixty-one years; his Dharma-years, more than forty. The master's conduct in life left men half doubting, half believing; but this last, swift and easy move of his — when high and low alike heard of it, there was none who did not sigh in admiration. Ah! To the master, birth and death — he looked on the four elements as a worn-out sandal to be kicked off. What Dharma could bring this about? The master often showed people the verse of Viśvabhu Buddha. I asked him, “Do you also keep it?” He said, “I have kept it for more than twenty years and have made one and a half lines familiar; if I made two lines familiar, I should have no anxiety about birth and death.” Was this not its proof? After the master's passing, he awaited the mandate six days, and his countenance did not change. When he was brought out, his body was moved and given temporary burial outside Cihui Monastery. In the spring and summer of the next year there were continuous rains; in the autumn, Mr. Lu Xiyuan wished to bring the master's flesh-body back south, and had it opened — it lay calm and unmoved. My disciple Dayi escorted the master's coffin. Passing the Lu River, the censor Ma Jinglun, moved by the master's affair and that of Li Zhuowu, was most grieved at heart; he had the coffin opened, wiped the face, and wept bitterly over it. When they reached Jingkou, the disciples of Jinsha and Qu'a escorted him back to Jingshan and enshrined him at Jizhao Hermitage. At the point of death the master had a verse: “No wonder the Twin Paths are the Twin Trees; / The palm-leaf scriptures like clouds, the sun of itself withdraws.” It was for this reason. It was the ninth month of the autumn of the jiachen year. Eleven years later, in the yimao year, his disciples buried the master's whole body behind Mount Shuangjing. The Director of Education Zhu Guozhen, paying homage at the master's stūpa, learned that there was water there, and charged the disciple Fakai to open it. The lay disciple Miao Xiyong divined and found a site within the Five Peaks, behind the stūpa of Dahui, to the left of the second founding generation, called Mañjuśrī Terrace. The cremation was divined for the nineteenth day of the eleventh month of the bingchen year; on the twenty-third the sacred bones were gathered, and the stūpa was built here. I was then among the marching ranks; hearing of the master's death I wished to go in person to mourn, but delay carried me through a full twelve years, and my original wish was not fulfilled. Lately I have come several thousand li from Nanyue, without any thought of meeting at an appointed time, and yet the day of sacrifice had been set beforehand. Truly the communion of spirit is a wondrous thing. The master's last affairs it was my fortune to witness, so that I could render some small service of heart. Ah! The master's conduct in life — how could it be easily equaled? From the time he left home he never let his ribs touch a mat for more than forty years. His nature was fierce and bold, his effort vigorous; he disciplined himself with the utmost strictness, so that those near him shivered though not from cold. He often sat in the open, never shrinking from wind or frost. In childhood, having received his mother's instruction not to sit on the threshold, he stood all his life rather than sit near the door. He held the diamond mind and bore the great Dharma alone in his heart. Whenever he saw an ancient monastery lying waste, he would see it restored: beginning with the Surangama and ending with Guizong and Yunju and others, he revived fifteen monasteries. Besides carving the great canon, he sought out and printed for the world the recorded sayings of ancient renowned elders, such as the collected essays on the sutras by the Venerable Jiyin, and Su Zhanggong's commentary on the Yi — all were brought to light and printed. By nature he was enamored of mountains and waters; his life long he moved like a cloud and flew like a bird, with a single robe and nothing more, with not a foot of ground to call his own. He held in deep reverence the great principles of loyalty and filial devotion to ruler and parents. Entering a Buddha hall, when he saw the tablet of the Ten Thousand Years, he would always pay his respects. Opening a calendar, he would raise it to his forehead before reading. Once, reading the gazetteer of Changsha, he came upon the loyal minister Li Fu: when the city was about to fall, unwilling to die at the rebels' hands, he gave a sword to a subordinate officer and ordered him to cut down his whole family. The officer, weeping bitterly, obeyed; and having done the deed, he killed himself as well. When the master reached this point, his tears gushed forth. A disciple attending nearby did not weep, and the master rebuked him, saying, “You should be pushed down the cliff.” His devotion to loyalty and righteousness was of this kind. The master's spirit was heroic, his frame full; his face and eyes were stern and cold, yet his heart was most compassionate. Whenever he instructed his disciples he always made them investigate for themselves, to bring forth their awakening, and would not rest until the root of doubt was wholly pulled out. He did not take ordinary feeling as his rule in receiving people; he sought men as a gray hawk seizes a hare, wanting to take them alive the moment he saw them. So for those who entered his room and did not accord, the more compassionate his heart, the deeper his regret; beneath a single blow of the staff he wanted straightaway to cut off the root of life. Hence those who drew near him were few. The austere and the warm — the master truly possessed both. Ah! How could the master be an ordinary man? In his direct, swift, steady, and subtle insight he must rank with the ancients. In his compassionate vows to benefit beings and his zeal in protecting the Three Jewels, he is rightly called a mahāsattva of the manifestation body. Someone asked what manner of man the master was. I said, “In the age of the true Dharma, Linji and Deshan might be dispensed with; in the age of the decline of Dharma, this old man could not be dispensed with.” The master often grieved that the cardinal tenets of the five houses were not flourishing, and would constantly bring this up for people. I once sighed, “If the cardinal tenets do not flourish, what is to become of the life of wisdom?” As for origins: the Caodong house presides solely at Shaolin; the Weiyang house's circular symbols have long been hidden; since Elder Han of Yunmen it is hard to find a man of that line; the Fayan house flourished greatly under Yongming and afterward flowed into Korea. Only the Linji line spread throughout the world; down to Dahui of the Song it revived the Way; and in the early years of our dynasty there were such great elders as Chushi and Wunian. Later it passed down to the end of the Hongzhi and Zhengde eras, when there was the retreat-master Jiguan, whose disciple was my late master, the monk Yungu, and the norms still survived. For fifty years now the master's lute has fallen silent; of late, before the rush mat is even steady and the true eye is not yet clear, men recklessly style themselves “the so-and-so-th generation of Linji.” Ah! Demons wreak havoc on the Dharma — must one not grieve? In my view, the master's insight can truly follow Linji from afar and connect above with Dahui; but as he had no master's line before him, I dare not recklessly press the claim. Take the Way of Yao and Shun: it was transmitted to Confucius and Mencius, and after Mencius's death there was no one to receive it, until the scholars of Lianxi and Luoyang in the Song remotely continued its vein. By this token, the master is surely not unworthy to be a true son of the wheel-turning king. I set down here a rough record, to await the clear-eyed masters of later days and those who will continue the Transmission of the Lamp, for them to draw upon. Because the master never took up an abbacy, there are no records of his mounting the hall, giving universal discourses, or instructing the assembly; only the instructions he gave on the occasions of visitors' inquiries. His disciples gathered these, and there are several volumes of inner and outer collections circulating in the world. His disciples who entered his room, monks and laymen alike, were very many, and among officials and lay devotees especially numerous. The master's conduct in life cannot be fully recorded here; there is a separate biography. So I made an inscription for him. The inscription reads:

Before the Buddha came to birth,
Before the Patriarch came from the west,
Who struck the poisoned drum on earth,
Who stood and answered to that test?
On Vulture Peak a flower was raised,
At Shaoshi’s cave he faced the wall.
“How quick! How easy!” all men praised —
Yet it became a tangled fall.
At Huangmei, in the midnight deep,
Old Lu in secret stole away.
Who guessed that south of Lingnan’s steep
A barbarian would hold the sway?
Nanyue, Qingyuan — those two men,
Who wiped the pus and wiped the tears;
How many fools, a witless crew,
Were swindled, duped, through all their years!
The Five Houses’ hands were swift to play,
As one who strokes Lord Shun’s own lute;
The south wind breathed a sudden day —
Only the knower knew the tune.
Their heirs were fierce, their tempers hot;
Whoever touched them first was slain.
Yet let one single line be got,
And that man’s house shall long remain.
The gate stands lonely, without peer;
Its life hangs on a single thread.
Whoever comes to save it here
Must be a son of the true bed.
Like Zhang Liang of the Han of old,
Who swore to avenge a fallen land;
Though the kingdom’s tale was told,
The ancestral line could stand.
And so my master came to light,
A bamboo shoot from stone that springs;
Out it bursts in soaring flight —
Who knows the root of all such things?
He fought for Dharma with all his might,
His whole body sweat and blood;
Much like Li Ling in desperate fight,
Bare-handed, unafraid he stood.
His body fell among the foe,
His heart was never wholly slain;
A thousand autumns hence shall show
His homeward road to the king again.
The master’s vajra heart, we know,
Was wholly turned to bone at last;
It fills and chokes the void below —
How could a hillside hold it fast?
The master did not know me here;
Who then shall know the master’s way?
One dies, one lives, from year to year —
Spring rests upon the flowering spray.
Tower Inscription for Great Master Zhuhong, Lianchi of Yunqi

The three poisons blaze; the five heats spread.
Who has the medicine to cool them in a breath?
The ocean of desire runs wild, its waves reach the sky.
Who can ferry them over, and pilot the great Dharma ship?
Only our Great Master, riding the power of his vows,
Cast himself into it, and tuned himself to each.
He cut the root of craving early, like a lion slipping its chain.
Scarce had he left the dust of toil than his horns showed.
He opened the gate of Pure Land and spread the net of the Dharma-realm,
Fishing out the three faculties, and they came to him like echo.
With the diamond lance he scraped the film from clouded eyes.
When the root is not born, branch and leaf fall of themselves.
The great forge, the red furnace: the power of compassion and patience.
Smelted in that crucible, delusion and madness stilled at once.
Light streams from every pore; the whole body is hands and eyes.
Out of what has no use, the Dharma wheel turns on.
If he was not the one entrusted, then surely he welled up from the earth.
How could he be counted ordinary? He had great courage and daring.
Master and disciples came from emptiness and go from emptiness too.
Though he was skilled at hiding his body, the more he hid, the more he showed.
Bells and drums ring in chorus; clouds and sunset weave and glow.
The pagoda's shadow rises high; the Dharma-body ever abides.
Stupa Inscription for Master Kongyin Zhencheng of Bamboo Grove Monastery on Mount Qingliang, Bestowed by Imperial Decree

The Dharma-body of all Buddhas rests upon the prajñā of words and letters. Therefore, when the Tathāgata appeared in the world, he gave singular weight to Dharma masters who uphold the scriptures, wishing that their wisdom-life should not be cut off. And so, from the time the white-hair mark withdrew its radiance, in the age of images, those who spread the scriptures were Aśvaghoṣa, Nāgārjuna, Asaṅga, and Vasubandhu, who set forth the schools of nature and of characteristics, each excelling in his own beauty. When the great Dharma flowed eastward, it was Master Qingliang alone who dredged the source of the Dharma-realm, upheld the net of the teachings, and gathered in gods and men. Because he was penetrating in his own nature, he spread abroad the four unhindered eloquence of teaching, in perfect unobstructed fusion. From Guishan onward, such a man has been hard to find. In recent times, one who far continued the fragrant rule and stood out as a model for masters was our Master Kongyin Zhencheng of Bamboo Grove Monastery. The master's personal name was Zhencheng, his style Kongyin. He was a son of the Li family of Sangyu in Wanping, Jintai. His father was Zhongwu; his mother, née Lü. At his conception his mother dreamed that a monk carrying a staff entered the room, and when she woke she gave birth to him. From childhood he was intelligent and unmatched; in his childish play he delighted in Buddhist observances, and early he had the will to leave the world. At fifteen he took refuge with Master Yin of Guangying Monastery in the Western Hills and was ordained a novice monk. After three years of diligent service he ascended the ordination platform and received the full precepts. Yijiang Li, Xifeng Shen, and Shouan Zhong, the great Dharma masters who spread the teachings in the great capital, were followed by the master one after another; he studied in the lecture halls and fathomed the essential purport of nature and characteristics, penetrating the Avataṃsaka Sūtra and mastering it all without exception. This went on for over ten years. He then studied under the two great teachers Xiaoshan and Xiaoyan, fathoming the secret meaning of the coming from the West, and wondrously sealed the mind-seal. For a time the scholars of doctrinal study acclaimed him foremost.
Earlier, when I was wandering in the capital, among the assembly of the Dharma gathering I singled him out as one who would be a master craftsman of the Dharma. Later he joined Chan Master Miaofeng in retreat at Wutai, where they were about to convene an unrestricted Dharma assembly and gather the venerable elders of the land; Miaofeng was urged to summon him with all his strength. The master did come, and I was overjoyed, taking it as a sign that Mount Tai had found its man. That was the renwu year of Wanli. When the assembly ended, Miaofeng and I parted. As I was about to set out, I could not bear to take leave of the master, and we talked through the night; I earnestly urged him, saying, “The times have fallen to the latter age, the Dharma gate lies desolate, and one who can hold it up is hard to find. Be careful not to dwell in the busy world; keep your mind on this mountain and store up your sharp tool deeply. In time you will be the master of the golden realm.” The master asked why. I said, “Long ago Sima Toutuo read the physiognomy of Weishan, and it was simply that his form matched the mountain.” The master gladly agreed. I then had him dwell in the Zixia Hermitage where I was living. There he sat in wall-gazing for three years and had a great awakening.
The patron of the stupa court, Elder Dafang Guang, asked him to revise the Record of Qingliang, and he stayed on to lecture on the various scriptures. His fame and light blazed forth, and scholars from every quarter gathered daily in greater numbers. Before long, with Xuefeng he founded the Lion's Lair and built the Vairocana Pagoda of Ten Thousand Buddhas, and it became a great monastery. There he lectured on the great Avataṃsaka Sūtra; his students numbered a thousand fingers. Sitting on cold cliff and ice and snow, they were as though within the Vajra Cave. The Empress Dowager and the Emperor prayed for the realm's blessing and fixed their attention on Mount Tai; hearing of the master's refinement, they esteemed him and specially bestowed the venerable canon of the Great Treasury for enshrinement and offering. Soon after they again commanded the master to lecture at the Thousand Buddhas Monastery in the capital on his own work, True Contemplation of the Śūraṅgama, and again at the Ciyin Monastery to lecture on the various scriptures.
At that time Miaofeng had cast a bronze hall of a thousand Buddhas and installed it at the Great Xiantong Monastery. The Emperor praised his merit and practice, commanded that it be rebuilt, and changed its bestowed name to Yongming; he established the seven places and nine assemblies as a bodhimaṇḍa and invited the great Dharma masters to lecture on the Avataṃsaka, with the master presiding over the first seat. When the assembly ended, the master, noting that the old Bamboo Grove Monastery was the place where Mañjuśrī had appeared, restored it after long ruin, most of the cost coming from the inner treasury. Before long a great bodhimaṇḍa appeared as if by magic. He then gathered his disciples and once more lectured through the Avataṃsaka Commentary for one full round, and restored the South Terrace as a realm of Mañjuśrī's transformation. From this time the master was weary of bridge-building, and so he took leave of his disciples, single-mindedly raising the last move, and sat silently upright. When the assembly asked him to teach the Dharma, the master said, “I have followed illusory conditions and done what I could for the great Dharma, always keeping the great matter of birth and death in mind. Now I am old; how much of human life is left? For a student, fathoming the mind is what matters. How could I take wagging the lips as attainment? You should exhort yourselves with this. I am about to go.”
After a short while he showed slight illness, sat upright for three days and nights, and talked and laughed as usual. In the middle of the night he passed away in silence. It was the fourteenth day of the sixth month of the ding-si year of Wanli. The master was by birth calm and grave, sparing of speech and laughter, strict in disciplining himself and generous in governing the assembly; without severity he was awe-inspiring. He taught the Dharma for over thirty years and lectured on the Avataṃsaka three times. Though he ascended the jeweled seat surrounded by a thousand fingers, his mind was as if no one were there. Though heavenly kitchens came to him daily, he was content with coarse fare. In dwelling he ever concentrated on contemplation of principle; his ribs never touched the mat. Deep and still, silent and quiet, in old age he showed no sign of slackness. His Dharma-receiving disciples numbered in the thousands and hundreds, and those who came from his gate were for the most part plain and without superficial habits, for he had been their model. In lecturing he grasped the outline and seized the essentials, and from time to time brought forth new meanings. For the flourishing of lecture seats in the north, if one examines the seniors of the past, none surpassed him. His works include True Contemplation of the Śūraṅgama, The True Eye of the Diamond, A Treatise on the Illumination of Reality by Prajñā, and commentaries on Buddhist Logic, The Awakening of Faith, the Mahāyānasaṃgraha, and the Yongjia Collection, all circulating in the world.
The master was born in the ding-wei year of Jiajing; his worldly life was seventy-one years, his monastic age over fifty. His whole body was buried to the left of Bamboo Grove. When the Emperor heard that the master had passed away, he bestowed treasury gold to build a stupa, inscribed “The Stupa of the Emanation Body of the Great Dharma Master Kongyin.” In the early years of our dynasty, Chan and lecture masters often moved the imperial heart and received abundant favor, yet in two hundred years none has had such depth of merit and virtue as to bring down such profound gracious regard. Was he not one who came as an emanation of Mañjuśrī, or else a reflection of Qingliang? The disciples he ordained, Weidong and seven others, and the Dharma heirs who received his teaching, Yuanqing and several hundred others, were mostly able to open and transform their own regions. The next year, the winter of the wu-wu year, his Dharma-grandson Fangmao and his disciple Daqian brought the master's conduct record and came from afar to Mount Kuang, seeking an inscription for his stupa. The master and I counted as bosom friends within the Dharma gate; if I do not write it, who will? So I made this inscription, saying:

The Dharma-body has no form;
It shows when it meets with things.
Letters blaze forth:
The light of prajñā.
So those who hold the scriptures —
The wisdom-life rests on them.
They fathom the emptiness of nature,
And speak the unspeakable.
West Heaven, this land —
No age lacked its heirs.
Then there was Qingliang,
Emanation of Mañjuśrī.
The ocean of nature surges;
The sky of meaning blazes with stars.
The Dharma-realm in perfect fusion
Shines forth all at once.
He dwells in the golden realm,
Seated on the jeweled lotus throne,
And puts forth the broad, long tongue:
A rain of flowers falls.
A thousand years and more below,
This great master appeared in time.
The fragrant rule, continued from afar:
A true lion's cub.
He sits aloft in his cave
And gives a mighty lion's roar;
The hundred beasts, all shaken,
Hear the sound and flee.
He lifts up nature and characteristics,
And flings wide the treasure-store;
One rain moistens all alike,
Three faculties, each its measure.
His fame reached the nine-fold court;
Its deep grace turned toward him.
The Brahma monastery rose;
The Dharma banner stands on high.
For over thirty years
He taught and never tired,
By the power of knowing and seeing
Following skillful means.
In discipline strict and refined,
In spirit still and plain,
He turned back the wild gale
And restored the simple and pure.
He showed this body as illusion,
A teacher for gods and men;
In the Dharma's latter age
Truly a jewel of the saṅgha.
The pagoda's shadow props the sky;
The Dharma-body stands alone, revealed.
Wind moves; water flows:
The perfect sound spreads everywhere.
A thousand-foot cold cliff,
A million years of snow and ice.
Sun and moon without end:
His light is never extinguished.
Dream Roaming Collection of Old Man Hanshan, Volume Twenty-Eight
Stupa Inscription for Chan Master Wuming Huijing of Shouchang in Xincheng

The Way of the buddhas and patriarchs is like the vast void: through all antiquity it has been so, and cannot be brightened or dimmed by the alternation of day and night. Only one who has attained it is like one who has won the wish-fulfilling jewel, its uses inexhaustible. That inconceivable power is complete within one's own nature; it is made clear in the mind and is not sought from without. From the patriarchs above downward, none has been otherwise. Why then is it so sparse in recent times? One cannot say there is no Chan — there is simply no master. And is it really so that there is none? In Chan Master Shouchang I have seen such a man.
According to his conduct record: the master's personal name was Huijing, his style Wuming. He was a son of the Pei family of Chongren in Fuzhou. His father was so-and-so; his mother, née so-and-so. At his birth there was a difficult labor; his grandfather recited the Diamond Sūtra, and the delivery came. He was therefore named Jing. The master was bright and extraordinary from birth, his bearing grave and ancient, like a crane soaring aloft. By nature he was calm and had no cravings. At nine he entered the village school and at once asked what the vast flowing vital force might be. His teacher thought him strange. He dwelt always as though he had no interest in the human world. At seventeen he cast aside brush and inkstone, and with deep feeling set his will on the Way. At twenty, visiting a layman's house, he saw the Diamond Sūtra on the desk, read it through in one sitting, and was delighted as though recovering something long lost. He at once told the layman what he understood, and the layman thought him remarkable. From this he gave up meat and wine and resolved to leave the world; his parents also let him go.
Chan Master Yunkong Zhong was teaching at Mount Lin, and he went to rely on him. When asked his original name, he said, “Huijing.” He served and attended him for three years, and never went against what he was taught, like one without understanding. He once doubted the four-line verse of the Diamond Sūtra. One day, seeing the verse of Mahāsattva Fu — “If you would speak of the four-line verse, it should never be apart from the body” — the master felt suddenly freed. He then composed a verse containing the line “light shining throughout the whole realm.” From this he knew it to be the ripening of habitual prajñā from former lives. He was then twenty-four.
One day, reading the great canon until he came to the chapter on the eye of the school, he first understood that there is a meaning transmitted apart from the teachings. As for the differences among the five houses, he was privately perplexed, and sat in confusion for eight months, as though seeing and hearing nothing; people of the time thought him simple. After a long while he had an awakening, and thereupon firmly resolved to investigate. So he took leave of Mount Lin and wished to live in seclusion. He visited E Peak, saw how deep and secluded were its wooded valleys, and cut thatch to dwell there, vowing that until he clarified the great matter he would never leave that mountain. He lived there three years, and no one knew of him.
Reading the Transmission of the Lamp, he saw a monk ask Xingshan, “What is the Way?” Xingshan said, “A very good mountain.” The master was utterly at a loss, and his doubt surged up at once; day and night he held it before him until he forgot sleep and food. One day, while moving a stone that was too firmly set to lift, he pushed with all his might and was suddenly greatly awakened. He then composed a verse: “Would you inquire into the supreme bodhi-way? / Hasten to clear the way through the good mountain. / When you know the Way, you know the mountain is not good; / Then turn and leap beyond the patriarchs' gate.” He presented it to Mount Lin, who recognized him as a vessel of the Dharma.
The master was frail from birth, as if he could not bear the weight of his clothes; but once he dwelt on the mountain he strove with all his might. He tilled and planted with his own hands, cut stone and opened fields, shrinking from no toil and giving no thought to his body. Whenever he heard the empty mountain's racket, he would say, “This old monk makes no distinction, no end to it.” So he dwelt with his door unbarred, and walked the mountain alone by night. At twenty-seven he had still not shaved his head; when someone urged him, the master said, “Wait until I have a monk's appearance.” Only then did he shave, dye his robes, and receive the full precepts. For twenty-four years his shadow did not leave the mountain, as though it were a single day.
Baofang in his district was the old monastery of Chan Master Shibao of the Song. When they asked the master to restore it, he accepted. He first went to Mount Lin, swept his teacher's stupa, and then went on, having a line about “suddenly thirty years, forgetting the road by which I came.” The master was then fifty-one, in the wu-xu year of Wanli. Dwelling at Baofang, he daily increased his vigor. In every task he put himself first. Wasted and gaunt, all bone, he never tired of the toil. Within a few years a hundred walls were made new, fields were opened, and the Buddha hall, the three gates, the halls and the kitchen were all complete. Monks in patched robes from all quarters, hearing the wind of him and coming, gathered daily in greater numbers. A monk asked the master, “Dwelling on this mountain, whom have you ever met?” The master said, “I have never gone on pilgrimage at all.” The monk prodded him: “How can you make the whole world small from one corner?” The master thought well of his words, and so took his staff and traveled far.
He crossed to the South Sea and visited Yunqi; then went on to the Central Plain and entered Shaolin, bowing at the First Patriarch's stupa and asking about the meaning of the single transmission from the West. Then he went to the capital and called on Chan Master Daguan, who esteemed him deeply. He entered Wutai and studied under Venerable Duanfeng. Duanfeng's gate was solitary and steep; the master met him once and was in accord. He asked for instruction: “I have doubts about several of the ancient worthies' cases; I beg you, Master, to point them out.” Feng said, “Speak.” The master said, “Linji said the Buddhadharma has nothing much to it. What exactly is that?” Feng said, “You ask what has nothing much to it — and what is that?” The master said, “Xuansha told Lingyun, ‘I dare guarantee, old brother, that you are not yet through.’ Where is it that he is not through?” Feng said, “It is very much Xuansha who is not through.” The master said, “Zhaozhou said, ‘The old woman of Mount Tai — I have seen through her for you.’ Where did he see through her?” Feng said, “Rather, it was the old woman who saw through Zhaozhou.” The master asked further. Feng said, “Knowing it is this sort of thing and that is the end of it.” The master bowed, and they sealed their mutual accord. Feng in turn questioned him, and the master answered each with a verse; the words are recorded elsewhere. The last verse, on Zhaozhou, read: “Spring's colors hidden in the dark, / Autumn's light revealed in the open. / Though you have eyes, you cannot see it; / Though you have wisdom, it is hard to measure. / One who has reached home does not walk the road to Chang'an — / Let the wind, flowers, snow, and moon blow as they will.” Feng deeply approved.
Watching the master — his words avoided the ten-tenths, his workings valued turning and exchange, wondrously matching the five positions — one knew that the Caodong line's wind would surely rise again from this. From then on the master's heart too grew weary of wandering, and he returned his staff to Baofang. There he first opened the hall and taught the Dharma, with Master Lai of Boju as his chief seat. Teacher and student were finely matched, drumming up this Way and rousing its essential purport. Monks in patched robes from all quarters, hearing the wind and coming, grew ever more numerous.
In the wu-shen year, Shouchang in his district — founded long ago by Chan Master Xizhu — had long been in ruin, and the assembly asked the master to dwell there. An old prophecy had been handed down: the master and Zhu were from the same district and bore the same surname, so all said the master was Zhu come again. Dwelling at Shouchang, he sought no outside support and sent out no fund-raisers, but simply used whatever came. Within a few years his expenditure ran to myriads, and the monastery's adornment was radiant and grand; whatever befits a great monastery was complete down to the smallest detail. Within ten years a thousand fingers were gathered around him. Was this not the master's effortless wondrous power conjuring it into being?
By birth the master was plain and upright, gentle in temper yet firm in will, even of heart yet steep in conduct. Though he neglected outward polish, his bearing was grave and reverent; under his stern frost and blazing sun no one grew angry, yet all felt awe. A monk of the patched robe would lose his old self at first sight. He guided each according to capacity, giving each what suited him. Whenever he met a sick monk, he would mix the medicine himself; when one died, he would shoulder the firewood and cremate the body with his own hands. In all matters of the monastery, great or small, he would give his own mind to it, so that things came right without contriving. He did not pick clean or foul, but always gave his whole strength to what he did. His breast was broad and vast; his ears and eyes seemed to see and hear nothing. Past seventy, he still mingled with the toiling brethren, never ceasing to plow and dig, always first out and last back, leading by example in opening fields. The yearly income of his three monasteries could feed three hundred. So all his life the Buddhadharma never left the edge of his hoe.
For over forty years he never took a single breath for his own ease. Though he stood before great assemblies, he never set himself up as a teacher. When it came to repartee, verses, and Dharma words, they flowed like a river and surged like clouds — truly what is called the light of prajñā, like a maṇi jewel's perfect illumination, responding without thought. Among the lamp-transmitting elders of old, each had his own unobstructed liberation, but the one who never tired of the ten thousand practices was Yongming alone — and even he did not reach the master's coarseness. As for the master, one may say his Way matched the single transmission and his mind fused with the ten thousand dharmas; how could his vigor and diligence have been like this? The Prince of Yi admired the master's virtue and deeply praised him, sighing, “The sages are far off in time; how fortunate that this old man remains.” Such was the regard in which he was held.
On the seventh day of the twelfth month of the ding-si year, returning from the fields, he told the assembly, “From now on I shall lay no more stone.” The assembly was astonished. On New Year's Eve he ascended the hall and said, “This year only this moment remains. I ask you all — do you know it or not?” His admonitions were earnest, and afterward he said, “This is the old monk's last move. I entrust it to the assembly; take good care.” On the third day of the New Year in the wu-wu year he showed slight illness and stopped eating, saying, “The old monk is not sick; it is simply time to go.” The assembly gathered around him, joyful as in former days, while he remained untroubled. He instructed them with a verse: “In life there is receiving, not repayment; / Do not panic at old age, sickness, and death.” On the seventh day he gave a verse to Boju, and one by one wrote out his testament for Baofang and Shouchang, saying, “The ancients guarded the monastic property as their own life; this old monk does not spare his life, but secures the property.” On the fourteenth he wrote letters to clergy and laity far and near, urging them on in the Way. On the fifteenth, Xiao, a licentiate of Jishui, came to consult him; the master instructed him, “Simply look into the one to which the ten thousand dharmas return,” and urged him to press his inquiry with all his strength. On the sixteenth he gave instructions for his cremation and composed his own verse for the raising of the fire, ordering his attendant Chezong to chant the verse and light the fire. The next morning he rinsed his mouth, washed his face, and wiped his body, instructing them, “There is no need to bathe me again; it would waste the monastery's firewood and water.” He warned the assembly not to follow vulgar custom and go into mourning, saying, “Whoever disobeys is no disciple of mine.” Then he called for a brush and wrote in large characters, “Today I clearly show the way.” He threw down the brush, sat upright, and passed away. It was the seventeenth day of the first month of the wu-wu year of Wanli, at the hour of wei. At the cremation the fire's light was five-colored, and the flame at his heart was like a lotus, its fine petals like bamboo leaves. His skull and teeth remained unbroken; the rest were white as jade, heavy as gold, and veined in five colors. He was buried at a certain place, and a stupa was raised. The master was born in the wu-shen year of Jiajing; his worldly life was seventy-one years, his monastic years over forty. He had a number of Dharma-heirs, of whom the foremost, Yuanlai, now teaches at Boju; the rest guard the monastic property of the three mountains. There are three assemblies' worth of recorded sayings.
I once heard of the master's manner. In the bing-chen year, while passing the summer at Mount Kuang, a disciple brought me a portrait of the master. When I unrolled it, I knew at once that he was a man beyond the ordinary, and I regretted never having met him. So I composed a praise for it, with the line, “He stands out on the good mountain; a thousand miles apart, we meet in the distance.” When Boju saw it, he took me for one who knew the master deeply within the Dharma-gate, and so he set out the master's conduct in full and asked me for an inscription for his stupa. I grieve to think how the Chan gate has fallen desolate, with none to raise it up; the lion's string is about to fall silent. Now as to the master's conduct — his insight was steady and subtle, his working of the pivotal and the discerning was free. Not only was the eye of Dharma perfect and bright, so that he single-handedly lifted the fallen discipline; his lofty integrity and solitary wind are truly enough to rouse the decadent age. As for his great vigor and power of patience, one must seek their like among the ancients. Though his shadow never left the mountain, his voice and light reached far — was he not one who “dwells like a corpse yet appears as a dragon, is silent in the abyss yet thunders”? Seeing how plainly he faced birth and death, one knows his practice was real. So, having set down his actual conduct in order, I made this inscription. The inscription reads:

The Great Way is vast and boundless, like empty space itself.
Sages and ordinary beings are phantom leaves, their shadows falling there.
Though one may seek it with all haste, in the end it is never found;
To weigh and ponder it is but to club the moon with a stick.
Gautama wore himself to a fever; Bodhidharma hurried here,
And at the last what each obtained was a single leather sandal.
He set up the drum of poison to make the true command fully known;
Whoever dares to strike it loses body and loses life.
But one who does not cling to life, when the hour comes, gives it a blow:
Three days of deafness follow, a thunderclap in a clear sky.
Body and mind are shattered both; demons and buddhas hide their tracks.
The maṇi jewel blazes bright, and all eight faces stand wide open.
Only I, Shouchang, fell by mishap into that poison;
Through every pore of my body samādhi rises and sinks away.
I turned the pit of birth and death into a gathered mass of light.
In all the doings of the day there is no place that is not so.
Lifting up the hoe, it is like a diamond sword;
In the dense forest of afflictions, buddhas and patriarchs appear.
For more than forty years I tilled the soil and dug the ground;
Rubble and thorns I paved instead with pure seven-treasure brick.
Body, mind, and world crumble into finest dust;
And in every mote of dust, buddha-lands where one may walk, sit, and lie.
Buddhadharma and the way of Chan I set aside to one side;
When someone comes to ask, I point him straight to what is there before him.
Like a great and perfect mirror, the five colors all arrive as one.
It does not go out, it does not come in; birth and death are but a play.
Of my own accord I fell into it; I have never truly dwelt in the world,
And now I go at once, yet I have never gone away.
If you do not believe it, only look: in a blade of grass, a speck of dust,
What single thing is there that is not the whole body?
The green mountain's shadow of the stūpa, the long tongue of the pine wind:
The sound of the dharma being spoken never for a moment ceases.
Tower Inscription for Master Wugou of Jiuhua Mountain

The master's monastic name was Xinglian; his courtesy name was Wugou. He was a son of the Wang family of Xianyuan in Taiping. He was set apart from others from birth, delighted in Buddhist works as a child, and early held the resolve to leave the world. At first, when the Buddhadharma had not yet spread in that region, various non-Buddhist teachers gathered and proclaimed their doctrines, and the master would often go to observe and listen. One day he said to the crowd, “These are words spoken in a dream. What can they do about birth and death?” Thereupon he resolved firmly to leave household life. At the age of twenty-two he abandoned wife and child, broke up his household, and scattered his property. He went to Qixia Temple on Mount She in Nanjing and was shaved and given full ordination by Master Jie of Su'an. He stayed by the lecture seat, studying the meaning of the scriptures and treatises, then set the scrolls down with a sigh and said, “I left home for the great matter of birth and death. How could these settle the great matter?” So he abandoned them as well. He then found Niutou Mountain in his home region, cleared the brush, and settled there, burning off the ground and farming with a blade, keeping the matter beneath his own feet as his sole concern. After a long time he still had found no entry, so he left again. He went to Qinghe and called on Elder Fatang, who taught him the samādhi of nianfo; in this he came to believe deeply and enter in. Soon after, he visited old Master Bianrong in the capital. Bianrong took one look and esteemed him, and kept him in his chamber for a long while. Later, when Master Miaofeng began teaching at Luya, the master went especially to see him and gained much refining. He returned again to Dashan Mountain in his home region. Monastics and laity from all quarters came at the news, but he sighed and said, “Am I, a man who has left home, to keep a bit of thatch to catch the dripping water and block out this life?” So he abandoned that too. He vowed to travel through every famous mountain, to call on every good and wise teacher, and to make his way on foot in many directions; in this way he tasted hardship to the full for seven years. One winter day, crossing a river, the ice split with a crack and he fell into the water, chilled to the bone, and suddenly there was a breakthrough. He said, “The eyebrows were always crosswise, the nose always straight. When thirsty, drink; when hungry, eat. What further matter is there?” Thereupon the doubts of a lifetime melted away like ice. He went straight back and planted his staff on Shan Mountain in Chiyang, and monks from the ten directions came in ever greater numbers. The master then built a monastery and made receiving and entertaining guests his work. Those who came found in him no other skill: only fine and simple gruel, rice, tea, and broth. He had not the least of Chan talk or Buddhadharma, and those who watched came to trust him deeply without doubt. The sacred ground of Jiuhua welcomed him as abbot of the monastery. The master governed himself with austerity and hardship and forgot himself for the sake of the many. When he transformed hard and wicked natures he always used tactful means, bowing and pleading this way and that; and even if it came to scolding and abuse, he would wait until great faith arose before he stopped. People of his time called him “Never Disparaging.” In this way nearly twenty years passed, and monastics and laity near and far gave him their hearts as though he were a buddha or patriarch. Whatever was needed appeared in answer like an echo, and he never once sent out a single mendicant master to the streets. Wherever his footprints reached, even a place for one meal or one night's rest became a place of practice. In Chiyang there was Shan Mountain; at Jiuhua, Vajra Peak; at Guanyin Mountain, the Golden Hall; at Dashan, the thatched hut; at Lian Ridge, the quiet room; in Nanjing, Huashan; and besides these, Qintou Peak, the Popo Ridge, the Cenfeng Cave, Baisha Mountain, and auspicious heavens beyond number. Everywhere he built dozens of small monasteries and settled those who cultivated in quiet retreat, and each had disciples of his to head its work. Was this not one who forgot himself for the sake of beings, accomplishing the transformation of others without contrivance? In the second month of spring in the bing-shen year, in answer to the entreaties of the assembly, he was at Wan Mountain of the Third Patriarch. Within a few months a hundred neglected things were set in order, and near and far were stirred. The master then returned to Jiuhua. The following year the four assemblies of Wan Mountain earnestly begged him to come, and the master nodded, saying, “I will go, I will go; but I still need three days.” The next day he happened to pass Nine Dragons and visited an abbot in his hermitage. Gazing about, he was delighted, and said to the assembly, “My great task on this mountain is finished.” No one understood what he meant. Two days later he showed a slight illness and in the end passed away there, his whole body enshrined in a stūpa to the right of the hermitage. It was the third day of the ninth month of the ding-you year of Wanli. The master was born on the eighth day of the fourth month of the jia-chen year, and lived fifty-four years, with twenty-five years of monastic ordination. He had a great many disciples, each of whom managed the affairs of his own monastery. Among his lay devotees who sought the Buddhadharma, only the brothers Shao Jigong, and Cha Ruding and Xiao Bogu, were closest to him, sworn friends beyond the world in life and death. A month after the master passed away, Ruding went straight to Lingnan and sought me out among my travels, bearing the record of the master's life and begging me for an inscription. Having read it over three times, I was moved by the master's preservation of his resolve, which may truly be called a mastery of forgetting the self. So I made this inscription:

Forgetting the self for things, like an insect boring wood.
To see things as the self is water washing water.
When self and things are both forgot, no point or edge is ever caught.
A stone man dances in the day; the golden crow shines at night.
The master's body was like drifting cloud;
The master's mind, still as the valley spirit.
It neither comes nor goes: who dies, and who is born?
Jiuhua towers to the sky, yet deafens the ear;
Wan Mountain cuts the heavens, yet blinds the eye.
Singly and tall, one stūpa stands, planted in that empty space.
Would you seek the master's place of walking? Ask it of the nine peaks.
Tower Inscription for Master Zhu of Yingzhai at Qixia

Mount She was opened as a mountain site by Emperor Wu of Liang and flourished in the Tang. In past times many masters of renown taught the dharma there, but it had long lain in ruin. In the Jiajing era, Master Lu of Wutai looked about and was moved, and through the monastic superintendent invited the late Master Yungu to practice quiet contemplation there. Master Shan of Songshan restored the temple and brought in Master Su'an to open wide the dharma seat, and for a time students from within the seas gathered like clouds. Among the disciples beneath that seat were a number of men, and the foremost of them was Master Zhu of Yingzhai. The master was a son of the Li family of Anlu. He was sharp and extraordinary from birth, and his father reverently served the Three Jewels. As a child the master followed his father into the temple and was stirred by hearing a monk recite the Avatamsaka Sutra, and he begged to leave home. He bowed to Master Yue of the district as his disciple and served him for several years. He had the resolve to travel far, and so left, going to Qixia in Nanjing, where he received the full precepts under Master Xi, a disciple of Su'an. He listened to lectures on the scriptures and treatises and plumbed the tenets of nature and characteristics, devoting his mind to the teachings and contemplations for fifteen years. One day he asked his teacher about the meaning of the special transmission outside the teachings. The teacher said, “This matter of going beyond is something that has its own transmission from a teacher. Old Master Huanxiu is now presiding over the dharma at Shaolin; you should go and call on him.” So the master went to Shaoshi and met Xiu, asking at once, “What is the matter of going beyond?” Xiu said, “The moon on the peak of the five breasts, the lamp within the hall of the single transmission.” The master was not in accord, and so asked to lodge there. He trained long with the assembly and entered the master's chamber, and one day, as he took up the Shishuang koan, he had a breakthrough. He presented a verse: “Step out the door and it is all weeds; the cold grove blooms, and spring returns early. How laughable that the footless one knows how to walk, yet tramples Mount Sumeru flat.” Xiu said, “The phrase before sound is subtly conveyed in the wondrous leaf; the true wind beyond the kalpas is deep and subtle and fine. This matter handed down hand to hand from the buddhas and patriarchs above is not something thought or consciousness can reach, nor is it something a mysterious road can penetrate. Do not spread it about as a worldly truth.” The master bowed. He served in office for four years in all, then returned to Qixia. From then on his mind did not touch conditions and his tracks did not enter the world; day and night he cultivated with care, single-minded and never slack. One day, without illness, he asked for a bath, changed his robes, and passed away serenely. It was a certain month and day of a certain year of Wanli. The master lived some decades, had some summers of dharma age, and ordained a number of disciples; his whole body was enshrined in a stūpa at a certain place on the mountain. In my youth I served Master Yungu, and whenever I passed Qixia I loved the master's lofty and rugged frame of the Way, and knew him to be a vessel of the dharma. In the end he did not betray his life's vow and grasped the nose-bar of going beyond. How could such a one be spoken of in the same breath as those bound by ordinary learning and understanding, fettered by birth and death? So I made this inscription:

Tower Inscription for Master Gujing Xuan, Founding First-Generation Abbot of Puxing Chan Monastery in Yunzhong

When the sun and moon hang in the sky, even the blind gain benefit; when spring returns to the great earth, the dark valleys bring forth life. So too is the dharma-body of our World-Honored Buddha all-pervading: there is no sentient being in whom it is not complete. Though one dwell in a frontier land of crude and violent folk, if the conditions of karma meet, there is none who may not be brought to enter the Buddha's knowledge and vision, and to turn a reeking and rank place into a Pure Land; all of this depends on how well the work of teaching and transformation is done. On Master Xuan I have reflected with deep feeling. The master's monastic name was Yixuan; his alternate style was Gujing. He was a son of the Jia family of Yunzhong; his father was Lin and his mother of the Li family. He was born with unusual signs, and in childhood wearied of the world. He bowed to Master Dingsheng of the prefecture and left home, his resolve fixed on the matter of going beyond. When grown he took leave of his teacher and traveled widely. He first came to the capital and received the complete precepts at the Wanshou ordination platform. He bowed at every famous mountain within the seas and called on teachers far and wide, deciding the matter beneath his own feet and gaining some clarity. Reflecting that blessings and wisdom were not yet complete and his practice not yet full, in middle age he returned to his home region and undertook Buddhist works on a broad scale. He formed karmic ties by feeding monks beyond counting, made gilt images to adorn buddha-lands, painted water-and-land murals to rescue the dark realms, repaired bridges to aid those who waded and lifted their skirts, and built stūpas to mark the way for gods and men. He knelt and recited the Rebirth Mantra three hundred and sixty thousand times to further his pure karma. In whatever brought benefit, he never failed to give his whole heart and strength in order to guide and profit many people. Thereupon the four assemblies took refuge in him and kings and ministers revered him. Yunzhong was a frontier region pressed by the northern tribes, and the people's temper was fierce and violent; through the master's teaching, killing intent was turned into seeds of goodness. Was he not one who manifested the body of a bhikṣu to speak the dharma? The master's frame was full and generous and his nature gentle; those who saw him rejoiced and followed him like shadows. Inner and outer texts alike he mastered without omission; rich in learning and lofty in conduct, he drew the reverence of the lords of the Dai principality for three generations, while the princes Jiyang, Duan, and Hui and others all became his outer protectors. They built Puxing Chan Monastery, and he became its founding first-generation abbot. The master was born in the ding-hai year of Jiajing and entered nirvāṇa in the yi-si year of Wanli; he lived eighty years, with more than forty years of monastic ordination. His stūpa stands outside the walls of Yunzhong. In the long-summer month of the bing-chen year, while I was mourning Old Man Zibai at Shuangjing, my old friend Yue Qingtan of Longhua in the great capital sent a letter and a record, begging me for an inscription. So I made this inscription for him, saying:

The dharma-body is universal,
nowhere does it fail to reach;
like the moon shown in water,
clear and turbid both it flows.
Thus for every living being,
the sentient all possess it whole;
good and evil though they differ,
their nature is not two.
The hinge of their transforming
rests upon a skillful guide;
water poured into water —
not wondrous, yet wondrous still.
Therefore the utmost one
manifests wherever he stands;
if the karmic bond is absent,
he is unseen though face to face.
But should he turn his wondrous use
and enter living beings' minds,
like the moon within the water,
the clearer, the deeper it grows.
He can by goodness transform
the killing intent in others;
since he is selfless,
those who know him are few.
The sun shines at mid-heaven,
spring returns to the great earth;
when the hour has truly come,
there is no place that is not.
The master appeared by karma,
and by karma passed away;
birth and death, going and coming,
utterly cannot be spoken.
The memorial spire pierces the sky,
the dharma-body ever abides;
thus we know that our master's
true working stands alone revealed.
Stūpa Inscription for Chan Master Dafang Qian of Longgang Monastery, Imperially Bestowed

What the Chan lamp-records transmit is all rooted in the Five Houses, and the length of each dharma-lineage differs from one another. Since Master Xueting of the Yuan dynasty revealed the one school of Caodong, it passed through twenty-four generations at Shaolin down to Chan Master Dazhang Shuchan, who revived its way. Now Master Qian is his true heir. The master's dharma name was Ruqian, his style Dafang, his other sobriquet Songgu. He was a man of Qishan in Fengxiang, Shaanxi, of the Li clan. His father's name was Duo, his mother's Zhang. The master was born at Luoxing Village. As a child he loved Buddhist matters; whenever he came to a Buddhist temple it was like returning to his old home, and he would linger fondly and forget to go back. Early on he entered the village school and studied the Confucian arts, but his heart took no delight in them. He often told his parents, “I have heard that the Buddha's teaching is the cause of leaving the world; my vow is to leave the household life.” When he was seventeen his parents could not turn his resolve, so they gave him up to take refuge with Master Wuzong Ben of that commandery as his teacher, and he had his head shaved and took the dyed robes. After three years he roused his will and girded himself for travel, seeking teachers far and wide to settle the matter beneath his own feet. He first called on Elder Xi of Yue'an, who administered the full precepts to him and pointed out the road beyond; soon after he entered Qingfeng Mountain, dwelling alone shadowed by his own form, and there he had an awakening. Hearing that the patriarch Dazhang had opened the hall at Shaolin, he went to seek his confirmation. In the xinyou year of the Jiajing era he called on Zhang in the Stand-in-the-Snow courtyard and stayed on to attend him. Morning and evening he entered the master's room, where he was tempered and forged through the patriarchs' old koans, and so he received the master's seal of approval, with the charge “a jade thread in the eye of a needle, an iron ox at the bottom of the sea; toil day and night — remember this and keep it.” From this he understood the Caodong lineage's style and the purport of the five positions of the real and the partial; down to his time these had still not been lost. Once he had obtained the Dharma, with his bundle at his waist and a single bowl, he wandered all the famous mountains within the seas. Returning to the capital, he passed through the various lecture halls and plumbed deeply the tenets of nature and characteristics. Later he came to Huaiqing, where the Heir Apparent of Zheng had yielded his principality and was quietly cultivating pure karma. Hearing that the master had arrived, he received him with ceremony and invited his instruction, and they sealed a deep mutual accord. So he built a retreat at Longgang and invited the master to dwell there in tranquil silence. At that time students from every quarter came from far away at the mere rumor of him. In the dinghai year of Wanli he answered an invitation from Ciyun Nunnery in the capital and raised up the essential teaching. In the wuzi year Qianfo Monastery asked him to lecture on the sutras, and day by day ten thousand fingers encircled him. In the gengyin year, by the gracious decree of the Empress Dowager Cisheng, he opened the Pure Land dharma-gate at Cishou Monastery, with twelve hundred in the assembly; a gilded great Buddha image was reverently made and the Great Canon bestowed, with the imperial autograph in four characters, “Great Dharma-Treasure Canon,” to guard the decree. In the spring of the jiawu year he was invited back to Longgang, where a monastery was founded to enshrine and maintain these gifts. In the autumn of the wuxu year, on the eleventh day of the eighth month, he first showed a slight illness, and then passed away seated upright. The master was born in the wuxu year of Jiajing and lived sixty-one years in the world, with over forty years of monastic standing. His whole body was buried on the western plain of the monastery. Twenty-two years after the master's death, in the jiwei year of Wanli, his disciple Haiyun came on foot to Mount Lu to call on me and seek an inscription for his stūpa. I once met the master in the capital at Cishou and saw how his solitary bearing was stern and cold, like a tall pine standing in snow; when monks came to consult him he granted them no soft words or looks, and when he raised up the school and its teaching he always pointed to the beyond as the ultimate standard. In meeting circumstances and receiving people he was wholly and purely sincere, and in movement or rest he was never for a moment lax. He had the model of the ancients. When he talked with me for ten days and nights, there was nothing at which we did not slap palms and beat time in delight. He used to tell his students, “Master Han is the true eye of the Chan school in our age.” When I was exiled beyond the passes and the master returned to his old mountain, he would often speak to his disciples of his longing across ten thousand li. So this inscription was waiting for me to write it. Moved that the master was a knower of me in the Dharma-gate, I made this inscription for him:

One flower, five leaves;
two branches, five houses.
Their gateways and devices
each excelled in their own style.
Caodong's true source —
its pivot prized in mutual turning;
jade thread and golden needle —
in real and partial it dwells not.
Old Xue took it up again,
Master Shu carried on the work;
to our own Master Qian
the very bone and blood were handed.
An iron ox at the sea's bottom,
sealed at the moment's point.
Meeting a condition, that is the school;
fully he raised the true command.
Wherever he stood he pointed it out —
a bright mirror set on its stand;
no fair or plain is hidden,
opened wide as the character eight.
For more than twenty years,
entering mud and water with all,
hand in hand he served others,
wholly forgetting himself.
His fame reached the ninefold height,
his Dharma-light shone in a failing age;
the Dharma-treasury came down from heaven,
the dragon-spirits revered him.
Merit forgotten, works laid down,
he rested in woods and springs;
body and mind extinguished,
his light of wisdom wholly round.
Illusory conditions now exhausted,
he let go and straightway went;
what was never born cannot die —
how then could there be birth again?
The stūpa seals Longgang,
the dharma-body ever abides.
Ask him for the final word:
day breaks and it is not shown.
Stūpa Inscription for Master Gonggan Jing of Qianfo Monastery on Mount Lu

The master's dharma name was Renjing, his style Gonggan, his other sobriquet Huanshi. He was a son of the Wu family of Xiangyang. From birth he was unlike the crowd, and while still a child with hair unbound he had the will to leave the world. At Futian Monastery on Mount Funiu he took refuge with Dharma Master Gao'an, had his head shaved, and received the full precepts. He listened to lectures on the sutras and treatises and investigated the tenets of nature and characteristics, toiling day and night without slackening for three years, and in the teachings and contemplation he came to a deep faith and acceptance. His teacher said, “A student's aspiration should be vast and far; do not measure the sea with a tube or the ocean with a shell and think yourself sufficient.” So he went to the capital, where great Dharma Masters such as Dongyuan and Xianli were all the masters and craftsmen of the day. The master attended their lecture halls and exhausted the depths of their meaning. When Patriarch Dazhang opened up the purport of Bodhidharma's single transmission at Shaolin, the master cast aside all his doctrinal learning and went once more to investigate it. He lodged and relied there for more than ten years, then sighed and said, “This is mouth and ear only; the Way lies in the mind's realization. What use are empty words?” So he abandoned it and went to the demon-smelting ground at Mount Funiu. Within that great forge he let go of body and mind and sat long retreats for three years, and there he had an entry into awakening. Then he traveled everywhere to consult the wise and seek confirmation. Passing through Jinling, he found Chan Master Shouxin in seclusion at Hongji, whose hidden practice and secret conduct were esteemed by all his contemporaries. At first sight he found the master most remarkable, and he told him, “The Way lies in the mind's awakening, and is guarded in quiet and secrecy. Climbing mountains and crossing rivers only wastes your straw-sandal money.” So he kept the master in retreat, and together they cut and polished, daily reaching deeper mysteries, until his profound interpretations were wholly swept away. Thus it went for three years. When the retreat ended he at once, without hesitation, entered Mount Lu, intending to form a hidden retreat there for the rest of his life. That was the jimao year, the seventh of Wanli. When the master first entered the mountains he divined for a site and came to Jinzhu Terrace; seeing how broad and level it was, he sighed, “This is a dwelling place for five hundred people.” So he made a vow with the spirit of the mountain, willing to give his body and life here as an offering, to form a bond with monks from the ten directions. He cleared the brush and bound together a hut, and dwelt there shadowed by his own form, carrying the pestle and doing the work, while his disciple Zhilian assisted him. Thus the master was able to cut off all traces for three years. The next year, gengchen, Chan Master Daguan Ke came wandering there; seeing him, he found him remarkable and said, “You can set your mind at ease in such solitude; the progress of your practice must be beyond measure.” So they became inseparable friends, and after lingering more than a month he departed. In the guiwei year he answered an invitation from Wuzu Monastery in Huangmei and expounded the Lotus Sutra. Three years later, in the yiyou year, at the invitation of Lord Wu Guolun of Xingguo, he expounded the Śūraṅgama Sutra. That region had long been known as fierce and violent, yet many were moved and transformed by him. Lord Wu led the way and built halls and shrines for him, the work going on for five years, until in the jichou year the three halls, the meditation hall, and the kitchen and storehouses were finished. The master then went to Nanchang to raise funds for a great thousand-petaled jewel-lotus Vairocana image, with the Hanlin scholar Lord Deng Dingyu as his advocate. Before the work was half done, the master showed a slight illness and passed away. It was the seventh day of the sixth month of the xinmao year, the nineteenth of Wanli. He lived fifty-one years in the world, with over thirty years of monastic standing. Lian raced down from the mountain and wailed, not wishing to live on. Lord Deng urged him to continue the master's purpose and carry on his work, and so at last the master's vow was fulfilled: the great image was completed, and he bore the master's sacred bones back to the mountain and buried them behind the monastery. It was a certain month and day of the bingshen year of Wanli. The master had nine disciples whom he had brought to ordination, but Lian alone attended him longest. To him the master's wheel of vow was entrusted. Twenty-eight years after his entry into quiescence, in the dingwei year, his various dharma-grandsons each donated robes and bowls to build a stūpa and asked me for an inscription. The inscription says:

The great Way is like space —
there is nowhere it does not pass.
Only leave off obstruction,
and there is nothing it does not hold.
Deep and vast as the sea,
it flows hidden beneath the earth;
whoever bores into it
must reach the ground of reality.
Therefore one who bears the Way
rests upon forms and vessels;
when the heart's measure is like space,
the Way is complete of itself.
I observe our master:
forgetting self, he served all things;
he spread his mind like the earth —
only then was his vow fulfilled.
Look at that empty mountain:
a single handful of thatch;
yet he meant to shelter the ten directions,
letting whoever came come.
His vow was not yet ended
when he cherished his aim and took his leave;
but a son able to carry the house
at last raised up his work.
The Brahma-monastery rose splendid,
gatherers came like clouds;
they ate when hungry, rested when tired,
and none knew why it was so.
The master's mind ever abides,
his dharma-body is not extinguished;
it endures to the end of the future,
though stone rot and the seas run dry.
The stūpa's shadow stands on high;
pine-sough and spring's echo —
such is the wheel of Dharma,
for the one who knows the tune to prize.
Stūpa Inscription for Master Jingtang Zhong of Yunzhong Monastery on Mount Lu

The Buddha tamed living beings by countless skillful means; bodhisattvas sought the Buddha-way through various causes and conditions. Thus we know that to be a disciple of the Buddha and continue the Buddha's wisdom-life, one need not only sit on the jeweled seat, lift the mallet, and raise the whisk as the matter beyond; even one who turns his will to the mist and clouds and practices secretly and invisibly never fails to make the sound of springs and the voice of the wind his broad and long tongue. Was not Master Zhong of Yunzhong one who, within the white-hair radiance, sat at ease in mountain forests and sought the Buddha-way? The master's dharma name was Fazhong, his other sobriquet Jingtang. He was a son of the Cao family of She county in Xin'an; his mother was of the Cheng family. From birth the master was keen and extraordinary, and as a child with his hair in tufts he loved to sit upright and would not play with the other boys. At twenty he tired of the Confucian arts and took no pleasure in managing property, having early shown the will to leave the world. At nineteen he visited Lingyin Monastery in Qiantang, where he met Elder Daji, the monk of Yunshan, and at once asked to leave the household life. He had his head shaved and dyed his robes, and attended him for three years. At twenty-one he ascended the ordination platform and received the full precepts, and then attended the lecture halls, and in time he studied under many teachers. Yet he had no confidence in himself, so he went on pilgrimage as far as Shaolin, where Chan Master Daqian Run had opened the hall and was expounding the Dharma. The master relied on him and probed the purport of the single transmission. Before long he went to Chang'an and called on the two great elders Bianrong and Yuexin, who pointed out the essentials of mind. Soon after he returned to Mount Wutai. I was then living with Chan Master Miaofeng at the Dragon Gate of the north terrace, and the master visited us amid ice and snow. At one meeting our minds sealed a mutual accord, and he stayed on for a full year. In the renwu year of Wanli Master Miao took leave of me and went to Luya, dragging the master along with him. Soon a forest monastery was opened there, and in all that was founded and established the master had a hand. After three years he abandoned it and entered the fire-ground of Mount Funiu to temper and refine his three karmas. Returning south, he climbed Mount Lu and loved its secluded beauty, so he cleared brush on the Sutra-Chanting Terrace and dwelt there three years; then he returned to Five Elders Peak and lived there shadowed by his own form for four years. One day he climbed and surveyed Yangtian Flat, the very summit of Mount Lu, and delighting in its height and vantage, he settled there. For several years he was a lone man; gradually he repaired and built dwellings, and in time monks began to gather. With his own hands he planted more than a hundred thousand pines, hoping to make a forest monastery. The master was by nature ever level and plain, without ornament; he governed the assembly without setting up rules, and in every small matter he always put himself first, never tiring as he grew old. He kept to his lot as conditions came, and apart from a single robe he had no extra possessions; a grain of rice or a stalk of vegetable he was sure to share. He looked on all as one, practicing kindness with an even mind, and whether people were wise or foolish, worthy or unworthy, in time they were silently transformed without knowing it. Thus those who came were like children returning home to serve their parents. Whenever he spoke a word it was earnest and piercing to the heart, and no hearer failed to grasp it in his inmost mind. Therefore, though he did not ascend the hall or enter the room to instruct, the whole assembly was grave and orderly, like a great forge — for he taught by his own person. In the dingwei year I retired to Five Milk Peak and visited the master at Yunzhong; we rejoiced and talked over old times. One day the master came to me and we talked the night through, lying on joined beds, and he asked me to compose a record of the ten-direction permanent dwelling. Three years later, in the autumn of the gengshen year, he showed a slight illness. At the end he sat upright and told his disciples, “I see the red sun in the sky and golden lotuses covering the ground. I am going now.” Having spoken, he passed away in silence. It was the twenty-first day of the seventh month. The master was born in the xinchou year of Jiajing and lived eighty years in the world, with sixty years of dharma standing. In his later years he brought three disciples to ordination: Nenghuan and Nengwo were both men of She county, and Nengcheng was a man of Qianzhou. Wo performed the cremation for the master and collected his sacred bones, and a stūpa was built for their burial below Peach Blossom Peak. He brought a written account and asked me for an inscription.
