Stroking the page, I sighed and said, “When the master visited me at Mount Wutai, I saw him drifting like a lone crane riding the wind, and my heart deeply loved his soaring aloofness; so I firmly pressed him to stay, and said, ‘Can you be buried here with me?’ The master answered, ‘If there is a bond, it will surely come about.’ After that we parted, and I thought there would be no chance of meeting again. Who would have thought that in our declining years we would return to the same place, and that I would be the one to recount the master's life?” The inscription says:

The great Way is like space;
all dharmas share one body.
Whoever can use it well —
meeting a condition, that is the school.
Adverse or favorable, all as fits,
with nothing lacking anywhere;
this is the wise one's
many and various skillful means.
Pine-sough and spring's echo
pour forth the broad and long tongue;
how much more when at the very moment —
is this not skillful speech?
Therefore the utmost one
taught by his own person;
his secret practice fully displayed,
every thing was wondrous.
Breaking the soil, digging the earth,
carrying firewood, hauling water —
the great function stands before you;
what binds him to this or that?
To meet when there is a bond,
to act with no mind at all —
every dharma, every head,
all becomes liberation.
Shadowed by his form on the crags
as though facing a great assembly;
for more than twenty years,
lofty and unmoved.
Every pore of his whole body
spreads through the ten directions;
whoever enters there
is cooled through and through.
A monastery raised in Yunzhong,
monks coming from beyond the world;
rice gruel follows them as it comes —
a world of fragrant accumulation.
It lies with our master,
his effortless wondrous power:
using it without hiding it,
casting it away into emptiness.
His great vow was not yet ended
when illusory conditions ceased;
brushing his sleeves, he went,
with no word to say at all.
One stūpa props up the sky,
his sacred traces are lodged there;
his dharma-body ever abides
through the end of the future.
Stūpa Inscription for Master Fazhen Duo, the Practitioner of Huayang Mountain in Xuancheng

The master's dharma name was Daduo, his style Fazhen. He was a son of a certain family of Wanling. From birth he stood above the crowd, with a clear spirit and an open bearing. In childhood he attended the village school and read the Analects; coming to the line “If one hears the Way in the morning, one may die content at evening,” he said, “What thing is the Way, that hearing it should let one die?” and a great doubt arose in him. Again and again he asked the elders of the day about this, and none satisfied him. One day he met a wandering monk and asked, “What is the Way?” The monk said, “This is the Buddha's supreme and wondrous Way, and not merely the human virtues of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom.” From this the master came to believe firmly in the Buddha-way, and he took refuge with that monk and had his head shaved. He was then just twenty. The monk instructed him, “I am not your teacher; you should go and consult Yunqi.” So the master went straight to him and received the novice precepts. He had not long followed the assembly when he joined Xue Lang's lecture seat and studied the various tenets of the teachings. He constantly sought to awaken to his own mind but could not find the pointing. So he returned to Yunqi to receive the full precepts and asked for the essentials of cultivating the mind. He was shown the gate of Buddha-recitation, with single-mindedness as its guiding purport, and was given the book Chan Admonitions for Advancement as the formula for his investigation. The master accepted and treasured it. He returned to Shilong Cliff in his home commandery and kept retreat for three years, singly upholding one thought. After a long time he had an awakening. He went again to Yunqi to seek confirmation, and then followed the assembly, being winnowed there for several years. Taking his leave, he returned to Huayang Mountain in his home commandery and cleared brush to dwell there. Huayang traces its ancestry to Mount Huang and White Peak; it stretches about a yojana in every direction and is ringed by four counties. His hut stood amid ten thousand mountains, the most secluded and remote spot of all. The master lived there, planting only taro and tea, gathering acorns and pine pollen to make his food, and had utterly cut off all thought of the human world. Only one novice, Zhihao, attended him. When Hao read the Śūraṅgama Sutra and came to the passage questioning the mind, he asked, “The mind is sought in seven places and nowhere found; where after all is the mind?” The master struck the table once, and after a long while asked, “Do you understand?” Hao said, “No.” So he showed him the case of the Second Patriarch. After a long time he sent Hao to consult the teachers everywhere. The master dwelt alone. Monks and laymen asked him to expound the essential meaning of the Diamond Prajñā, and the master took up “All that has marks is delusion and falsehood; if you see that marks are no marks, then you see the Tathāgata,” and asked the assembly, “Do you understand?” The assembly said, “No.” The master said, “All conditioned dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow; like dew, like lightning — thus should they be contemplated.” Then he said, “Great assembly, each of you take good care of yourselves. I am going now.” He bathed at once and changed his robes, and passed away seated upright in Buddha-recitation. It was the eighteenth day of the seventh month of the wuwu year of Wanli. The master was born on the twenty-fourth day of the eighth month of the jiaxu year of Wanli, lived forty-five years in the world, and had twenty-eight years of monastic standing. He was buried at a certain place by the hut. When Zhihao returned from consulting teachers to visit him, the master had already entered quiescence three years before. Hao then crawled on his knees to Mount Lu and begged me for an inscription for the stūpa. Reading the account, I learned that the master had first roused his mind from the single saying that hearing the Way lets one die, and at once cast off the human world; though he drew near to the teachings, he did not prize words, but cut off all thought on the lonely shores of an empty mountain, singly upholding one thought and taking birth and death as the great matter. As for his conduct, so solitary and absolute, he was aloof like the ancient recluses of the mountains — this is what is hard to achieve in the final age. Alas, if such a manner as the master's could prevail, it would make the greedy among our followers dispassionate, the wild ones still, and the restless ones calm. What need then to sit on a jeweled seat to expound the Dharma? Moved by this, I made this inscription for him:

The root and spirit of prajñā
is planted in the earth;
when conditions meet it sprouts,
by timely rain brought forth.
One word of the Way he hears —
old habits are its own;
by chance a single touch,
and the thought before him shone.
Death may come, then, and welcome;
why long for life again?
He casts off worldly bonds
and enters the mountain glen.
No traffic with the tongue,
but raises the huatou high;
one thought, solitary and bright,
till self and other die.
On acorns and on pine bloom
he keeps the wasting frame;
floating clouds and phantoms
he counts as empty name.
In the silent, lonely hills,
lone wind and no companion.
Ask not about the guest —
look to the host in the host.
Death and life unchanging,
a lightning flash in space;
in quiescent extinction,
past feeling and past views.
Once stirred, he simply goes,
as if he had never come.
Empty flowers veil the eye,
wild dust-motes in the sun.
The stūpa’s shadow round,
steamed in mist and locked in cloud.
Ask him his final word:
green hills, bloom upon bloom.
The Stūpa-Banner Inscription of Bhikṣu Xingci

Bhikṣu Xingci was a son of the Pan family of Piling. By nature he loved to leave the world behind, and in childhood, hearing Dharma Master Yuezhu expound the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, he aroused the mind to leave home. He paid reverence to Dharma Master Yuguang on Mount Hua and sought to be shaved, and was taught the Pure Land Dharma-gate. Single-minded and wholehearted, he nobly cultivated the pure life. He delighted in nursing the aged and the sick, and his heart never tired of it. He trained himself in the Buddha-deeds of chanting and ritual. Later he met the monk Xingyu of southern Yunnan, and the two became companions on a journey to the Southern Sea. They cut thatch and dwelt together for more than ten years. Yu was ill year after year, and Ci tended him with diligence as though serving his own parents, never once showing a weary look; in the end Yu came through unharmed. In the jiwei year of Wanli they went together to Mount Kuang to receive the full precepts, and returned to Putuo, where Yu fell ill again. Ci nursed him with still greater care. In the gengshen year, moved by the milk of the Dharma, Ci came once more to pay his respects at Mount Kuang. His boat put in at Digang, and there he was seized by a slight illness; so he passed away sitting up in the boat, charging the three companions with him to cremate him on Zisha Island. It was the first day of the fifth month of the gengshen year of Wanli. When Yu heard of it he hurried to carry back the sacred bones, buried them at Putuo, and then went to Mount Kuang to relate the whole story and beg me to record it. Hearing it, I was moved and said: “The Book of Songs has it that brothers may quarrel within the walls. Yet in this world there are many of one flesh and blood who become bitter enemies — how much more so those of two surnames? But as for Ci and Yu: meeting all at once, they grew close through the Way, one in mind and never at odds, tending the sick for ten years as though it were a single day. Ci gave his whole heart in life, and Yu repaid the debt of gratitude after death. Truly this is what is meant by saying that only when one has died and the other lives is the friendship seen. I have therefore set their story in order; and further, to open up the meaning of the Dharma-gate, I would say that nursing the sick should be taken as the foremost practice. Ci was born on the seventeenth day of the first month of the guisi year; his worldly span was twenty-eight years. Yu was a son of the Xu family of Kunming in southern Yunnan, whose generations practiced Confucianism. I therefore record them together.” Then he made this inscription, saying:

Their roots long set in the Way,
they met without design.
In form apart, in mind one —
brothers in hardship, brothers true.
Each looked on the other’s body as his own;
in death and life they were not two.
Feeling that passes beyond all feeling —
and so it was with these two.
His bones lie buried at White Flower;
his mind is fixed in the ultimate real.
Let me ask the great being:
where did he come from, where go?
Stūpa Inscription for Master Yu’an Guangji of the Bowl-Casting Hermitage on Huangshan in Xin’an

The Master’s personal name was Guangji and his courtesy name Yu’an; he was a son of the Yu family of Kaihua in Quzhou. Born intelligent and wise, he had the will to leave the dust behind. At fifteen he told his parents and was permitted to leave home, entering Zhanggong Mountain in the prefecture, where Dharma Master Wuwei made him a śrāmaṇera. He loved learning and was capable in many things, broadly cultured and skilled in the arts, and he was forever going back and forth between Xiuning and Wuyuan. For a time there was no man of letters or official who did not hold him in esteem and delight in his friendship despite the difference in years. At twenty-four he sighed and said: “Human life is a colt glimpsed through a crack; if one drifts on like this, what is the good of having left home?” He therefore resolved to wander abroad and call upon teachers of knowledge. Several times he set out, but was detained by kin and friends and never got away; so he slipped off by night. With a single gourd and one staff he went straight to Yunqi. The Great Master saw him, thought highly of him, gave him the full precepts, and instructed him in the gate of Buddha-recitation, saying: “Buddha-recitation has no other device; it lies solely in single-mindedness undisturbed.” The Master bowed to this teaching, and so he was appointed to serve as wei-na. In daily life he was ever intent on pure cultivation, holding to a single thought, carefully restraining the three karmas, strictly ordering his deportment, harmonizing those within and without, and gladdening the hearts of the assembly. One day the Great Master addressed the assembly: “When the court appoints an official, fitness for the post is the highest mark. This holds not only for the state; so too in a monastery. In Sanskrit it is wei-na; in our tongue, one who gladdens the assembly. As for Monk Ji in the wei-na’s seat, he may be called truly fit for the post.” From this the whole assembly honored and respected him. He sat in one place for eight years, then returned to his home mountain to visit his teacher, and shut himself in retreat for three years. In the gengxu year of Wanli he entered the Chancellor’s Plain in Huangshan, cut thatch, and hid himself away in cultivation, spurring himself on in diligence, his single thought unmoving, as though he had forgotten the human world. After a long time the monks and laity of the region came to believe in him in great numbers, and Lord Wang Tunan built him a hermitage to dwell in, where he sat for twelve years. Then he was suddenly stricken with a grave illness, yet he said nothing at all and went about as usual, so that no one knew of it. In time the illness grew critical, and the country people asked a physician to examine him. The Master said: “Death and life are but a guest; when it is time to go, one goes. What is the use of anything else?” In the end he took no medicine, only sat calmly upright as though he had no body. One day he called his disciples and said: “I am going. This last matter — bear it in mind.” Having spoken, he crossed his legs and passed away. It was the second day of the second month of the xinyou year, the first of Tianqi. At first the disciples had not expected the Master to depart so soon and had prepared no burial niche, so they set him sitting on a low table; and fearing his form would change, they quickly heaped firewood to cremate him. But a great snow fell and they could not move him, and so it went for seven days. Monks and laity far and near, hearing of it, broke through the snow and ran to offer condolence. They saw the Master’s countenance as though alive, a joyful look as if he would speak, his lips still red, his hands soft as silk. All said: “This is a living man; how could we bear to burn him?” And they firmly stopped it. So they borrowed a Buddha niche to receive him and enshrined him in the abbot’s quarters where he had lived. Then the snow stopped. The disciples said to one another: “Is this not the last matter?” And so they too dared not burn him. Through the heat of summer and autumn his form and vital air did not change, and they meant to honor him three years before burial. In the third month of the following year, renxu, the disciple Dashou went to Mount Kuang and told the whole affair, asking for an inscription. Hearing it, I sighed and said: “In the conduct of us monks what is prized is true cultivation and real attainment, not the flaunting of fame and repute or the setting up of a house and hall as the goal. With the Master’s brilliance and many gifts, his wide learning and broad knowledge, once he entered the Dharma-gate he swept them all away and gave his whole heart to the Way, seeming dull and slow of speech. His single thought in daily life was dense and continuous. He would not utter a word when he met people, and to those who questioned him he gave only a single smile. As for his dealings with his fellows, forgetting self and other and casting off bodily form, there was none who did not love and reverence him. Was this not one who converted beings by his deportment, who awakened others by a dignified countenance, who taught the Dharma without words? Alas! As for the Master and death and life, his spirit departed while his form remained, turning rot and stench into the wondrous — was this not because of the perfuming of precepts and samādhi, the fusion and penetration of a refined mind? Even the Buddha’s and patriarchs’ adamantine indestructibility, their permanence and incorruption, comes about by this. Otherwise, before a single morning had passed, one would be no better than a piglet feeding at its dead mother.” Here I am moved, and so I made this inscription, saying:

All dharmas of the three realms
the mind alone has made;
to perish or not perish
in one single gate is laid.
The firefly’s light, the pearl’s —
though small the gleam they throw,
it too is exquisite,
a treasure’s rounded glow.
How much more the Buddha-nature,
the jewel-awakened mind,
which is our own by birth —
how fathomless, how deep!
Perfumed by precepts and samādhi,
the adamantine seed:
hence come the śarīras,
clustered as thick as ants.
Since there is a phantom form,
what phantom sickness spares?
The bond of fruit still holds;
our karma was fixed beforehand.
The Master’s bodily form,
kept long and never foul —
I think that there within
his mind’s light knows no stain.
From this refine and train,
life after life unretreating;
you shall surely arrive
at the adamantine ground.
To burn it or to keep,
no course is not well-taken.
But wait three years,
then come and tell me again.
I make this inscription
not for the Master alone:
I proclaim it to all —
let everyone strive on!
The Dream Roaming Collection of Old Man Hanshan, Volume Twenty-Nine
Stūpa Inscription for Master Danju Fake of Huacheng Monastery at Jingshan

Looking over the heroes of ancient and modern times: some had the talent to quell rebellion, yet could not subdue their own minds; some had the strength to uproot mountains, yet could not cut off attachment. Hence we know that to pass through the barrier of feeling and turn one’s back on death and life is not something even a great man can easily do unless his seeds were sown deep in former lives. In Master Kai I found something rare. The Master’s personal name was Fake, his courtesy name Renzhi, his other style Danju; he was a man of Jiangyin, of the Zhao clan, a family reputed to be of great standing. His mother dreamed of a monk sitting cross-legged in the hall, and so the Master was born. Born bright and wise, he delighted in Buddha-deeds as a child at play, and was unrestrained and far above his fellows. Grown, he studied the learning of the examinations and his talent and fame shone brightly, but he looked on worldly honor as dust and set his mind on the study of nature and destiny. His parents arranged a match for him, but he would not consent. When his father died he took up his staff and wandered alone, climbing Mount Taihe, where he met a Taoist adept who taught him the art of long life. Passing through Wuchang he met scholars who lectured on the innate knowledge of the good, and he shook his head and left them all. One day he entered a monk’s cell and saw the Diamond Sūtra. Reading as far as “all such minds the Tathāgata teaches are not minds,” he was suddenly awakened and said: “This is where I belong.” Returning by way of Fushan, he sat in the Three Bends Cave and wrote out the Classic of Filial Piety in his own blood. In the guisi year he traveled to Wan City. Chan Master Daguan was crossing the river there, and the Master went to call on him but did not meet him face to face; he bowed outside the gate. Only on a second visit did he see him, and when he asked to be tonsured he was not yet permitted. The Master then climbed to Mazu Hermitage, and the Master came there with Lord Ruan, arriving from Hua. That night the Master dreamed of a man clad in white armor attending at his side; and when the Master arrived, dressed in white, earnestly begging to be shaved, the Master consented and gave him his present name, shaved his head, and conferred the full precepts. He was then thirty-three. The Master charged him to investigate the matter of his own person, and so he took his leave and entered Mount Tianmu, cutting thatch at the Sutra-Dividing Terrace, where he hid himself in cultivation, solitary as a shadow, raising the huatou on high and striving in investigation with all his might. He ate vegetables without grain and wore a single robe with elbows bared; whenever the deluded mind rose he burned incense on his arm. Thus for three years, and he opened up greatly. Lord Yue Shifan came into the mountain and saw the Master in a worn robe and unkempt hair, face grimy and feet bare, a sickle at his waist gathering firewood. He asked him: “What are you to Monk Dan?” He answered: “I am the one he sends on errands.” Lord Yue laughed aloud and said: “A true man of the Way.” After a long while he came down from Tianmu and passed through Xuancheng, where he shut himself in retreat at Xile. There he trained himself to bear heavy loads, walking with forty catties on his shoulder to toughen his sinews and bones and to regulate his drowsiness, and his Way advanced the more. Later he left the retreat and went on pilgrimage to Mount Kuang. Whenever he passed a monastery he would sit beneath the eaves, and suddenly it would be dawn: waking and sleeping were one. In the xinchou year he came to the capital and visited his own teacher at Cishou. At his first entry into the room he asked: “I, so-and-so, am here for the great matter of birth and death; I beg the Master to instruct me.” The Master at once gave him a painful blow of the staff, and so it was a second time. One day he asked again: “Yongjia says, ‘Once enlightened, karmic hindrances are originally empty.’ What of the Venerable Siṃha, the Second Patriarch, Master Sengzhao and the rest — were they enlightened or not?” Before the words were out, the Master rained blows on him, saying: “Do you understand? Do you understand?” He said: “I do not.” The Master said: “This ‘originally empty’ — what sort of dry shit-stick is it?” The Master woke with a start and simply nodded. From then on his insight was steady and subtle. In the autumn of the renyin year he returned south and entered Fushan, lodging at Huisheng Cliff — the place where Master Yuan of the Song and Ouyang the Six-One discoursed on the Dharma over a game of chess. It had long since become lay property, and Lord Ruan Danyu of Wan City gathered his clan and restored it, inviting the Master to dwell there. He rebuilt the stūpa of Master Yuan and wrote out the Brahmā Net Sūtra in his own blood, daily reciting the Diamond Prajñā for his mother’s long life. In the wushen year, at the invitation of Lord Wu Guanwo, a court historian, he became abbot of the Great Huayan Monastery at Fushan. In daily life he made the fundamental matter his Buddha-work, and to patch-robed monks who came from all quarters he pointed out only what was direct and immediate. He gathered the accounts of how the patriarchs entered the Way and had them printed. At first Master Da had made Shuangjing Jizhao the site for carving the Great Canon, and the Master’s reliquary was brought there too. Wishing to fulfill his own teacher’s vow, the Master went there. In the gengxu year he came to the mountain and saw how misty and damp it was; below there was the old site of Huacheng, once the practice ground of Chan Master Fori Xuan of the Song. The court historian Lord Feng Mengzhen, known as Juqu, proposed restoring it as a place to store the printing blocks. The Master found a letter in his own hand and showed it to Lord Wu Benru, the left provincial administrator, who surveyed the site, marked the boundaries, wrested it from the hands of the powerful, and made it Buddha-land again. He also redeemed a hundred mu of the fields of Taiping Monastery in Lin’an to support the resident community. Thus the canon project found its home. In the jiayin year Lord Wu took up the governorship of Shu, and the Master went to discuss the affairs of the canon, and so climbed Mount Emei to worship Samantabhadra. In the spring of yimao he left Shu together with Lord Xu Ruogu, an investigating censor. That autumn he returned to Jingshan. The Great Master’s reliquary had already been interred, and Lord Zhu Wenning, Director of the Directorate of Education, paid reverence at the Master’s stūpa; following the geomancers’ words he learned that there was water in the ground, and proposed reburial. The Master, with Miao Zhongchun, a Dharma-protecting disciple of the Master, traveled about seeking a good site and chose a new place on the sunny side of Pengtuan Peak. In the winter of bingchen I came from Mount Nanyue to attend the mourning, fulfilling the Dharma-gate’s duty of death and life, and at Jinsha I composed a eulogy to sacrifice to him. The day had been set beforehand for the nineteenth of the winter-solstice month, and when I arrived at the assembly the cremation took place that very day. I applied the torch and asked that the sacred bones be placed in the stūpa, to repay a lifelong friend who knew me. Master Da’s final radiance was owing to the Master’s strength. The proverb says: “Under the stick the filial son appears.” The Master truly lived by it. I returned to Mount Kuang. The Master, weary of bridging and ferrying, handed Jizhao over to Master Gao and made Huacheng a receiving monastery of the ten directions for the resident community, charging his disciples: “Beneath your robes each of you has a patch of sitting-mat ground; why cling so fondly to this place?” In the seventh month of the autumn of xinyou he took leave of all his donors, passed through Baimen, and entrusted the canon project to Lord Wu Benru. In the tenth month of winter he returned to Shuangjing. One day, leaning on his staff below the hall, he turned to the assembly and said: “The antelope hangs up its horns and does not go beyond the twelve.” No one could fathom it. That evening he burned incense and paid homage to the Buddha, bathed and changed his robes, and sat cross-legged in silence. At dawn he suddenly passed away. It was the thirteenth day of the twelfth month of the xinyou year, the first of Tianqi. His disciples, certain of them, cremated him and buried him at a certain place. The Master was born on the twenty-first day of the third month of the xinyou year of Jiajing; his worldly span was sixty-one years, his monastic years twenty-eight. I had often seen how steep and lofty Master Da’s gate was, and always thought that afterward a man to match him would be hard to find. When I came to Shuangjing and met the Master, his countenance was pure and his bones firm, with a sharp and soaring heroic spirit. Those who came from all quarters to attend the burial arrived in droves, and a hundred affairs bristled and clustered together. The Master carved them up with a running blade and directed all as he pleased, his spirit at ease, his voice and face unmoved. In escorting the dead and giving him new life, in spending his form and ending his life for him, in continuing his will and setting forth his work, glorifying what went before and cutting off what came after — in this he was Master Da’s last disciple, not unworthy to be his true bone and blood. I say in private that the Master’s talent was enough to meet the world and his strength enough to carry the burden. As to the Way, there was no hardship or toil he did not fully undergo; as to affairs, when he saw what was right he did it with courage, not shrinking from the knife or the saw. He looked on gain and support as empty flowers and the moon in water, and at the brink of death and life he was detached as one kicking off worn-out sandals. Ah! Had he not been a great man whose roots from former lives were laid bare, whose mind was attuned to the unborn, who dwells and rests beyond the formed — how could he have been like this? The Master’s disciple Yuanliang prepared a full account and came to Mount Kuang to beg me for an inscription. Mindful of the bond of the Dharma-gate, I made this inscription, saying:

In Chan groves, autumn late is shed;
The Great Dharma’s net hangs by a thread.
In winter’s cold, in frost and snow,
Zibai shines out with steady glow.
His Way once bright, his gate grows steep,
Its courts and portals ever more deep.
Wall-like, a hanging cliff it stands;
Worlds apart from the common lands.
Who looks on it must shake with dread;
Who comes near turns away instead.
One staff of bramble, nothing more,
No caution kept, no bolted door.
The lion in his cavern deep
But now lets claws and fangs out-peep.
He is the lion’s cub indeed;
No turning back, no cautious heed.
Beneath one staff’s descending blow,
He flips and leaps up from below.
With sweeping strides he roams at will;
The road back home is wondrous still.
His whole body takes up the load,
And spares no strength along the road.
The Dharma store of Ganges sands
He scatters freely with his hands.
The Dharma wheel, an endless round,
Turns on, its turning never bound.
Ferry and bridge at last grow tired;
He follows conditions as required.
A traveler lodged, at peace, at rest,
A wall and shield where he walks, blest.
All that he did, he did for all;
The ten directions’ ever-abiding hall.
In life, he held no thing his own;
At the last, no thing was shown.
Not a speck of dust remains;
Fundamentally, thusness reigns.
The antelope hangs high its horn,
A sign made plain for all the born.
He lifts his hem and straight departs;
Lets fall his hands and homeward starts.
One stūpa stands, alone, on high,
Raised in the void of empty sky.
The dharmakāya, fully bare,
In the wind’s voice and moonlight fair.
Inscription for Master Ruiguang Faxiang, Lord of Mount Nanyue

Throughout the whole measure of the Dharma-realm, there is not one thing that is not the dharmakāya; within all the gates of affliction, there is not one practice that is not Buddha-work. How much more so for one who disciplines the three karmas, fixes his whole heart on one point, withdraws far from the world, and diligently walks the Pure Land path. Thus the white-hair light of our Buddha illumines eighteen thousand worlds to the east, and within that light bodhisattvas seek the Buddha-way by countless means. Was Master Xiang of Nanyue not one revealed within that light, gathering his thoughts in mountain forests and single-mindedly seeking the Buddha-way?

According to the record: the master’s dharma name was Faxiang, his courtesy name Ruiguang, his style Yinnan, a son of the Zhou family of Sheng County in Yue. Lofty and free by nature from birth, he studied the Confucian texts but failed the examinations, and with a sigh conceived the will to leave the world. He traveled to the capital with his uncle and went to consult the elder Xiaoyan. Xiaoyan pointed him to the ultimate. The master said, “Your disciple is a man amid the dust of affliction; I dare not take that upon myself.” Xiaoyan said, “The gate of Buddha-recitation is the most swift and essential of all.” The master nodded in assent.

Not long after, he returned south and resolved firmly to leave the household. He bowed to Master Kai of the Joy Hermitage in his home district and had his head shaved; he was then thirty-two years old. He paid his respects to Dharma Master Su’an of Qixia and received full ordination; he relied on the lecture halls of Qixia for three years, then gave them up and left. Journeying north to the great capital, he consulted the venerable Bianrong. At their first meeting Bianrong asked, “How do you practice?” The master said, “I left home for the sake of birth-and-death, and have all along practiced the gate of Buddha-recitation. I do not know whether this is the supreme truth.” Bianrong said, “You must not seek the supreme truth anywhere apart from Buddha-recitation.” The master received the instruction and bowed.

The Empress Dowager Cisheng undertook great Buddhist works and established a Pure Karma session, inviting him to hold the chief seat. When the three-year session ended, he traveled to Wutai and to Funiu, consulting all the venerable elders. At that time the monk Baisong was an old resident of Mount Niu; meeting him, the master spoke with him and their minds were in accord. He was kept in a stone chamber, alone with his shadow and cut off from all traces, eating only plants for three years. One day, as he sat cross-legged, snow piled up over his seat, the fire had gone out, and his clothes were soaked through. The attendant came to look, and ran off in alarm to tell Baisong. Baisong came to see and found the master in samādhi; he struck a chime to rouse him and asked, “Smoke cold, ashes chill — what state do you make of it?” The master said, “The mountain was always stone; the ice was always water; snow flies over the cliffs — I do not know why.” Baisong said, “This is only a temporary rest from the toil of affliction, a mere ease and lightness. If you cling to this state, you fall into one-sided emptiness. Do not linger here; you should go on pilgrimage. Where you meet the south, stop there.” He gave him a bowl and a bag, and instructed him: “Southward the Chan monk makes his way;
Report the number seventy-nine.
My own time is not long to stay;
Let us keep our watch, yours and mine.”

The master then, with gourd and bamboo hat, went straight to Mount Emei to pay homage to Samantabhadra. He stayed at Great Emei Rock for eight months, investigating with keen urgency, yet his mind-ground was not at peace. Remembering Baisong’s prophecy of meeting the south, he went to Nanyue and climbed to the summit of Zhurong Peak. Gazing toward ancient Daming, where the mountain forests grew thick and fair, he went there to choose a dwelling. Before long the monk Churan of Chidi Peak asked him to preside over a reading of the canon. The master arrived and stayed one night; at midnight, as if in a dream, a voice told him, “This is not where you should dwell. Leave quickly.” At dawn he was about to go elsewhere when the monk Dakuan pressed him to stay at Chedao Peak; the master agreed. Three days later the canon was destroyed. Since Xiaoyan had revealed to him the gate of Buddha-recitation, the master resolved to devote his whole life to it. He wished to use beans as counting beads, and Dakuan volunteered to be the alms-collector, gathering forty-eight piculs of beans. From then on the master put down body and mind; his shadow never left the mountain. Day and night he practiced with diligence, using beans for beads, pure mindfulness continuing without a break, to the end of his life. Hence he was called the Bean Buddha.

Dwelling on the mountain, the master had no outside ties at all, yet his fame and light shone out more each day. Monks from the ten directions came from far away to take refuge with him; the four requisites arrived unlooked for; a monastery took shape without his building it. Nanyue, long silent and deserted, was stirred to life by him alone. In daily conduct he constantly admonished his disciples: “You have shaved head and beard, yet you do not know that there is the great matter of birth-and-death. Leaning on walls and propping against posts, your karmic consciousness vast and blind — what would you call that? Is it not what our Buddha rebuked? To wear the robe in idleness and falsely call yourself a forest-dweller — if you do not single-mindedly devote yourself to the Pure Land practice, when the final limit comes, how will you answer King Yama?” Those who heard were moved to tears.

Though the master had cut off all intent toward the world, gentlemen of the age who heard of him admired him from afar. Mr. Liu, provincial administrator of Guangxi, while visiting the shrine, sent a letter asking to meet him once; the master firmly declined and did not go. Mr. Lu, vice-prefect of Hengzhou, while sacrificing at the shrine, fined those who missed the appointed hour and pledged more than thirty piculs to be sent to the master. The master said, “Would this old monk, for the sake of a single bowl of rice, gather up the resentment of the crowd?” In the end he would not accept it. The Prince of Ji in Changsha admired the master and sent an inner envoy to invite him. The master said, “This mountain monk, wearied by wandering, has rested his shoulders here. I have sworn to follow Master Huiyuan even unto death; my traces do not enter the world. I dare not accept the command.” The prince sent the same envoy again, bearing two copies of the Avataṃsaka Sutra, one copy of its Great Commentary, and a hundred taels for a vegetarian feast. The master accepted the prince’s command; he distributed the feast funds throughout the mountain to spread the prince’s bounty, and kept the rest to secure the mountain gate. The prince esteemed him all the more.

The master received all comers without judging good or bad, with one flavor of equal compassion. Seven great bandits of Jingxiang — Jia Er, Tang Jiu, and others — hard pressed by pursuit, came to take refuge, confessed and repented, and pleaded piteously for their lives. The master pitied their sincerity and took them in; he gave them Daoist head-wraps to wear and had them work with the community. When the arresting officer arrived and saw the master’s kindly, gentle heart, and heard the sound of Buddha-recitation, he was moved: he untied the three pieces of gold at his waist, provided a feast, and departed. The bandits too were transformed into ascetic monks. In the famine year of xinchou, 1601, the community ran out of food for three days and gathered ferns to eat. The master prayed day and night to the Dharma-protecting deities, and a young monk appeared who had collected more than a hundred piculs of rice and beans from donor households below the mountain and delivered them; when they asked after that monk, he was nowhere to be found.

From the time he settled at Chedao Peak, the master cultivated the Pure Land practice with devotion for more than thirty years, never pausing even briefly. As a rule his ribs never touched a mat. He did not set up an abbot’s quarters, but only sat in a single niche in the Buddha hall; he kept no storehouse, and his chest held no surplus. On the day of his passing there were only a bottle of pepper and a few scraps of old cloth. He did not trouble attendants, did not send out alms-collectors, did not form outside alliances, and did not consort with the powerful. He ate coarse fare, often making cakes of bran and chaff for his meals. When monks threw scraps on the ground, the master would pick them up, roast them, and eat them. Whenever he walked in recitation, he carried a hoe out with him, and whenever he saw refuse or filth he covered it with earth. Someone asked, “Why does the master trouble himself so?” He replied, “This is a pure and clean land; I fear the mountain god might see the filth.”

All his life the master followed the community; past seventy, he still had no dharma heir. A layman of Linjiang, Mr. Fu, who had long traded on the rivers and lakes, one day abandoned wife and children and left home at Mount Emei, taking the name Tongrong. In the winter of the renyin year of Wanli, 1602, he came to consult the master; their minds sealed in mutual accord, and the master at once transmitted robe and bowl, with the verse: “If you ask the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West,
Has it been seen, right up to now, or not?
When nothing arises in the mind, what seeing could there be?
Suruṣṭi svāhā.” Tongrong stayed with him to the end.

The master moved among the community as always, untiring in his dealings with them. One day he asked for a bath, bowed to the Buddha, and told the assembly, “The melon is ripe; it is just the time for it to drop from the stem.” No one in the hall understood. At that time Tongrong was living at Pifo Cave, and someone was sent to summon him. As Tongrong reached the front of the peak he heard music; entering the room, all was silent. The master sat cross-legged; Tongrong bowed. The master said, “I am going. I earlier entrusted bowl and bag to you; now I leave you my recitation beads and staff in farewell. Guard them well.” After a long while he had the chief seat lead the assembly in Buddha-recitation. Sitting cross-legged, the master admonished the assembly: “Do not make false displays or fabricate marvels to deceive the world. Just single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name in all honesty.” When he had spoken, he joined his palms, sat upright, and passed away. It was the sixth day of the second month of the gengxu year of Wanli, 1610, at the hour of yin, between three and five in the morning. The master was born on the full-moon day of the ninth month of the renchen year of Jiajing, 1532; his worldly span was seventy-nine years, his dharma age forty-three. The assembly made offerings to him in the hall for seven days; his countenance did not change. His whole body was buried to the right of the peak, and a stūpa was built.

I recall that long ago, when I was in the Eastern Sea region, Mr. Zeng of the Ministry of Rites told me of the master’s austerities and lofty conduct, no less than those of the ancients; I took it to heart at the time. Fourteen years after the master’s nirvāṇa, in the guihai year, 1623, I returned to Caoxi, and Master Tongrong prepared a record and came to beg an inscription for the stūpa. Stroking the record, I sighed deeply and said: Alas! The age is far from the sages, the Dharma gate is withered and decayed, and the model of the monastery has nearly been swept from the ground. Drifting on the waves, all are swallowed up in fame and profit and lose their original truth; the decline of the Dharma has come even to this. But as for pure conduct and bitter discipline, one thought held for a lifetime, unchanging from first to last — one like the master may be said to have taught the Dharma with his own body. What need was there for him to mount the curved seat, raise the mallet, and hold up the whisk, to be called “upward”? Seeing how the master came and went through death and life with no hindrance at all — was he not one who entered the Unborn through the mind of Buddha-recitation? Ashamed that I cannot reveal the master’s hidden depths, I have made this inscription. The inscription says:

In all the worlds of the ten directions,
The dharmakāya gives responses.
Through every gate of toil and dust,
This is the wondrous practice, just.
How much more, with a single heart,
Pure mindfulness that will not part.
Unchanged from first to last degree,
By day and night, unceasingly.
Alas, in the Dharma’s latter day,
Chasing after things, we lose the way.
But our master, all for the Way,
Forgot himself from day to day.
Once within the thousand peaks he came,
He walked as if on knives of flame.
Thus he gained samādhi’s door,
Named No-Contention, evermore.
All outer conditions he cut away,
And used beans for beads, day by day.
Luminous, distinctly clear,
Mind and world are thus, right here.
His shadow never left the peak,
His traces shunned the worldly street.
His bitter discipline, edged and bare,
His pure breeze blowing everywhere.
The four assemblies came to stay,
Gruel and rice along the way.
One flavor and an even heart,
Each one doing his own part.
With a mind on Buddha bent,
Straight into the Unborn he went.
So his last word, plain and clear:
Tuck up your robe and go from here.
Stark naked, one body alone,
Not an inch of thread was sewn.
Seventy-nine years he passed,
Then the whole body dropped at last.
Coming, he clung to nothing here,
Going, he left no footprint clear.
Therefore I name him, and I say,
A true good friend upon the Way.
The stūpa’s shadow spans the sky,
Its light flows over Nanyue high.
With the broad and lengthy tongue,
Ever blazing, ever sung.
Water flowing, wind in flight,
Buddha and Dharma they recite.
This is our master, none beside,
The precious raft across delusion’s tide.
Stūpa Inscription for Master Gufeng Chun, Founding First Abbot of the Imperially Established Great Nation-Protecting Cishou Temple

When the World-Honored One taught the Dharma, as the three baskets set it forth, he declared that manifesting a body according to kind is in every case the true mark of reality; and when he held up a flower before the assembly and Kāśyapa smiled, he declared that touching a thing one understands the mind, a single transmission directly pointing. Those who studied the Buddha-way in ancient times — to understand this may be called possessing the eye of the true Dharma.

As for Chan Master Gufeng: he began as a layman and ended with the marks of a bhikṣu. Following conditions to benefit beings, no one could fathom his hidden accord. How could such a one be sought through the two truths?

Reverently perusing the master’s record: his name was Juechun; he was a man of Xincheng in Baoding. His father was Song Qin; his mother was of the Zhang family. From birth his nature would not take meat or wine. As a child he loved to sit cross-legged. When he grew up he had no liking for managing property. His parents married him a wife, and though he complied under constraint, he was skilled at contemplating emptiness and practiced the way of freedom from desire. He often gathered good men together to hold Prajñā and Perfect Enlightenment assemblies, and the master was the eldest among them, naturally keen and awakened.

At twenty-seven he left home and traveled far, going to the capital, where he mounted the platform and received the lay precepts. The great good teacher Baozang Cheng was teaching the Dharma in the royal city; the master went to consult him and felt a deep accord, and was at once shaved, taking up the duties of a disciple. He always kept to the lowest rank; though it meant tending the stove and carrying grain to the mortar, he never failed to put himself first in labor. Though Cheng at times disapproved of him, his resolve to serve only grew firmer. After three years, Cheng finally had him receive full ordination. He studied under the two Dharma masters Shouxin and Wu’ai, hearing the Avataṃsaka, the Perfect Enlightenment, the Śūraṃgama, and other sutras. At the words “when the four elements disperse, where is the deluded body?”, he had an understanding and accord.

From then on, wherever he went he established Avataṃsaka and Perfect Enlightenment Dharma grounds, with no empty day in the year. The royal city was moved and transformed, as though Kapilavastu had taken on a new face, and his fame flowed through court and country. Thus for more than ten years.

In the xinyou year of Jiajing, 1561, Mr. Huang of the Directorate of Ceremonial and Mr. Jiao of the Embroidered-Uniform Guard, among others, rebuilt Pu’an Temple and invited the master to reside there, for nearly twenty years. The master simply occupied the abbot’s room and invited such Dharma masters as Yijiang, Daqian, and Zhi’an to propagate the tenets of the Tiantai and Xianshou schools. In the renshen year of Longqing, 1572, the late emperor first honored the Buddha’s way; at Pu’an a Hall of Auspiciousness was established, and the master presided over the altar. His sincerity moved heaven, and imperial favor was bestowed in abundance, the provisions for the feasts all coming from the inner palace. In the first year of the present emperor, 1573, the two palace empress dowagers, praying for the altars of state, undertook great Buddhist works; whenever a vegetarian altar was set up, it was mostly at the master’s place. He was once granted a brocade kāṣāya of a thousand Buddhas. All within the inner Sutra Printing Office, and all who wished to perform Buddhist services, generally followed him.

In the bingzi year of Wanli, 1576, the present emperor, carrying out the gracious intent of the Empress Dowager Cisheng Xuanwen Mingsu, completed the imperially established Great Cishou Temple and at once transferred the master to be its abbot. He was commanded to ordain one śrāmaṇera as his disciple, and was charged with editing the continuation of the Great Canon; the master led this work. Whatever Buddhist undertakings he propagated, all met with the imperial approval. At that time the whole Dharma gate within the seas knew the master as a great Dharma banner.

In daily life he received the four assemblies, but he would raise only the verse from the Perfect Enlightenment — “Knowing illusion, one is free of it at once, without resort to means; freed from illusion, one is awakened, with no gradual stages” — and the Śūraṃgama’s samādhi of illusoriness; or he would take up the ancients’ ultimate cases to alert and awaken them. At leisure, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, he would often cluck and mutter to himself. Those who saw or heard him changed countenance, and none realized that he was a hidden practitioner. Throughout his life, wherever he went, he never left the place at hand, yet he spread the school’s wind far and wide; none could fathom his limits. Many called him a flesh-body great being.

One evening he summoned his disciples and told them he was slightly unwell. He sat upright for three days, then calmly gathered the assembly to recite the Buddha’s name and, as the sound went on, passed away in silence. It was the seventeenth day of the fourth month of the ninth year of Wanli, 1581. The master was born in the xinwei year of Zhengde, 1511, and died in the xinsi year of Wanli, 1581; his worldly span was seventy-one years, his monastic age more than forty. He ordained fifteen disciples and had more than eighty dharma grandchildren. Among them, Benzai was by imperial appointment Shanshi of the Buddhist Registry and served as abbot of the present Cishou Temple. His whole body was enshrined and buried in the rear garden of the temple. The Empress Dowager mourned him and granted a sum of gold to build a stūpa in his honor. The inscription says:

The Dharmakāya is like empty space.
Neither sound nor form it knows;
Responding to things it shows a shape,
As in water the moon appears.
Wherever it touches, all is so —
What is true, and what is mere?
Even this monk's body here
Is likened to an empty vale.
Venerable indeed is Gufeng,
Born in an age of image and simile.
Lofty his bearing and aspiration,
Doing the great Buddha-work.
True and conventional both displayed,
Form and spirit alike sublime.
He did not leave the market town,
Yet spread the utmost Way abroad.
His responses were clear and bright,
Gods and men revered him still.
Silently he turned the pivot of the sphere,
Dragons tamed and tigers quelled.
His spirit reached the purple palace,
His sincerity turned the Northern Dipper.
The Dharma Way flourished and grew great,
Pearls rolling round a polished plate.
The Brahma cloister had scarce arisen,
The jewel palace but newly built,
When his wind filled all within the bounds,
Swift as wind and lightning joined.
One pipe of breath brought spring to life —
The reed-ash rose within the tube.
The whole earth shone with radiance;
Truly it began from here.
Who then was this Master —
A transformation, or a phantom made?
How could he have received a secret charge,
And come to practice skillful means?
Seventy years and more he lived,
Yet to him it seemed a moment's meal.
The onlookers are dazed, in doubt,
Their fevered dreams not yet awake.
With a snap of the fingers he returned to emptiness,
Breaking into a smile.
On a ten-thousand-fathom pool
He merely let one fishing line hang down.
The marker stūpa soars into the sky,
Tall pines trailed with mist.
Moonlight and the sound of wind —
The true mechanism stands revealed alone.
Tower Inscription for Master Rui'an Zhen, Eighth Abbot of Longhua Monastery at Jintai

The Master's dharma name was Guangzhen; his courtesy name, Rui'an. He was a son of the Sun family of Jintai. By nature he was full of strange and uncanny traits; as a child he was not counted among the ordinary boys, and all who saw him thought him extraordinary. In his heart he loved Buddha-work, and would often murmur words of renunciation. Rong'an Mao of Longhua Monastery, who held the post of Left Expounder of the Teaching in the Buddhist Registry and was a man of weighty conduct, happened one day to be at a vegetarian feast among the Sun family, and saw the Master, then just seven years old, possessed of a singular spirit. He begged for him as a novice, and so had him become a disciple of his own senior disciple, Master Cang. As he grew up, he delighted in making the Buddha-work out of sound, disciplining the three karmas and cultivating the six daily periods with diligence. In daily life he always set his resolve on the matter that lies above. At thirty he mounted the ordination platform and received the full precepts. Master Datong's teaching flourished widely, and he served him with diligence, hearing many essentials of the Dharma. With the beginning of the Longqing era, the Minister of Rites recommended him as abbot of Longhua. The Master then threw open the Dharma community, inviting Chan and doctrinal masters and gathering scholars from the four quarters to read through the great canon and expound the two cardinal teachings of Shaoshi and Tiantai. Masters such as the Chan teacher Darun of the Qian, who revived the Caodong lineage, and all who became teachers and masters of the regions, for the most part began their careers here. When the Chan teacher Miaofeng Deng was still obscure, he came to the Master over the matter of the great canon, and the Master brought him to the notice of the nobles and ministers, so that his reputation for the Way became great. Master Miaofeng, being one whom the Dharma gate advanced, also relied on this support. His present Majesty esteems the Three Jewels; throughout the land, famous monasteries and men of knowledge, all who perform Buddha-work, mostly come from the Master's gate; he was generally known as a treasury of merit. In the spring of the dingchou year, Master Miaofeng and I were living in reclusion at Qingliang. The Master, inclining his heart toward us in admiration, traveled to the five peaks and sought us out through snow and ice. After a short stay he left his staff and journeyed south, bowing to Avalokiteśvara at Putuo. He entered Tiantai and hid himself on the summit of Tongxuan Peak, perching like a bird and eating like a nestling for three years, devoting himself wholly to the single-practice samādhi, and gained some awakening thereby. Soon after he took his leave and turned east into Wu, bowing to the śarīra at Changgan. He traced the Yangtze upward, climbed Jiuhua, ascended Mount Lu, tamed the Yellow Dragon and the White Deer, bowed to the Five Elders and gazed toward Incense Burner Peak. He circumambulated the Mañjuśrī sutra platform three times, then cleansed his profound contemplation and rested. Passing through Huangmei, he sought confirmation of his understanding there. Again he let his eyes wander over Wudang, reached Nanyue, and sought the place where the Dharma Flower samādhi was realized. He returned and entered the community of practitioners at Funiu, staying three months before going back. In the spring of the ninth year of Wanli, the xinsi year, the Master was fifty-four years old. After a short while, Master Miaofeng and I convened a great assembly at Qingliang, and the Master, together with Master Ping of Shuanglin and Master Yun of Wuzhe, entered the Dharma community. In the spring of the renwu year the assembly concluded, and the Master and I again went into retreat together in the Taihang Mountains. By early winter the Master had returned to his old dwelling. The following year I too crossed east to the seacoast, vowing to return home together with the Master. The year after that, the jiashen year, in obedience to the command of the Empress Dowager Cisheng, the Mother of His Majesty, I joined Master Miaofeng in offering food to the monks at the famous mountains of Qin, Jin, Yi, and Luo. Thereupon I went out through the pass to Luya, crossed the river and climbed Mount Hua, toured Chang'an, viewed the lingering shadow at the Wild Goose Pagoda, and sought out the place where Kumārajīva had translated the sutras at Caotang. We kept the summer retreat at Guifeng, gazing toward Taibai and Taiyi, passed lightly through Xiao and Han and went east, and entered Funiu once more. I visited Songshan and Shaoshi, investigating the single transmission of the ancestral patriarch, mourned Master Run, and knocked at Baima before returning. Before long I again received the compassionate decree and carried the great canon to Tiantai and Mount Lu, then sent word back from Qingliang. The Master sighed deeply and said: A single humble monk has time and again presumed upon the compassionate command; examining my heart and reviewing my virtue, I am ashamed — how can I bear it? So he pleaded illness and dwelt alone, shutting out men and cutting off his traces, and long since handed the affairs of the monastery over to his disciples, content in his daily life and with no thought for the world. All his life he put himself last and others first, taking no account of things. His precept-jewel and mind-moon were like autumn dew on the cold sky; his features were ancient and his spirit clear, like a tall pine or a solitary crane. Distant yet warm, he could be loved but not approached, could be treated lightly but never ignored. Surely he was a flower of the Dharma eye, a model for a whole generation of monastic communities. Master Daguan Ke once said to me: Longhua in our gate is like the mirror of Qin — it can truly reflect a man's liver and gall. It is also like a wish-fulfilling gem wrapped in floss: take it up at will, and there is nothing wanting. Such was the esteem in which he was held by his contemporaries. The Master nursed his illness for a full year, and I came from the seacoast to inquire after him. He took my arm, wept, and said to me: Birth and death are a dream, a phantom; going and coming are night and dawn. That is not what grieves me. Only that I cannot return home together with you — I have failed the covenant of the mountains and the sea. When at last we part forever, I shall strain my eyes toward you from within the Pure Land. As for the dregs I leave behind, let my disciples serve you as they would have served me in life, and do you regard me as one who has not died. He said again: The Dharma gate is desolate and fallen — this weighs on my grief anew. Masters Miao and Da, and the gentlemen of the secret treasury and the rest, are all the outstanding talents of our time. Our true covenant, yours and mine, should be to forget the mind for the sake of the Dharma. Pray convey my thanks for me. Before long he summoned his disciples and said: I have relied on being a son of the Buddha, and am ashamed that I have added nothing to the Dharma gate. Only this heart of mine through life has never dared betray the Buddha's grace. In life you may count me insufficient; in death I shall have abundance. Do you strive at it. I am going now. Do not forget the Eastern Sea. Prepare robes for me as an offering. With these words he passed away. It was the twenty-third day of the fifth month of the seventeenth year of Wanli. The Master was born in the wuzi year of Jiajing; his worldly span was sixty-two years, his Dharma-seniority over thirty. He had two disciples whom he ordained; Sun Zhitan tended the Master's reliquary chamber, and his whole body was buried on the left of Longxi Monastery at Haidian in the northwest of the capital. In the tenth month of that winter, Zhitan, in obedience to the Master's command, brought a single set of his robes and came crawling on his knees to the seacoast to report the death to me. Alas, how sad. Alive, or dead? Who then was the Master? So I set out the record of his conduct as follows, and made this inscription.

A body filling the whole Dharma-realm,
Cultivating Samantabhadra's deeds.
The ocean-seal's awe-inspiring power
Shines out as one, made manifest.
Now appearing as a dhūta ascetic,
Now dwelling in the marketplace —
Dusty town or mountain grove,
Nothing but the Buddha-work.
It was our Master who
Took the form of a monk.
Precept-eye and compassion-flower,
A model for all men.
A bodhimanda of perfect enlightenment,
Where the ten directions gather.
Let those who come know this:
No within, no without.
Like a wish-fulfilling pearl,
Like a treasury of merit,
Bringing forth wonderful blessings
And offerings countless as the sands.
From above it is lifted up —
A single bowl of fragrant rice.
All who see or hear of it
Are granted deliverance.
He split Tiantai asunder,
Trampled Mount Lu flat.
As a lotus flower opens,
As from a great dream one wakes.
He journeyed through the whole world,
Gathering the sand-realm in his bag.
With bare hands he came home,
With no money for buying and selling.
Over sixty years and more,
Death and birth as night and dawn.
Call him, he will not turn his head —
He was first to reach the other shore.
He cast off the skull,
And buried it in a heap of sand.
A stūpa marks the long sky,
Its shadow sunk in autumn water.
This is the Master's constant body,
Shining clear as this.
Stele Record and Inscription for the Vow-Power Stūpa of the Layman Xu Zhengguang at Longquan Monastery on Mount Wutai

Observe how the true realm stands still and whole, while the signs of its responsive transformation are never one; sages and ordinary beings walk different roads, and the traces of benefiting others are therefore distinct. Hence phantom shadows take many forms, and floating light wears ten thousand postures. As for one who relies on vow-power to sustain his mind and uses a stūpa to express his vow — this is what is seen in the layman Zhengguang. The layman's surname was Xu; he was a man of Baoding County in Bazhou. His father was Xu Shen, his mother of the Gao family. He was born with unusual marks: at one year old he could speak of matters from former lives, and in movement and rest he was measured like a heavenly being. In the thirty-fourth year of Jiajing, when he had just turned seven, he was selected to enter the palace apartments and was placed in the Inner Hanlin Bureau to study. He advanced to be a bureau official, was taught the rules of inner conduct, and put in charge of the secret archives; and already he could master the precedents with ease. With the beginning of the Longqing era he was promoted to serve before the throne, diligent and cautious with merit. At the start of Wanli, when His present Majesty came to the throne and the roll of merit was recorded, he was raised to the Palace of Heavenly Purity as palace memorial transmitter. He served three reigns with cautious reverence, attending the Empress Dowager's daily life with vigilance morning and evening, harmonizing the hub and pivot and aiding the workings of transformation, in which his strength was great. As his virtue and rank grew daily, his faith in the Three Jewels deepened. Outside Chongwen Gate in the capital he built the Mingyin Monastery, one compound, printed and distributed one complete Buddhist canon, and invited the monk Yongqing to be its abbot. At the old road ridge of Mount Wutai in Shanxi he restored Longquan Monastery, reported it to the Empress Dowager, ordained the novice Yuanjian and granted him the post of Left Awakener of Meaning in the Buddhist Registry as abbot of that monastery. He also restored a Fengxiang Monastery north of Quyang County in Zhending, and set aside over three hundred mu of land to supply incense and fire for Longquan and to receive visitors from the ten directions. Throughout the realm, at every famous mountain and great monastery touched by the Empress Dowager's merit, he never failed to assist in silence the imperial design and spread the compassionate teaching, so that one rain fell everywhere and living beings obtained blessing. Though the layman dwelt in the deep palace, he wore only plain cloth and was content with vegetable food. He always wearied of birth and death and set his mind on liberation. Morning and evening he paid reverence and made obeisance, unchanging through cold and heat. He pricked his blood to write out the Diamond Prajñā Sutra, the Practices and Vows of Samantabhadra, and several fascicles of the Lotus Sutra's mind chapter. He built a stūpa at the southeastern foot of Longquan to express how his vow-power sustained his mind, his merit flowing through vast kalpas, quenching this fierce flame, dwelling forever in coolness, looking to future lives for refuge, and resolving to accomplish it within this one life — as a Vajra seed and a spiritual sprout, a field of blessing to endure forever. Ah — was not the layman one who came bearing a personal entrustment? Or did he use an illusory body among gods and men to perform the Buddha-work? How else could his wisdom be so deep and his resolve so firm as this? When the merit was accomplished, he commanded his household official Cheng Jin, holding a staff, to bow his head before the Wayfarer of the Ocean Seal and beg that the matter be recorded. So I made this inscription.

Heaven and earth's creating work
Bred spirit, bore the fair.
Then came down a wise one —
How tell the left from right?
Who was this wise one then?
None but a son of Xu.
In spirit a true man,
In phantom form a woman.
A woman — what of that?
Her rule the inner training.
Without that one, who
Could aid the Empress Dowager?
Three reigns he served,
Ranked in the nine degrees.
He aided change and tuned the source,
And set these great deeds forth.
Vast and boundless his compassionate wind,
Radiance on radiance, the Buddha sun.
The whole land, all under heaven,
Nothing but service to the state.
Every place a bodhimanda,
Everywhere a jewel abode.
He wished but for adornment —
Who divides self and other?
His body dwelt amid the dust of toil,
His mind sought the Pure Land.
He received and kept the Three Refuges,
And practiced the Six Pāramitās.
Writing out, receiving, holding
The Mahāyāna's sutras and verses,
He vowed to cast off this body
And go straight to the Buddha-ground.
Alas, the dreamers lie in the long night, dim;
How great the awakened, who make of death a hymn.
His traces bound to the royal palace,
His heart among the hills and streams —
A staunch joint piercing the clouds,
A tall pine, a solitary crane.
The Yan Master made a man of straw —
Who is the fake, who the true?
The dragon girl who offered up her pearl —
Her story seems divine.
The stūpa marks the Long Wall,
Anchoring the capital's heart.
Above, we pray for voice and blessing —
As long as heaven and earth endure.
